Immediate extraction (Option A) is contraindicated as laterally luxated teeth have an excellent long-term retention rate when properly repositioned, splinting in a displaced position (Option B) perpetuates occlusal interference and periodontal destruction, and immediate pulpectomy (Option C) is inappropriate because pulpal revascularization or survival can occur, especially in developing roots, and endodontic intervention is only initiated if pulpal necrosis is confirmed during follow-up.

anatomy-607772291.question: A 9-year-old male presents with an anterior crossbite involving the permanent maxillary left central incisor (tooth 21). Clinical examination shows tooth 21 occluding lingual to the mandibular left central incisor (tooth 31), creating an anterior functional shift of the mandible upon closure and localized gingival recession on the labial aspect of tooth 31. What is the MOST appropriate initial interceptive management?
options: Deliver a removable anterior inclined bite plane appliance
Extract the primary mandibular canines to relieve crowding
Delay orthodontic treatment until all permanent teeth have erupted
Initiate comprehensive fixed orthodontic appliance therapy with premolar extractions
anatomy-607772291.explanation: Option A is correct because an anterior inclined bite plane (or removable appliance with a finger spring) is the indicated interceptive appliance to tip the displaced maxillary incisor (tooth 21) labially across the bite, eliminating the anterior functional displacement and arresting traumatic occlusion-induced gingival stripping on tooth 31. Extracting primary canines (Option B) fails to correct an isolated dental crossbite, delaying treatment (Option C) allows traumatic occlusion to worsen periodontal attachment loss and bone dehiscence on tooth 31 while perpetuating skeletal adaptation, and comprehensive fixed extraction therapy (Option D) is overly aggressive and premature for a localized single-tooth crossbite in the mixed dentition.

anatomy-603837981.question: A 78-year-old female presents with chronic dry mouth and burning under her maxillary complete denture. Her medical history includes Sjögren syndrome, hypertension, and depression managed with multiple daily medications. Clinical examination reveals atrophic oral mucosa, negligible unassisted salivary flow, and erythema of the palatal mucosa confined to the denture-bearing area, diagnostic of denture stomatitis (erythematous candidiasis). What is the MOST appropriate initial management strategy?
options: Prescribe topical nystatin for the palate and denture base, reinforce denture hygiene, and recommend salivary substitutes
Prescribe systemic fluconazole (100 mg daily for 14 days) and systemic pilocarpine
Advise the patient to discontinue her prescribed antihypertensive and antidepressant medications
Apply a soft tissue conditioner to the existing denture base and prescribe 0.12% chlorhexidine rinses alone
anatomy-603837981.explanation: Option A is correct because Canadian guidelines (CDA, RCDSO) recommend topical antifungal therapy (such as nystatin suspension or cream applied to the tissues and denture fitting surface) combined with meticulous denture disinfection and salivary substitutes as the safest, first-line management for localized denture stomatitis and xerostomia. Systemic fluconazole (Option B) is contraindicated as first-line therapy in an elderly polymedicated patient due to significant risks of cytochrome P450 drug-drug interactions and hepatotoxicity, advising medication cessation (Option C) violates dental scope of practice and endangers systemic cardiovascular and mental health, and placing soft tissue relines (Option D) without antifungal treatment provides a porous matrix that accelerates fungal colonization.

anatomy-405299539.question: When evaluating cross-sectional cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) imaging prior to the surgical extraction of an impacted permanent mandibular third molar (tooth 38 or 48), which of the following is the MOST common anatomical position of the mandibular canal relative to the root apices?
options: Lingual to the root apices
Directly between the roots (interradicular)
Superior and coronal to the root apices
Inferior or buccal to the root apices
anatomy-405299539.explanation: Option D is correct because anatomical and CBCT cross-sectional studies demonstrate that the mandibular canal (inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle) is most commonly situated inferior (50–60%) or buccal (25–40%) to the root apices of tooth 38 or 48. Option A is incorrect because a lingual course is observed in only 10–20% of cases, representing the least common position. Options B and C are incorrect because an interradicular pathway is an uncommon variation, and a superior/coronal position does not represent the normal anatomical path of the inferior alveolar canal.

anatomy-402878255.question: A 22-year-old male presents with severe pain and localized swelling associated with a necrotic permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 36). If an odontogenic periapical infection from this tooth perforates the lingual cortical plate of the mandible, into which anatomical space will it directly spread?
options: Submandibular space, inferior to the mylohyoid muscle
Submental space, between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles
Sublingual space, superior to the mylohyoid muscle
Parapharyngeal space, medial to the superior pharyngeal constrictor
anatomy-402878255.explanation: Option C is correct because the mylohyoid line slopes downward anteriorly, placing the root apices of the permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 36) superior to the mylohyoid muscle attachment; lingual cortical perforation thus directly enters the sublingual space above the mylohyoid muscle. Option A is incorrect because perforation into the submandibular space inferior to the mylohyoid muscle typically arises from mandibular second (tooth 37) or third (tooth 38) molars, whose apices lie below the mylohyoid line. Options B and D are incorrect because the submental space receives direct drainage primarily from mandibular anterior teeth, and the parapharyngeal space is a deep fascial space involved secondarily rather than by primary lingual cortical perforation from tooth 36.

anatomy-903582343.question: Which of the following morphological characteristics is a distinctive anatomical feature of the primary maxillary canine (tooth 53 or 63) when compared to the permanent maxillary canine (tooth 13 or 23)?
options: A blunt, rounded cusp tip at initial eruption
A mesial cusp slope that is shorter than the distal cusp slope
A prominent cervical ridge on the labial aspect with marked cervical constriction
A lingual surface that lacks a cingulum and marginal ridges
anatomy-903582343.explanation: Option C is correct because the primary maxillary canine (tooth 53 or 63) characteristically displays a prominent labial cervical ridge and pronounced cervical constriction, which are defining hallmarks of primary anterior teeth. Option B is incorrect because the primary maxillary canine uniquely features a mesial cusp slope that is longer than the distal cusp slope, which is the reverse of the permanent maxillary canine. Options A and D are incorrect because primary canines erupt with a distinctly sharp, pointed cusp tip rather than a blunt one, and they possess a well-developed cingulum and distinct marginal ridges on the lingual aspect.

anatomy-989930813.question: A clinician is preparing a cavity on a permanent mandibular first premolar (tooth 34 or 44). Which of the following anatomical features is characteristic of this tooth and must be accounted for during operative preparation?
options: A distinct mesiolingual developmental groove separating the mesial marginal ridge from the lingual cusp
A lingual cusp that is equal in height and occlusal function to the buccal cusp
A prominent mesial concavity extending from the crown onto the root trunk
Two distinct lingual cusps separated by a lingual developmental groove
anatomy-989930813.explanation: Option A is correct because the permanent mandibular first premolar (tooth 34 or 44) possesses a unique mesiolingual developmental groove that originates in the mesial pit and crosses onto the mesiolingual surface, separating the mesial marginal ridge from the diminutive lingual cusp. Option B is incorrect because the lingual cusp of tooth 34 or 44 is small, non-functional, and approximately two-thirds the height of the buccal cusp. Options C and D are incorrect because a prominent mesial concavity extending onto the root is the classic feature of the permanent maxillary first premolar (tooth 14 or 24), and two distinct lingual cusps are characteristic of the three-cusp mandibular second premolar (tooth 35 or 45).

anatomy-479266350.question: A 2-week-old male neonate presents with poor feeding and difficulty suckling. Clinical examination reveals hypermobile natal mandibular central incisors (teeth 71 and 81) with Grade III mobility causing sublingual ulceration on the ventral surface of the tongue (Riga-Fede disease). What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Topical application of 5% sodium fluoride varnish
Initiation of systemic broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
Observation and periodic monitoring for spontaneous stabilization
Extraction of the hypermobile natal teeth
anatomy-479266350.explanation: Option D is correct because hypermobile natal teeth (teeth 71 and 81) with Grade III mobility pose an imminent risk of airway aspiration and cause ongoing traumatic sublingual ulceration (Riga-Fede disease) that impairs neonatal nutrition, making prompt extraction the standard of care. Option A is incorrect because topical fluoride varnish does not resolve mechanical trauma or aspiration risk and is contraindicated in neonates. Options B and C are incorrect because Riga-Fede disease is a mechanical trauma rather than an infectious process requiring antibiotics, and hypermobile natal teeth lack root development and will not spontaneously stabilize.

anatomy-503468657.question: Which morphological feature is characteristic of the permanent maxillary first molar (tooth 16 or 26) and reliably distinguishes it from the permanent maxillary second molar (tooth 17 or 27)?
options: Presence of an oblique ridge extending from the distobuccal cusp to the mesiolingual cusp
Presence of a Cusp of Carabelli on the mesiolingual cusp
Presence of three distinct roots with two buccal and one palatal
A rhomboidal occlusal table outline with acute mesiobuccal and distolingual angles
anatomy-503468657.explanation: Option B is correct because the Cusp of Carabelli, located on the lingual surface of the mesiolingual cusp, is a distinctive morphological hallmark of the permanent maxillary first molar (tooth 16 or 26) that is typically absent on the maxillary second molar (tooth 17 or 27). Option A is incorrect because a prominent oblique ridge is a common anatomical feature shared by both maxillary first and second molars. Options C and D are incorrect because both maxillary first and second molars possess three roots (two buccal, one palatal) and a rhomboidal occlusal outline, making neither feature a distinguishing difference between them.

anatomy-96480176.question: A 25-year-old male patient requires endodontic therapy on a permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 36). During access cavity preparation, the clinician searches for root canal orifices in the mesial root. What is the MOST common anatomical root canal configuration in the mesial root of this tooth?
options: Two canals (mesiobuccal and mesiolingual)
One canal (single broad mesial canal)
Three canals (mesiobuccal, middle mesial, and mesiolingual)
Four canals (two mesiobuccal and two mesiolingual)
anatomy-96480176.explanation: Option A is correct because anatomical and endodontic studies demonstrate that the mesial root of the permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 36 or 46) most commonly contains two separate canals—the mesiobuccal and mesiolingual canals—in approximately 85% of cases. Option B is incorrect because a single canal in the mesial root is an infrequent occurrence observed in less than 10% of mandibular first molars. Options C and D are incorrect because a middle mesial canal is an anatomical variation identified in only 1–15% of cases, and four mesial canals is an exceedingly rare anomaly.

anatomy-539788218.question: A 50-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of painful unilateral swelling in the submandibular triangle, just inferior to the lower border of the mandible and anterior to the mandibular angle. The symptoms characteristically worsen during meals. Bimanual palpation reveals a firm, tender mass in the floor of the mouth. If sialolithiasis is diagnosed, which salivary gland is MOST commonly involved, and through which duct does it drain?
options: Submandibular gland, Wharton's duct
Parotid gland, Stensen's duct
Sublingual gland, Bartholin's duct
Sublingual gland, ducts of Rivinus
anatomy-539788218.explanation: Option A is correct because sialolithiasis overwhelmingly occurs in the submandibular gland (80–90% of all salivary stones), which drains via Wharton's duct into the floor of the mouth; its upward tortuous ductal path, higher saliva viscosity, and alkaline pH with high calcium content promote stone formation. Option B is incorrect because the parotid gland (draining via Stensen's duct) accounts for only 10–15% of sialoliths due to serous, watery saliva. Options C and D are incorrect because sialolithiasis is rare in the sublingual gland (under 5%), which drains through the major sublingual duct of Bartholin and smaller minor ducts of Rivinus.

anatomy-138108587.question: A 60-year-old male presents with unilateral facial pressure, nasal obstruction, and dull pain in the right posterior maxilla two weeks following dental implant placement in the edentulous site of the permanent maxillary first molar (tooth 16). Cross-sectional imaging reveals implant fixture penetration beyond the superior cortical floor of the alveolar process. Which anatomical membrane was directly breached during implant osteotomy and fixture insertion?
options: Mucoperiosteum of the nasal cavity floor
Periosteum of the pterygopalatine fossa
Fibrous lining of the incisive canal
Schneiderian membrane of the maxillary sinus
anatomy-138108587.explanation: Option D is correct because the floor of the maxillary sinus lies directly superior to the alveolar ridge of the permanent maxillary first molar (tooth 16); vertical implant over-preparation directly breaches the Schneiderian membrane (the ciliated pseudostratified respiratory mucoperiosteum lining the sinus floor), predisposing to maxillary sinusitis. Option A is incorrect because the nasal floor is located superior to the anterior maxilla (incisor region) rather than the molar region. Options B and C are incorrect because the pterygopalatine fossa is located deep and posterior to the maxillary tuberosity, and the incisive canal is located in the anterior midline of the palate.

anatomy-442057982.question: A 40-year-old male presents with recurrent, painful preauricular and retromandibular facial swelling that intensifies during meals. Clinical examination reveals erythema and purulent exudate expressed from a mucosal papilla located on the buccal mucosa opposite the crown of the permanent maxillary second molar (tooth 27). Which major salivary gland is primarily affected by this suppurative inflammatory process?
options: Parotid gland
Submandibular gland
Sublingual gland
Minor palatine salivary gland
anatomy-442057982.explanation: Option A is correct because the parotid gland lies in the preauricular and retromandibular region and empties via Stensen's duct, whose papilla opens on the buccal mucosa opposite the permanent maxillary second molar (tooth 27); purulent drainage from this orifice confirms acute suppurative parotitis. Option B is incorrect because the submandibular gland is located in the submandibular triangle and empties via Wharton's duct at the sublingual caruncle. Options C and D are incorrect because the sublingual gland drains through the sublingual plica in the anterior floor of the mouth, while minor palatine salivary glands are located in the hard and soft palate.

anatomy-718613616.question: A 55-year-old female presents with localized deep periodontal pocketing on the buccal aspect of a permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 46). Clinical and radiographic examinations demonstrate clinical attachment loss extending into the buccal furcation area. Which developmental anatomical feature of tooth 46 is MOST commonly associated with localized periodontal breakdown and significantly complicates mechanical subgingival debridement?
options: Palatogingival developmental groove extending apically from the cingulum
Pronounced mesial crown concavity extending onto the root trunk
Bifurcated pulp canal configuration within the distal root
Cervical enamel projection extending into the bifurcation
anatomy-718613616.explanation: Option D is correct because cervical enamel projections (CEPs) frequently extend into the buccal bifurcation of permanent mandibular first molars (tooth 46); because connective tissue fibers cannot form an insertion into enamel, only a weak junctional epithelial attachment is present, predisposing the site to rapid pocket formation and obstructing mechanical debridement. Option A is incorrect because palatogingival grooves are developmental anomalies primarily found on permanent maxillary incisors (teeth 12 and 22). Options B and C are incorrect because a mesial crown concavity extending onto the root is a hallmark of the permanent maxillary first premolar (teeth 14 and 24), and internal distal canal anatomy does not induce external periodontal attachment loss or impede root debridement.

anatomy-100787370.question: In an ideal Angle Class I molar relationship, which cusp of the permanent maxillary first molar (tooth 16 or 26) occludes directly within the central fossa of the permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 36 or 46)?
options: Mesiobuccal cusp
Distobuccal cusp
Mesiolingual cusp
Distolingual cusp
anatomy-100787370.explanation: Option C is correct because in ideal Angle Class I occlusion, the mesiolingual cusp of the permanent maxillary first molar (tooth 16 or 26) functions as the primary centric supporting (stamp) cusp and occludes directly into the central fossa of the permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 36 or 46). Option A is incorrect because the mesiobuccal cusp of tooth 16 or 26 aligns with and occludes in the mesiobuccal developmental groove of tooth 36 or 46. Options B and D are incorrect because the distobuccal cusp occludes in the distobuccal embrasure or groove of the mandibular first molar, and the distolingual cusp occludes against the marginal ridges of the mandibular first and second molars.

anatomy-819018699.question: A 68-year-old male presents with a dull, constant ache in the left mandibular quadrant that has worsened over several days. He notes localized tenderness on mastication. Clinical examination reveals extensive occlusal wear facets, and tooth 36 has a large amalgam restoration with secondary recurrent caries. The tooth is exquisitely tender to percussion and buccal sulcular palpation. Thermal pulp testing elicits no response. A periapical radiograph of tooth 36 demonstrates widening of the periodontal ligament space around the mesial root without a periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate periapical diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic apical periodontitis
Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
Chronic apical abscess
Condensing osteitis
anatomy-819018699.explanation: Option A is correct because symptomatic apical periodontitis is defined by exquisite tenderness to percussion and biting with radiographic widening of the periodontal ligament space in a non-vital tooth. Option B and Option C are incorrect because asymptomatic apical periodontitis and chronic apical abscess do not present with acute pain on percussion and characteristically display periapical radiolucencies or a draining sinus tract. Option D is incorrect because condensing osteitis produces a localized radiopaque bony proliferation rather than an acute radiolucent periapical inflammatory response.

anatomy-858638149.question: A 45-year-old female patient presents for a periodontal maintenance appointment. She was previously treated for generalized periodontitis (Stage III, Grade B) and completed active non-surgical periodontal therapy 6 months ago. Clinical examination reveals localized probing depths of 6 mm with bleeding on probing at the mesial aspect of tooth 16 and the distal aspect of tooth 46. All other sites demonstrate probing depths ≤4 mm with no bleeding. Bite-wing and periapical radiographs demonstrate stable alveolar bone levels with no progression of bone loss. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Prescribe a systemic regimen of amoxicillin and metronidazole.
Re-evaluate in 3 months without active subgingival instrumentation.
Perform localized subgingival debridement and consider adjunctive local antimicrobial delivery.
Recommend extraction of tooth 16 and tooth 46 due to refractory disease.
anatomy-858638149.explanation: Option C is correct because isolated 6 mm residual pockets with bleeding on probing during maintenance therapy require site-specific subgingival debridement and may benefit from adjunctive local antimicrobial delivery to re-establish periodontal stability. Option A is incorrect because systemic antibiotics are not indicated for localized residual pockets and risk systemic toxicity and antimicrobial resistance. Option B and Option D are incorrect because failing to debride bleeding pockets allows disease progression, whereas extraction is unwarranted for stable, non-mobile teeth without furcation involvement.

anatomy-703132312.question: A 50-year-old male patient with a history of stable angina pectoris controlled by sublingual nitroglycerin presents for the surgical extraction of tooth 46. His medical history reveals that he is taking clopidogrel 75 mg daily following coronary stent placement 18 months ago. According to Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) and Canadian Dental Association (CDA) guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate management regarding his antiplatelet medication prior to the procedure?
options: Instruct the patient to discontinue clopidogrel 5 to 7 days prior to surgery.
Continue clopidogrel without interruption and manage hemostasis using local measures.
Discontinue clopidogrel 24 hours prior to surgery and bridge with low-molecular-weight heparin.
Discontinue clopidogrel and substitute with acetylsalicylic acid 81 mg daily.
anatomy-703132312.explanation: Option B is correct because Canadian clinical guidelines mandate that single antiplatelet therapy such as clopidogrel be continued without interruption for routine dental surgical extractions, managing hemostasis with local measures like gelatin sponges and sutures. Option A and Option C are incorrect because discontinuing clopidogrel or bridging with heparin significantly increases the risk of life-threatening stent thrombosis and myocardial infarction without clinically meaningful reduction in bleeding risk. Option D is incorrect because altering antiplatelet regimens without medical indication disrupts cardiovascular protection and is unnecessary for dental procedures.

anatomy-796821025.question: Which of the following definitive luting cements provides chemical adhesion to tooth structure and sustained fluoride release, while offering higher tensile strength and lower early solubility than conventional glass ionomer cement?
options: Zinc phosphate cement
Zinc polycarboxylate cement
Self-adhesive resin cement
Resin-modified glass ionomer cement
anatomy-796821025.explanation: Option D is correct because resin-modified glass ionomer cement provides ionic chemical bonding to hydroxyapatite and continuous fluoride release, while its polymerizable resin matrix yields superior tensile strength and reduced early moisture sensitivity compared to conventional glass ionomer. Option A is incorrect because zinc phosphate bonds purely by mechanical interlocking and does not release fluoride. Option B and Option C are incorrect because zinc polycarboxylate has low tensile strength and negligible fluoride release, while self-adhesive resin cements rely on micro-mechanical retention with minimal fluoride exchange.

anatomy-619199346.question: A 42-year-old male patient presents for a periodontal examination. He reports no medical conditions and is a non-smoker with no history of tooth loss. Clinical examination reveals generalized gingival inflammation with bleeding on probing at 45% of sites, probing depths ranging from 4 to 5 mm, and interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm affecting 40% of his dentition. Full-mouth radiographs reveal generalized horizontal bone loss extending 20% to 30% of the root length. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Generalized gingivitis on an intact periodontium
Generalized periodontitis, Stage II, Grade B
Generalized periodontitis, Stage I, Grade A
Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C
anatomy-619199346.explanation: Option B is correct because interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm with 20% to 30% horizontal bone loss (coronal third) without tooth loss defines Stage II, involvement of >30% of teeth defines generalized extent, and a bone loss to age ratio of ~0.6 defines Grade B. Option A is incorrect because plaque-induced gingivitis requires an intact periodontium with no clinical attachment loss or radiographic bone loss. Option C and Option D are incorrect because Stage I is restricted to 1 to 2 mm attachment loss and <15% bone loss, while Stage III requires attachment loss ≥5 mm or bone loss into the middle third of the root.

anatomy-766215546.question: A 28-year-old female patient presents with mild sensitivity to cold and sweets on tooth 26. Clinical examination reveals an occlusal carious lesion with intact marginal ridges and no proximal cavitation. The cold sensitivity resolves immediately upon removal of the stimulus, and the tooth is non-tender to percussion and palpation. Radiographs show a radiolucency extending into the middle third of the dentin, with more than 1 mm of sound dentin remaining over the pulp chamber. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Indirect pulp capping with calcium hydroxide followed by a full-coverage crown.
Direct pulp capping followed by an intermediate restorative material.
Complete caries excavation followed by placement of a direct restoration.
Pulpotomy followed by non-surgical root canal therapy.
anatomy-766215546.explanation: Option C is correct because an occlusal carious lesion in the middle third of dentin with adequate remaining dentin thickness and reversible pulpitis requires complete caries excavation and placement of a direct restoration. Option A is incorrect because indirect pulp capping is reserved for extremely deep lesions approximating the pulp where exposure is imminent, and full-coverage crowns are excessively invasive for intact occlusal lesions. Option B and Option D are incorrect because direct pulp capping is indicated only for mechanical or traumatic pulpal exposures, and pulpotomy is an unnecessary invasive procedure for a vital, reversibly inflamed pulp.

anatomy-669748080.question: According to Canadian dental infection prevention and control (IPAC) guidelines (RCDSO/CDA), what is the standard protocol for handling critical or semi-critical dental items that cannot withstand moist heat or dry heat sterilization?
options: Immerse them in a 2% glutaraldehyde liquid chemical sterilant solution for 10 hours.
Replace them with heat-tolerant reusable alternatives or single-use disposable devices.
Process them through an unsaturated chemical vapor sterilizer cycle at 132°C.
Perform high-level disinfection using hospital-grade intermediate disinfectant surface wipes.
anatomy-669748080.explanation: Option B is correct because Canadian IPAC standards state that critical and semi-critical instruments must be sterilized by heat; if an item is heat-sensitive, it must be replaced with a heat-tolerant alternative or a single-use disposable device. Option A is incorrect because liquid chemical sterilants such as glutaraldehyde cannot be routinely monitored with biological spore tests and are proscribed for critical dental instruments in Canadian practice. Option C and Option D are incorrect because chemical vapor operates at 132°C and damages heat-sensitive items, while surface wipes achieve only intermediate disinfection and cannot sterilize invasive instruments.

anatomy-629371065.question: A 32-year-old female presents for evaluation of an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, firm swelling in the right submandibular triangle that has been present for 4 months. She reports no changes in size during meals. Extraoral examination reveals a well-circumscribed, non-tender, freely mobile 2 cm mass within the right submandibular gland. Intraoral examination reveals healthy mucosa and clear, unobstructed salivary flow from Wharton's duct. An occlusal radiograph shows no radiopaque calcifications. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Submandibular sialolithiasis
Submandibular space cellulitis
Odontogenic submandibular abscess
Pleomorphic adenoma
anatomy-629371065.explanation: Option D is correct because pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign salivary gland neoplasm, characteristically presenting as an asymptomatic, slow-growing, firm, well-circumscribed, and freely mobile mass without mealtime fluctuations. Option A is incorrect because sialolithiasis typically presents with recurrent pain and sudden swelling associated with salivary stimulation during meals, often accompanied by salivary duct obstruction. Option B and Option C are incorrect because cellulitis and odontogenic abscesses are acute, painful, indurated or fluctuant infectious processes accompanied by erythema and systemic signs rather than an indolent mobile mass.

anatomy-950787882.question: A 50-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension controlled by an ACE inhibitor and a myocardial infarction 6 months ago presents for a dental extraction. He reports no known drug allergies. Which of the following analgesic agents should be avoided or used with the MOST caution due to the specific risks of attenuating his antihypertensive therapy and increasing the risk of recurrent cardiovascular events?
options: Acetaminophen
Codeine
Ibuprofen
Tramadol
anatomy-950787882.explanation: Option C is correct because ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits renal prostaglandin synthesis, which blunts the antihypertensive efficacy of ACE inhibitors and significantly increases the risk of recurrent myocardial infarction and heart failure in post-infarction patients. Option A is incorrect because acetaminophen does not inhibit peripheral prostaglandin synthesis and is the recommended first-line analgesic for patients with cardiovascular disease on ACE inhibitors. Option B and Option D are incorrect because opioid analgesics such as codeine and tramadol do not interfere with renal prostaglandin-mediated vascular tone or antihypertensive medications.

anatomy-605248120.question: A 50-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of sensitivity to cold and sweet foods on tooth 26 that has gradually worsened over the past few weeks. Clinical examination reveals a deep amalgam restoration with recurrent caries along the distal margin. Thermal cold testing elicits sharp discomfort that resolves immediately upon removal of the stimulus. Percussion and palpation tests are negative, and there is no pain upon biting release. Radiographs show recurrent caries approaching the pulp chamber with a normal periodontal ligament space. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis and treatment plan?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis; initiate non-surgical root canal therapy.
Reversible pulpitis; excavate recurrent caries, evaluate the pulp, and place a definitive restoration.
Symptomatic apical periodontitis; prescribe systemic antibiotics and perform an extraction.
Cracked tooth syndrome; place an orthodontic band and evaluate for cusp fracture.
anatomy-605248120.explanation: Option B is correct because thermal sensitivity that subsides immediately upon removal of the stimulus in the absence of percussion or palpation pain is diagnostic of reversible pulpitis, which is treated by caries removal and restorative therapy. Option A is incorrect because irreversible pulpitis presents with spontaneous pain or pain that lingers after stimulus removal, necessitating endodontic intervention. Option C and Option D are incorrect because apical periodontitis requires tenderness to percussion or periapical pathology, and cracked tooth syndrome characteristically presents with sharp pain on release of biting pressure rather than thermal sensitivity to recurrent caries.

anatomy-740465369.question: A 35-year-old male patient presents with severe, spontaneous, throbbing pain in tooth 46. The pain is exacerbated by hot foods and lingers for several minutes after removal, whereas cold water provides temporary relief. Clinical examination shows tooth 46 is tender to percussion, but palpation of the buccal vestibule is non-tender with no swelling. Radiographs demonstrate a deep mesio-occlusal restoration approaching the pulp horn with slight widening of the apical periodontal ligament space and no periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate diagnosis and immediate treatment?
options: Reversible pulpitis; remove the existing restoration and place a zinc oxide-eugenol sedative dressing.
Pulp necrosis with acute apical abscess; prescribe systemic antibiotics and perform incision and drainage.
Cracked tooth syndrome; recommend a full-coverage crown without endodontic therapy.
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis; initiate non-surgical root canal therapy.
anatomy-740465369.explanation: Option D is correct because lingering thermal pain exacerbated by heat and relieved by cold indicates symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, while percussion tenderness with apical PDL widening without a radiolucency reflects early apical inflammation requiring root canal therapy. Option A is incorrect because reversible pulpitis involves only non-lingering provoked discomfort without spontaneous pain or percussion tenderness. Option B and Option C are incorrect because an acute apical abscess presents with localized fluctuant swelling and complete loss of pulpal vitality, whereas crowning without endodontics will not resolve irreversible pulpal inflammation.

anatomy-591944876.question: A 9-year-old male patient presents to your office 2 days after falling off his bicycle and sustaining trauma to his anterior teeth. Clinically, tooth 11 exhibits dark grey coronal discoloration and slight tenderness to percussion, with no abnormal mobility or crown fracture. Thermal pulp testing elicits no response. Periapical radiography shows a closed apex, an intact lamina dura, and no evidence of root or alveolar fracture. According to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Monitor the tooth clinically and radiographically at regular recall intervals.
Initiate immediate non-surgical root canal therapy.
Perform immediate coronal pulpotomy with calcium silicate cement.
Extract tooth 11 and fabricate a removable interim prosthesis.
anatomy-591944876.explanation: Option A is correct because International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines recommend monitoring traumatized teeth with transient coronal discoloration and negative initial sensibility testing, as post-traumatic neuropraxia and transient intrapulpal hemorrhage frequently resolve without pulp necrosis. Option B is incorrect because initiating root canal therapy immediately after trauma without confirming definitive, persistent pulp necrosis or periapical pathology represents overtreatment. Option C and Option D are incorrect because pulpotomy is indicated only for exposed vital pulps in crown fractures, and extraction is excessively destructive for an intact tooth with concussion or mild subluxation.

anatomy-104843945.question: A 42-year-old female presents with a fractured cusp on her maxillary right second premolar (tooth 15) extending subgingivally, resulting in thermal sensitivity. The remaining tooth structure is sound, and there is no pulpal involvement. She desires a strong and esthetic restoration. What is the MOST appropriate definitive restoration for this tooth?
options: Direct composite resin restoration
Glass ionomer cement restoration
Direct amalgam restoration
Indirect ceramic onlay
anatomy-104843945.explanation: Option D is correct because an indirect ceramic onlay provides the necessary cuspal coverage and structural protection to withstand occlusal forces, while ensuring precise subgingival marginal adaptation and excellent esthetics. Direct composite resin (Option A) and direct amalgam (Option C) do not provide adequate cuspal reinforcement for a fractured premolar under masticatory load, and glass ionomer cement (Option B) lacks sufficient mechanical strength for definitive posterior cuspal restoration.

anatomy-221868613.question: An 82-year-old female presents with difficulty chewing and a loose lower complete denture. She has worn complete dentures for 30 years and takes oral alendronate for osteoporosis, with no other significant medical history. Clinical examination reveals severe residual ridge resorption in the mandible. The existing mandibular complete denture is unstable and non-retentive, while the maxillary denture is stable. Her oral mucosa is healthy. What is the MOST appropriate treatment to improve the stability and retention of her mandibular denture?
options: Reline the existing mandibular complete denture
Fabricate a new conventional mandibular complete denture
Fabricate a new mandibular overdenture supported by two implants
Prescribe a denture adhesive for daily use
anatomy-221868613.explanation: Option C is correct because the Canadian McGill Consensus designates a two-implant supported overdenture as the first-choice standard of care for restoring retention and stability in an edentulous patient with a severely resorbed mandible, and oral alendronate for osteoporosis is not a contraindication to routine implant therapy. Relining (Option A), fabricating a new conventional denture (Option B), and using denture adhesive (Option D) cannot overcome the anatomical absence of bone height and will not provide satisfactory stability or masticatory efficiency.

anatomy-840256642.question: A 20-year-old male presents with severe pain, facial swelling, and trismus associated with his erupting mandibular right third molar (tooth 48). Clinical examination reveals an inflamed operculum partially covering tooth 48 with purulent exudate upon gentle palpation. His body temperature is 38.5°C. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate surgical extraction of tooth 48
Local debridement with irrigation and prescription of systemic amoxicillin
Surgical operculectomy under local anesthesia
Warm saline rinses and analgesics alone without antibiotic therapy
anatomy-840256642.explanation: Option B is correct because acute pericoronitis accompanied by systemic manifestations (fever of 38.5°C and trismus) warrants gentle local debridement, saline irrigation, and systemic antimicrobial therapy with amoxicillin per Canadian antibiotic stewardship guidelines. Immediate surgical extraction (Option A) and operculectomy (Option C) are contraindicated during acute fascial-space threatening infections due to surgical trauma and risk of spreading infection, whereas conservative rinsing without antibiotics (Option D) is inadequate when systemic signs and trismus are present.

anatomy-100102834.question: A 65-year-old female presents for a dental extraction. Her medical history reveals stable angina pectoris managed with sublingual nitroglycerin. During the procedure, she suddenly experiences substernal chest tightness radiating to her left arm. What is the MOST appropriate immediate step in managing this patient?
options: Administer 325 mg chewable aspirin
Administer sublingual nitroglycerin and position the patient comfortably
Activate emergency medical services (EMS) immediately
Place the patient in a supine position
anatomy-100102834.explanation: Option B is correct because the immediate clinical management protocol for a patient with known stable angina experiencing intraoperative chest pain is to terminate the procedure, position the patient comfortably (upright or semi-reclined), and administer sublingual nitroglycerin. Activating EMS (Option C) and administering aspirin (Option A) are indicated if the pain fails to resolve after three doses of nitroglycerin or if myocardial infarction is suspected, while placing the patient supine (Option D) is contraindicated because increased venous return raises myocardial preload and exacerbates angina.

anatomy-147644049.question: A 35-year-old female presents with a persistent dull ache and masticatory tenderness in her mandibular left first molar (tooth 36). She reports having a deep restoration placed on this tooth six months ago. Clinical examination reveals marked pain to percussion, no mobility, and no response to thermal pulp vitality testing. A periapical radiograph shows a widened periodontal ligament space around the mesial root without a discrete radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate periapical diagnosis?
options: Normal apical tissues
Acute apical periodontitis
Chronic apical periodontitis
Chronic apical abscess
anatomy-147644049.explanation: Option B is correct because pain to percussion and mastication associated with a non-vital tooth and a radiographically widened periodontal ligament space defines acute (symptomatic) apical periodontitis. Chronic apical periodontitis (Option C) is by definition asymptomatic with a well-defined periapical radiolucency, chronic apical abscess (Option D) presents with a draining sinus tract, and normal apical tissues (Option A) would not exhibit tenderness to percussion or radiographic alterations.

anatomy-591006779.question: A 40-year-old female presents with severe, unilateral, sharp, electric shock-like pain localized to the area of her maxillary right second premolar (tooth 15). The paroxysmal pain lasts only a few seconds and is triggered by light touch to her upper lip. Clinical and radiographic examinations reveal no caries or periapical pathology, and all teeth in the quadrant respond normally to pulp vitality testing. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Trigeminal neuralgia
Cracked tooth syndrome
Atypical odontalgia
anatomy-591006779.explanation: Option B is correct because severe, paroxysmal, lancinating electric-like pain triggered by innocuous non-noxious tactile stimuli within a trigger zone in the presence of completely normal dental and pulpal findings is classic trigeminal neuralgia. Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (Option A) causes continuous or lingering pain to thermal stimuli, cracked tooth syndrome (Option C) typically elicits pain upon release of biting pressure on a specific cusp, and atypical odontalgia (Option D) presents as a persistent, non-paroxysmal, dull burning or aching sensation.

anatomy-154407522.question: Which of the following nerves is MOST commonly associated with transient or persistent paresthesia following a standard inferior alveolar nerve block injection?
options: Lingual nerve
Inferior alveolar nerve
Mental nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
anatomy-154407522.explanation: Option A is correct because the lingual nerve accounts for approximately 70% of reported local anesthetic-related paresthesia cases following an inferior alveolar nerve block due to its unifascicular structure and superficial location in the pterygomandibular space. The inferior alveolar nerve (Option B) accounts for the remaining minority (approximately 30%) of cases, while the mental nerve (Option C) and mylohyoid nerve (Option D) are rarely implicated in standard pterygomandibular block complications.

anatomy-622955696.question: A 48-year-old male presents for a post-operative evaluation 10 days following a difficult extraction of his mandibular left first molar (tooth 36). He reports localized dull discomfort and food packing in the area. Clinical examination reveals incomplete soft-tissue closure over the socket. A periapical radiograph reveals a well-defined 4 mm radiopaque structure in the apical portion of the mesial socket displaying a visible root canal space and an intact periodontal ligament outline. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Retained root fragment
Alveolar osteitis
Acute osteomyelitis
Idiopathic osteosclerosis
anatomy-622955696.explanation: Option A is correct because the radiographic demonstration of a distinct radiopaque structure exhibiting root morphology, an internal root canal lumen, and a surrounding periodontal ligament space confirms a retained root fragment. Alveolar osteitis (Option B) presents within 2-4 days post-extraction with severe radiating pain and an empty socket without an organized root radiopacity, acute osteomyelitis (Option C) shows diffuse moth-eaten osteolytic changes with systemic features, and idiopathic osteosclerosis (Option D) lacks an organized root form and periodontal ligament space.

anatomy-846871740.question: A 58-year-old male presents with a fractured maxillary left first premolar (tooth 24) that had a large multi-surface amalgam restoration. Clinical examination reveals that the entire palatal cusp has fractured off subgingivally, but an adequate 2 mm ferrule can be established coronally. The tooth is asymptomatic and vital. Radiographic examination shows sound bone support and no periapical pathology. What is the MOST appropriate definitive restoration for this tooth?
options: Direct composite resin restoration
Complex pin-retained amalgam restoration
Porcelain laminate veneer
Full-coverage crown
anatomy-846871740.explanation: Option D is correct because a maxillary premolar with extensive structural loss and a fractured functional cusp requires a full-coverage crown to provide complete cuspal protection, establish a circumferential 2 mm ferrule, and resist lateral masticatory forces. Direct composite resin (Option A) and complex pin-retained amalgam (Option B) do not provide the necessary structural reinforcement and carry a high risk of catastrophic tooth fracture, while a porcelain laminate veneer (Option C) is contraindicated on a tooth with extensive posterior occlusal breakdown.

anatomy-169398599.question: A 40-year-old male presents for a periodontal re-evaluation 6 months following non-surgical periodontal therapy (scaling and root planing) for generalized periodontitis. Clinical examination reveals excellent patient oral hygiene, but a localized residual probing depth of 6 mm with bleeding on probing persists on the mesial aspect of his maxillary right first molar (tooth 16). There is no tooth mobility. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Maintain on a 3-month supportive recall without intervention
Prescribe systemic broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
Perform localized surgical periodontal therapy
Prescribe a 0.12% chlorhexidine mouthrinse for 2 weeks
anatomy-169398599.explanation: Option C is correct because a localized residual pocket depth of 6 mm with persistent bleeding on probing after thorough non-surgical therapy in a patient with good plaque control indicates the need for localized surgical periodontal access for definitive root debridement and pocket reduction. Continued supportive recall alone (Option A) and chlorhexidine rinses (Option D) fail to reach deep subgingival areas (>5 mm) to halt disease progression, and systemic antibiotics (Option B) are contraindicated as monotherapy for localized residual pockets under Canadian antimicrobial stewardship.

anatomy-3755764.question: A 35-year-old male presents with severe, spontaneous, throbbing pain in his maxillary left first molar (tooth 26). The pain is exacerbated by thermal stimuli and lingers for several minutes. Radiographic examination reveals a deep carious lesion approximating the pulp chamber with no periapical radiolucency. The tooth is also sensitive to percussion. What is the MOST appropriate pulpal diagnosis?
options: Pulp necrosis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Normal pulp
anatomy-3755764.explanation: Option B is correct because spontaneous, throbbing pain that lingers prolonged after thermal stimulation in the presence of deep caries indicates that the dental pulp is severely inflamed and incapable of healing (symptomatic irreversible pulpitis). Pulp necrosis (Option A) would be unresponsive to thermal vitality testing, reversible pulpitis (Option C) produces transient sharp pain that subsides immediately upon stimulus removal, and normal pulp (Option D) displays only mild, non-lingering thermal sensations.

anatomy-65156530.question: A 50-year-old female presents for a routine dental recall examination. She reports no pain but notices occasional gingival bleeding when brushing. Clinical examination reveals generalized gingival erythema and edema, with probing depths of 4 to 5 mm and bleeding on probing at greater than 30% of sites. Radiographic examination reveals generalized horizontal bone loss confined to the coronal third of the roots (approximately 20% bone loss) with no tooth loss. According to the 2018 AAP/EFP Classification, what is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Generalized periodontitis, Stage II
Generalized gingivitis
Generalized periodontitis, Stage IV
Necrotizing periodontitis
anatomy-65156530.explanation: Option A is correct because the 2018 AAP/EFP classification defines Stage II Periodontitis by probing depths up to 5 mm, horizontal bone loss limited to the coronal third (15% to 33%), and no tooth loss from periodontitis, with a generalized distribution affecting >= 30% of teeth. Generalized gingivitis (Option B) requires bleeding on probing >= 10% without clinical attachment loss or radiographic bone loss, Stage IV Periodontitis (Option C) involves bone loss extending to the apical third with tooth loss >= 5 teeth, and necrotizing periodontitis (Option D) manifests as painful necrotic ulcerated interdental papillae.

anatomy-611141795.question: A 45-year-old male with well-controlled hypertension is scheduled for the routine extraction of a non-restorable mandibular left second molar (tooth 37). His medical history is significant for a coronary stent placed 18 months ago, for which he takes clopidogrel daily. According to Canadian Dental Association and Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate management regarding his clopidogrel therapy prior to the extraction?
options: Discontinue clopidogrel 7 days prior to the extraction
Consult the patient's cardiologist to temporarily stop the medication
Continue clopidogrel without interruption and manage hemostasis with local measures
Hold clopidogrel and bridge with therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin
anatomy-611141795.explanation: Option C is correct because Canadian Dental Association and Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines state that antiplatelet monotherapy (such as clopidogrel) should not be discontinued for minor oral surgery; the risk of fatal coronary stent thrombosis far outweighs the risk of localized oral hemorrhage that is readily managed with local hemostatic agents. Discontinuing clopidogrel (Options A and B) places the patient at grave risk for acute stent thrombosis, myocardial infarction, and death. Bridging with low-molecular-weight heparin (Option D) is reserved for select patients on vitamin K antagonists (such as warfarin) and is completely contraindicated for antiplatelet regimens.

anatomy-916954952.question: A 40-year-old male presents to the dental emergency clinic with progressive trismus, severe dysphagia, and difficulty breathing 5 days after the extraction of a mandibular right third molar (tooth 48). Clinical examination reveals a toxic appearance, pyrexia of 38.8°C, marked bilateral woody induration across the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, and superior elevation of the tongue. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Ludwig angina
Submandibular space abscess
Parapharyngeal space infection
Acute alveolar osteitis
anatomy-916954952.explanation: Option A is correct because Ludwig angina is classically defined in Canadian and international literature as a rapidly spreading, bilateral cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental fascial spaces that causes elevation of the floor of the mouth and tongue with impending airway compromise. Isolated submandibular or parapharyngeal space infections (Options B and C) present with unilateral swelling rather than simultaneous bilateral involvement of all three spaces. Alveolar osteitis (Option D) is a localized post-extraction complication characterized by socket pain without facial cellulitis, dysphagia, or systemic pyrexia.

anatomy-264018843.question: A 30-year-old male presents with generalized gingival bleeding and halitosis. Clinical examination reveals generalized gingival inflammation, probing depths of 4 to 5 mm, and interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm affecting 45% of teeth. Radiographs demonstrate generalized horizontal bone loss in the coronal third of the root (20% to 25%), with no missing teeth. His medical history is non-contributory, and he is a non-smoker. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification system, what is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Generalized periodontitis, Stage I, Grade A
Generalized periodontitis, Stage II, Grade B
Generalized periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C
Biofilm-induced generalized gingivitis on an intact periodontium
anatomy-264018843.explanation: Option B is correct because under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm, radiographic bone loss confined to the coronal third (15% to 33%), and probing depths up to 5 mm without tooth loss define Stage II periodontitis, while involvement of more than 30% of teeth and a bone loss-to-age ratio of 0.83 (25% / 30 years) establish generalized Grade B disease. Stage I (Option A) is characterized by clinical attachment loss of only 1 to 2 mm and bone loss under 15%. Stage III (Option C) requires clinical attachment loss of 5 mm or greater with bone loss extending into the middle third of the root, whereas gingivitis (Option D) cannot be diagnosed when interdental attachment loss and radiographic bone loss are present.

anatomy-493761159.question: A clinician selects an addition silicone (polyvinyl siloxane) impression material for the fabrication of a multi-unit fixed partial denture. Which characteristic of polyvinyl siloxane is primarily responsible for its superior dimensional stability over time compared to condensation silicones and polysulfides?
options: High inherent tear energy at thin gingival margins
Addition polymerization reaction that produces no volatile byproducts
Complete absence of polymerization shrinkage during setting
High natural surface energy and wettability in the presence of saliva
anatomy-493761159.explanation: Option B is correct because addition silicones (polyvinyl siloxanes) undergo an addition reaction without the formation of volatile byproducts (unlike condensation silicones which release ethanol and polysulfides which release water), resulting in negligible dimensional change over time and allowing delayed or multiple pouring of accurate casts. While high tear strength (Option A) prevents marginal tearing upon retrieval, it does not govern long-term dimensional stability. Polyvinyl siloxanes still undergo minimal polymerization shrinkage, making complete absence of shrinkage factually incorrect (Option C), and unmodified polyvinyl siloxanes are inherently hydrophobic rather than wettable (Option D).

anatomy-269128719.question: A 68-year-old male presents with a chief complaint of a loose lower anterior tooth. Medical history reveals well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Clinical examination reveals Class III mobility, probing depths of 8 to 10 mm, and suppuration associated with the mandibular left central incisor (tooth 31). Periapical radiographs demonstrate severe alveolar bone loss extending to the root apex, and the tooth is diagnosed with a hopeless periodontal prognosis. What is the MOST appropriate management for tooth 31?
options: Extraction of tooth 31
Periodontal debridement and composite-wire splinting
Endodontic therapy followed by root amputation
Immediate implant placement and provisionalization
anatomy-269128719.explanation: Option A is correct because a tooth with a hopeless periodontal prognosis—characterized by Class III mobility, pocket depths of 8 to 10 mm, and alveolar bone loss extending to the apex—cannot be maintained and must be extracted to eliminate chronic infection and preserve the bone of adjacent teeth. Periodontal debridement and splinting (Option B) cannot halt progressive attachment loss in a periodontally hopeless tooth. Endodontic therapy (Option C) does not treat primary attachment loss, and immediate implant placement (Option D) is contraindicated in the presence of active purulent infection and extensive alveolar destruction.

anatomy-263960741.question: A 9-year-old male presents to the dental office 2 hours after sustaining trauma to his anterior teeth during a sports activity. Clinical examination reveals a crown fracture involving enamel and dentin on the maxillary right central incisor (tooth 11), with no pulp exposure. The tooth is non-displaced, demonstrates physiologic mobility, and responds positively to cold testing. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management for tooth 11?
options: Perform a full pulpectomy and place a calcium hydroxide dressing
Perform a partial pulpotomy (Cvek technique) and restore with composite resin
Seal the exposed dentin and restore the tooth with composite resin
Extract the tooth and deliver a space maintainer
anatomy-263960741.explanation: Option C is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an uncomplicated crown fracture involving enamel and dentin without pulp exposure requires immediate dentin sealing with a bonding agent or glass ionomer liner followed by composite resin restoration (or reattachment of the tooth fragment) to protect the vital pulp. Pulpectomy (Option A) is contraindicated in an immature permanent tooth with a vital, unexposed pulp as it halts root development. Partial pulpotomy (Option B) is indicated only when there is traumatic pulp exposure, and extraction (Option D) is contraindicated for a restorable, vital traumatized incisor.

anatomy-708794648.question: A 30-year-old female presents for a routine dental examination. She reports no pain but is concerned about a receding gumline on an upper anterior tooth. Clinical examination reveals 3 mm of localized facial gingival recession on the maxillary right central incisor (tooth 11), with a probing depth of 1 to 2 mm, absence of bleeding on probing, and no interdental clinical attachment loss. The adjacent periodontal tissues are healthy. What is the MOST likely primary etiology for this localized recession?
options: Biofilm-induced chronic periodontitis
Necrotizing periodontal disease
Traumatic mechanical toothbrushing
Primary occlusal traumatism
anatomy-708794648.explanation: Option C is correct because isolated facial gingival recession presenting with a shallow sulcus (1 to 2 mm), absence of bleeding on probing, and intact interdental papillae in an otherwise healthy mouth is characteristically caused by mechanical toothbrushing abrasion and hard-bristle trauma. Biofilm-induced periodontitis (Option A) produces interproximal attachment loss, elevated probing depths, and bleeding on probing. Necrotizing periodontal disease (Option B) presents with painful, punched-out interdental ulcerations, while occlusal traumatism (Option D) results in tooth mobility and widened periodontal ligament space rather than isolated facial soft-tissue recession.

anatomy-772683487.question: Which anatomical structure forms the lateral boundary of the oropharyngeal isthmus (isthmus of fauces), separating the oral cavity proper from the oropharynx?
options: Hard palate
Soft palate
Palatoglossal arch
Palatopharyngeal arch
anatomy-772683487.explanation: Option C is correct because the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of the fauces), formed by the palatoglossus muscle and overlying mucous membrane, establishes the anterior and lateral anatomical boundary of the oropharyngeal isthmus that demarcates the oral cavity proper from the oropharynx. The hard palate (Option A) forms the osseous roof of the oral cavity proper, while the soft palate (Option B) forms the superior border rather than the lateral boundary of the isthmus. The palatopharyngeal arch (Option D) constitutes the posterior pillar of the fauces and lies entirely within the oropharynx, posterior to the palatine tonsillar fossa.

anatomy-633419787.question: An 8-year-old male presents to the dental clinic 30 minutes after sustaining facial trauma from a fall. Clinical examination reveals that the permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth 11) is extruded by 3 mm and displays moderate mobility. Periapical radiographs confirm partial displacement of the root out of the socket with an open apex and no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for tooth 11?
options: Extract the extruded incisor and deliver an interim removable space maintainer
Gently reposition the tooth into the socket and stabilize with a flexible splint for 2 weeks
Observe the tooth for spontaneous repositioning without active intervention
Perform an immediate pulpectomy and apply a rigid wire splint for 6 weeks
anatomy-633419787.explanation: Option B is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an extruded permanent tooth should be gently repositioned into the socket under local anesthesia and stabilized with a flexible splint for 2 weeks to promote periodontal ligament reattachment and allow pulp healing, which is especially favorable in an immature tooth. Extraction (Option A) is overly aggressive for an extruded tooth with intact alveolar walls. Observation alone (Option C) leads to fibrous healing in an extruded, non-functional position, while immediate pulpectomy and rigid splinting (Option D) eliminate potential for pulpal revascularization and increase the risk of ankylosis.

anatomy-245943948.question: A 12-year-old male presents to the dental clinic 45 minutes after traumatic avulsion of the permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth 11). The tooth has a closed apex, has been stored dry in a paper towel, and has minor debris on the root surface. Medical history is non-contributory. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management for tooth 11?
options: Scrape the root surface to remove non-viable tissue and soak in 5% sodium fluoride
Gently rinse the root with sterile saline to remove debris and replant the tooth immediately
Perform extra-oral root canal therapy and curette the socket prior to replantation
Place the tooth in Hanks balanced salt solution and delay replantation for 24 hours
anatomy-245943948.explanation: Option B is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an avulsed permanent tooth with an extra-oral dry time under 60 minutes retains viable periodontal ligament cells; the root should be gently rinsed with sterile saline to remove contaminants and replanted immediately, followed by flexible splinting for 2 weeks. Scraping the root and applying fluoride (Option A) is indicated only when extra-oral dry time exceeds 60 minutes and total PDL cell death has occurred. Extra-oral endodontics and socket curettage (Option C) prolong extra-oral dry time and destroy surviving PDL cells, and delayed replantation (Option D) eliminates any chance of periodontal reattachment.

anatomy-722985127.question: A 42-year-old female requires an indirect restoration for a large MOD defect on the maxillary left first molar (tooth 26). She has a clinical history of heavy nocturnal clenching (bruxism) and has fractured two all-ceramic crowns in the past. Following preparation, there is adequate retention and resistance form, and the patient prioritizes functional durability over aesthetics. What is the MOST appropriate material choice for the onlay?
options: Conventional feldspathic porcelain
Direct microhybrid composite resin
Cast Type III gold alloy
Lithium disilicate glass-ceramic
anatomy-722985127.explanation: Option C is correct because cast Type III gold alloy is the gold standard material for posterior onlays in patients with heavy bruxism and a history of ceramic fractures due to its high ductility, fatigue resistance, and wear characteristics that closely match natural enamel without abrading opposing teeth. Ceramic restorations like feldspathic porcelain (Option A) and lithium disilicate (Option D) have low fracture toughness and carry an unacceptably high failure rate under heavy parafunctional occlusal stress. Direct composite resin (Option B) exhibits inadequate wear resistance and lower long-term mechanical survival in wide, load-bearing MOD preparations.

anatomy-293441255.question: A 65-year-old male with a 40-year history of heavy cigarette smoking presents with generalized severe periodontitis. His medical history is significant for rheumatoid arthritis, which is managed with low-dose methotrexate. Beyond the established effects of chronic tobacco smoking, which underlying systemic factor is the MOST likely contributor to the aggressive progression of his periodontal breakdown?
options: Chronic systemic inflammation associated with rheumatoid arthritis
Cytotoxic immunosuppression caused by low-dose methotrexate therapy
Physiologic tissue senescence associated with advanced chronological age
Drug-induced salivary gland hypofunction resulting in reduced salivary flow
anatomy-293441255.explanation: Option A is correct because rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by systemic dysregulation of pro-inflammatory mediators (including TNF-alpha, IL-1, and RANKL) that cross-react with periodontal tissues and significantly accelerate osteoclastic alveolar bone resorption. Low-dose methotrexate (Option B) is an anti-inflammatory disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) that suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines and does not accelerate periodontal tissue destruction. Advancing age (Option C) represents cumulative lifetime disease exposure rather than an aggressive etiologic driver, and salivary hypofunction (Option D) influences caries risk rather than primary alveolar bone loss.

anatomy-142530027.question: A 25-year-old male patient presents with a chief complaint of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling in the anterior mandible for the past 6 months. He denies any trauma or previous dental infections. Radiographic examination reveals a well-circumscribed, unilocular radiolucency attached at the cementoenamel junction of the crown of an impacted tooth 33. The adjacent teeth are vital to pulp testing. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Radicular cyst
Odontogenic keratocyst
Ameloblastoma
Dentigerous cyst
anatomy-142530027.explanation: Option D is correct because a well-circumscribed, unilocular radiolucency attached at the cementoenamel junction of an impacted tooth crown (tooth 33) is the classic radiographic presentation of a dentigerous (follicular) cyst. Radicular cysts (Option A) arise from non-vital teeth secondary to pulpal necrosis, while odontogenic keratocysts (Option B) and ameloblastomas (Option C) typically present as aggressive lesions that extend along the internal aspect of the bone without attaching strictly to the cementoenamel junction.

anatomy-994438685.question: A 55-year-old female patient presents with a chronically ill-fitting maxillary complete denture that is 10 years old and has never been relined. Clinical examination reveals moderately resorbed maxillary alveolar ridges, severe occlusal wear of the denture teeth, and loss of vertical dimension of occlusion, resulting in poor retention and stability. The oral mucosa is healthy with no signs of candidiasis. What is the MOST appropriate treatment option?
options: Fabrication of a new conventional complete denture
Chairside hard reline of the existing complete denture
Placement of two implants in the anterior maxilla to support an overdenture
Pre-prosthetic surgical ridge augmentation followed by a conventional denture
anatomy-994438685.explanation: Option A is correct because fabricating a new conventional complete denture is the definitive treatment to restore proper vertical dimension of occlusion, correct occlusal disharmony from worn teeth, and optimize peripheral seal and retention. Chairside relining (Option B) is contraindicated for a 10-year-old prosthesis with worn teeth and lost vertical dimension, placing only two implants in the maxilla (Option C) is strictly contraindicated in Canadian implant prosthodontics due to high failure rates requiring a minimum of four implants, and invasive surgical ridge augmentation (Option D) is not indicated before conventional prosthetic fabrication.

anatomy-856736604.question: A 40-year-old male patient presents three days after an uncomplicated extraction of tooth 38 with severe, throbbing pain radiating to his ear that is unresponsive to over-the-counter analgesics. Clinical examination reveals an empty socket with exposed bone, absence of a blood clot, and a foul odor, without fever, swelling, or purulent exudate. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Prescribe a 7-day course of systemic amoxicillin and analgesics
Gently irrigate the socket with sterile saline, débride debris, and place an analgesic medicated dressing
Curette the socket walls vigorously to induce bleeding and re-suture
Perform surgical re-exploration of the socket for retained root fragments
anatomy-856736604.explanation: Option B is correct because the clinical presentation indicates alveolar osteitis (dry socket), which is managed non-surgically by gently irrigating the socket with sterile saline to clear debris followed by the placement of an analgesic medicated dressing (such as an eugenol-based paste) for prompt symptomatic relief. Systemic antibiotics (Option A) are not indicated as alveolar osteitis is a localized fibrinolytic process rather than a bacterial infection, aggressive curettage (Option C) traumatizes exposed alveolar bone and worsens pain, and surgical re-exploration (Option D) is unwarranted without radiographic evidence of retained roots.

anatomy-773479627.question: A 9-year-old female patient presents with her parents concerned about an anterior crossbite. Clinical examination reveals an early mixed dentition with a Class I molar relationship, an anterior crossbite involving tooth 21, and adequate arch perimeter for tooth movement. What is the MOST appropriate initial interceptive orthodontic management?
options: Comprehensive full fixed orthodontic appliance therapy across both arches
Observation until the permanent dentition has completely erupted
Fabrication of a removable appliance with a finger spring to tip tooth 21 labially
Referral for orthognathic surgical correction of the crossbite
anatomy-773479627.explanation: Option C is correct because localized single-tooth anterior dental crossbites in mixed dentition should be treated interceptively with a removable appliance incorporating a finger spring (or Z-spring) to tip tooth 21 labially and prevent incisal wear or gingival recession. Comprehensive fixed appliances (Option A) are premature and unnecessarily complex in early mixed dentition, waiting until all permanent teeth erupt (Option B) allows traumatic occlusion and periodontal compromise to progress, and orthognathic surgery (Option D) is reserved for severe skeletal discrepancies after skeletal maturity.

anatomy-500683693.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of sharp, spontaneous pain in her maxillary right posterior region that lingers for several minutes after cold and hot stimuli, often awakening her at night. Clinical examination reveals extensive occlusal caries on tooth 16. Cold testing elicits severe, lingering pain lasting over 45 seconds, and the tooth is mildly tender to percussion. Radiographs confirm deep caries approximating the pulp chamber with a normal periapical ligament space. What is the MOST appropriate pulpal diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Normal pulp
anatomy-500683693.explanation: Option A is correct because spontaneous, nocturnal pain and an exaggerated thermal response that lingers for over 30 seconds are classic clinical indicators of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis requiring endodontic intervention or extraction. Reversible pulpitis (Option B) produces only transient discomfort that subsides immediately upon removal of the stimulus, necrotic pulp (Option C) fails to respond to cold or electrical sensibility tests, and normal pulp (Option D) responds normally without lingering symptoms or spontaneous pain.

anatomy-209920371.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with his parents concerned about a large cavity in his lower right back tooth. He reports transient cold sensitivity when eating, but denies spontaneous or nocturnal pain. Clinical examination reveals extensive occlusal caries on tooth 84 with significant loss of tooth structure. Periapical radiography shows deep carious demineralization approaching the pulp with no evidence of furcation or periapical radiolucency. Pulp testing confirms vitality. What is the MOST appropriate definitive restorative management?
options: Direct multi-surface composite resin restoration
Coronal pulpotomy followed by a stainless-steel crown
Indirect pulp therapy followed by a stainless-steel crown
Extraction of tooth 84 and placement of a band-and-loop space maintainer
anatomy-209920371.explanation: Option C is correct because Canadian Academy of Pediatric Dentistry and AAPD guidelines recommend indirect pulp therapy (IPT) followed by a preformed stainless-steel crown (SSC) as the treatment of choice for deep caries approaching the pulp in vital primary teeth with reversible pulpitis, yielding superior long-term pulpal survival. Coronal pulpotomy (Option B) is invasive overtreatment when the pulp is unexposed and vital, direct composite restorations (Option A) demonstrate high clinical failure rates in multisurface primary molar lesions, and extraction (Option D) is premature for a readily restorable tooth.

pharmacology-1.question: A 68-year-old male patient with a history of atrial fibrillation is currently taking warfarin with a stable therapeutic INR of 2.4. He presents for an uncomplicated extraction of tooth 46 and requires post-operative pain management. Which of the following analgesics is the MOST appropriate to prescribe for this patient?
options: Meloxicam 7.5 mg orally once daily
Acetaminophen 500 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed
Ibuprofen 400 mg orally every 6 hours as needed
Aspirin 325 mg orally every 4 hours as needed
pharmacology-1.explanation: Option B is correct because acetaminophen (up to 2-3 g/day for short durations) is the analgesic of choice in patients receiving warfarin, as it does not inhibit platelet aggregation or irritate gastric mucosa. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs including meloxicam (Option A) and ibuprofen (Option C), as well as aspirin (Option D), inhibit platelet cyclooxygenase and significantly increase the risk of severe gastrointestinal and postoperative bleeding.

pharmacology-2.question: A 45-year-old female patient with a prosthetic mechanical aortic valve requires antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis prior to a dental extraction. She reports a history of a mild, non-pruritic maculopapular rash when taking ampicillin ten years ago, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria. According to current Canadian Dental Association and AHA guidelines, which of the following is the MOST appropriate antibiotic regimen?
options: Metronidazole 500 mg orally, 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
Amoxicillin 2 g orally, 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
Clindamycin 600 mg orally, 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
Cephalexin 2 g orally, 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
pharmacology-2.explanation: Option D is correct because under 2021 Canadian Dental Association and AHA infective endocarditis guidelines, cephalexin (2 g orally) is the first-line bactericidal alternative for penicillin-allergic patients whose previous reaction was non-severe and non-IgE-mediated (e.g., mild maculopapular rash). Amoxicillin (Option B) is avoided due to the reported penicillin allergy history, clindamycin (Option C) is strictly contraindicated and was removed from prophylaxis regimens due to the high risk of fatal Clostridioides difficile colitis, and metronidazole (Option A) lacks antimicrobial coverage against oral viridans group streptococci.

anatomy-639574095.question: A 65-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of a persistent "sore spot" on her lower lip that has been present for 3 months and occasionally bleeds. She has a history of extensive chronic sun exposure. Clinical examination reveals a 7 mm, firm, indurated, non-healing ulcer with rolled borders on the vermilion border of the lower lip. The adjacent mucosa appears normal, and no cervical lymphadenopathy is palpable. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Perform an incisional biopsy
Perform an excisional biopsy with 1 mm margins
Prescribe a high-potency topical corticosteroid
Apply silver nitrate chemical cautery to promote healing
anatomy-639574095.explanation: Option A is correct because a chronic, indurated ulcer with rolled borders on the actinically damaged lower lip is highly suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma (lip cancer), which requires an incisional biopsy to establish a definitive histological diagnosis while preserving anatomical landmarks and oncologic margins. Excisional biopsy (Option B) is contraindicated for suspected malignancies as it breaches tumor margins and compromises future definitive surgical resection, topical corticosteroids (Option C) suppress local tissue immunity and dangerously delay cancer diagnosis, and chemical cautery (Option D) produces tissue destruction without yielding diagnostic pathology.

anatomy-604818333.question: A 42-year-old female patient presents for follow-up five days after the surgical extraction of an impacted tooth 38. She reports persistent numbness and loss of taste sensation on the left anterior two-thirds of her tongue, as well as numbness of the adjacent lingual gingiva. Sensation of the left lower lip and chin is completely normal. Which nerve was MOST likely injured during the surgical procedure?
options: Lingual nerve
Inferior alveolar nerve
Mental nerve
Long buccal nerve
