options: Placement of a standard-diameter implant combined with staged or simultaneous guided bone regeneration.
Placement of a wide-diameter implant to engage the full buccolingual width of the cortical plates.
Placement of a mini-implant (<3.0 mm diameter) as the definitive single-tooth restoration.
Placement of a 6 mm ultra-short implant without lateral bone augmentation.
implants-307.explanation: Option A is correct because an alveolar ridge under 5 mm in width cannot accommodate a standard-diameter implant while preserving the required minimum 1.5 to 2 mm of buccal bone plate thickness, necessitating guided bone regeneration. Option B is incorrect because placing a wide-diameter implant in a 4 mm ridge would cause complete buccal cortical dehiscence. Options C and D are incorrect because mini-implants are contraindicated for single-tooth posterior restorations due to fatigue fracture risk, and ultra-short implants address vertical, not horizontal, bone deficiencies.

implants-294.question: A 50-year-old female patient presents for implant placement to replace a missing maxillary right first molar (tooth 16). Pre-operative CBCT reveals a residual alveolar bone height of 5 mm inferior to the maxillary sinus floor, and a 10 mm length implant is planned. What is the MOST appropriate surgical approach to facilitate implant placement in this site?
options: Lateral window sinus floor augmentation.
Transcrestal osteotome sinus floor elevation.
Placement of a 5 mm ultra-short implant without sinus elevation.
Alveolar ridge split osteotomy without grafting.
implants-294.explanation: Option A is correct because when 5 mm of vertical sinus augmentation is required in an area with only 5 mm of residual bone height, a lateral window sinus lift is the evidence-based approach to ensure adequate visibility and graft volume. Option B is incorrect because transcrestal osteotome elevation is limited to 2 to 3 mm of elevation and carries high risk of membrane perforation with 5 mm residual bone. Options C and D are incorrect because 5 mm ultra-short implants have reduced long-term success in the posterior maxilla under occlusal loading, and ridge splitting addresses horizontal, not vertical, deficiency.

implants-215.question: A 38-year-old male patient with an osseointegrated implant at the site of the mandibular left first molar (tooth 36) presents for definitive prosthetic restoration. Clinical examination reveals a restricted interocclusal space of 4 mm between the implant platform and the opposing maxillary dentition. Which of the following restorative options is MOST appropriate to ensure retention and minimize biological complications?
options: A cement-retained porcelain-fused-to-metal crown on a custom zirconia abutment.
A cement-retained full-contour cast gold crown on a stock titanium abutment.
A screw-retained monolithic zirconia crown bonded to a titanium base (Ti-base).
A cement-retained monolithic zirconia crown on a short prefabricated abutment.
implants-215.explanation: Option C is correct because restricted interocclusal space (4 mm) provides insufficient vertical height for cement-retained abutment retention (requiring >=5 mm), making a screw-retained crown on a Ti-base ideal to ensure mechanical retention and avoid cement-induced peri-implantitis. Options A, B, and D are incorrect because all cement-retained modalities in limited vertical clearance are prone to frequent debonding and undetectable subgingival cement extrusion that initiates severe peri-implant soft tissue inflammation.

implants-317.question: A 40-year-old female patient receives a single implant to replace the mandibular right first molar (tooth 46). Primary stability is excellent, demonstrated by an insertion torque of 40 Ncm and an implant stability quotient (ISQ) > 75. The patient exhibits good oral hygiene and no parafunctional habits. According to current ITI consensus guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate loading protocol for this implant?
options: Immediate loading within 48 hours with a provisional crown in full occlusion.
Conventional loading after a minimum healing period of 3 to 6 months.
Early loading after 6 to 8 weeks with a definitive crown.
Delayed loading after 9 to 12 months to achieve maximal bone remodeling.
implants-317.explanation: Option C is correct because ITI consensus guidelines recommend early loading at 6 to 8 weeks for single posterior implants placed in good bone quality when high primary stability (ISQ > 70) is established. Option A is incorrect because immediate functional loading of an isolated posterior molar carries high failure rates from unpreventable masticatory shear forces causing micromotion. Options B and D are incorrect because extending healing to 3 to 12 months is an outdated, overly conservative protocol when objective stability criteria are met.

implants-327.question: A 48-year-old female patient presents for implant placement at the site of the missing maxillary right first molar (tooth 16). Pre-operative CBCT reveals adequate ridge width but a residual alveolar bone height of only 2 mm inferior to the maxillary sinus floor. What is the MOST appropriate surgical approach to facilitate implant placement?
options: Lateral window sinus floor augmentation with delayed or staged implant placement.
Transcrestal osteotome sinus floor elevation with simultaneous implant placement.
Placement of a 4 mm short implant without sinus augmentation.
Guided bone regeneration with horizontal ridge expansion alone.
implants-327.explanation: Option A is correct because residual alveolar bone of only 2 mm beneath the sinus floor cannot provide primary implant stability, necessitating a lateral window sinus augmentation with staged implant placement after graft maturation. Option B is incorrect because transcrestal osteotome elevation is contraindicated with <4 mm of residual bone due to extreme risk of Schneiderian membrane tearing and lack of primary stability. Options C and D are incorrect because a 4 mm implant cannot osseointegrate in 2 mm of bone, and horizontal ridge expansion fails to address vertical bone deficits.

implants-372.question: A 28-year-old female patient presents with a non-restorable tooth 21 (maxillary left central incisor) secondary to a subcrestal root fracture. The surrounding periodontal tissues are healthy with a thick biotype and no active infection. Radiographic evaluation shows an intact facial bone plate and 4 mm of native bone apical to the root fundus. What is the MOST critical surgical requirement for successful immediate implant placement in this scenario?
options: Selecting an implant diameter that completely fills the coronal circumference of the extraction socket.
Achieving primary implant stability by anchoring into native bone 3 to 5 mm apical to the extraction socket.
Advancing a full-thickness flap to achieve complete primary soft tissue closure over the socket.
Placing a definitive metal-ceramic crown into functional occlusion on the day of surgery.
implants-372.explanation: Option B is correct because achieving primary mechanical stability by anchoring into 3 to 5 mm of native bone beyond the extraction socket apex is the essential biological prerequisite for successful immediate implant placement. Option A is incorrect because oversized implants eliminate the required buccal gap, leading to facial bone resorption. Options C and D are incorrect because primary flap advancement distorts the mucogingival junction in the aesthetic zone, and immediate functional loading risks micromotion and early fibrous encapsulation.

implants-353.question: A 65-year-old female patient has an implant-supported fixed partial denture replacing teeth 13, 14, and 15 (maxillary right canine, first premolar, and second premolar). Which interdental cleaning aid is MOST recommended for daily home care to effectively clean around the implant abutments and underneath the prosthesis?
options: Standard waxed dental floss without a threader.
Tufted dental floss (Superfloss) or an oral irrigator.
Wooden interdental stimulation wedges.
Standard metal-core interproximal wire brushes.
implants-353.explanation: Option B is correct because tufted dental floss (Superfloss) and oral irrigators effectively cleanse concave subpontic areas and implant transmucosal contours without scratching titanium components or damaging peri-implant seals. Option A is incorrect because standard floss cannot navigate fixed connector joints without a threader and lacks bulk to clean pontic tissue surfaces. Options C and D are incorrect because wooden wedges can splinter subgingivally and metal-core wire brushes scratch titanium surfaces, facilitating pathogenic biofilm adhesion.

implants-5.question: According to the Lekholm and Zarb bone classification, which bone quality type provides the optimal balance between high primary implant stability and sufficient trabecular vascularity for predictable osseointegration?
options: Type II (thick compact cortical bone surrounding a core of dense trabecular bone)
Type I (homogeneous compact cortical bone with minimal trabecular space)
Type III (thin cortical bone surrounding a core of dense trabecular bone)
Type IV (thin cortical bone surrounding a core of low-density trabecular bone)
implants-5.explanation: Option A is correct because Lekholm and Zarb Type II bone provides the ideal anatomical substrate for implant placement, combining a thick cortical plate that ensures robust primary mechanical stability with a dense vascular trabecular core that promotes rapid osseointegration. In contrast, Type I bone contains minimal vascularity and carries a high risk of thermal osteonecrosis during osteotomy preparation, whereas Types III and IV feature thin cortical boundaries and low-density trabecular bone that significantly compromise initial implant anchorage.

implants-194.question: A 58-year-old male presents for the delivery of an implant-supported crown replacing the mandibular left first molar (tooth 36). The patient has a history of moderate bruxism managed with a nocturnal occlusal appliance. Which occlusal scheme is MOST appropriate to protect this posterior implant restoration from detrimental lateral shearing forces?
options: Group function occlusion distributing lateral contacts across all posterior teeth on the working side
Canine guidance with immediate disocclusion of all posterior teeth during lateral and protrusive excursions
Bilateral balanced occlusion with simultaneous posterior gliding contacts in eccentric movements
Lingualized occlusion maintaining light balancing contacts on the non-working side
implants-194.explanation: Option B is correct because canine-guided occlusion (mutually protected occlusion) provides immediate posterior disocclusion during lateral and protrusive excursive movements, shielding the implant restoration at tooth 36 from harmful transverse shearing forces and bending moments. Group function (Option A), bilateral balanced occlusion (Option C), and lingualized cross-arch contacts (Option D) introduce non-axial lateral loads to posterior fixtures, which significantly increase the risk of screw loosening, ceramic fracture, and peri-implant marginal bone loss in bruxing patients.

implants-179.question: A 50-year-old female presents for implant evaluation to replace a missing mandibular right first molar (tooth 46). Pre-operative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) reveals Misch D3 bone density at the edentulous site. What anatomical characteristics define D3 bone, and what osteotomy preparation protocol is MOST appropriate to ensure adequate primary implant stability?
options: Dense homogeneous cortical bone; utilize crestal countersinking and dense bone tapping with vigorous cooling.
Thick porous cortical bone with coarse trabecular bone; utilize a standardized full-diameter drill sequence.
Virtually absent cortical bone with sparse trabecular bone; utilize bicortical cortical plate engagement.
Thin porous cortical bone with fine trabecular bone; utilize an undersized osteotomy (under-drilling) protocol.
implants-179.explanation: Option D is correct because Misch D3 bone consists of a thin porous layer of cortical bone over fine trabecular bone (350 to 850 Hounsfield units), which requires an undersized osteotomy (under-drilling) or osteotome condensation to achieve acceptable primary implant stability. Dense cortical bone tapping and high-volume cooling to prevent thermal osteonecrosis are specific to dense D1 bone (Option A), while D2 bone features thick porous cortex with coarse trabeculae suitable for standard protocols (Option B), and D4 bone exhibits negligible cortical density (Option C).

implants-165.question: When planning dental implant placement in the anterior mandibular midline to replace teeth 31 and 41, which anatomical structure is MOST critical to identify on a pre-operative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scan to prevent life-threatening hemorrhagic complications?
options: Mandibular incisive canal
Lingual foramen
Mental foramen
Superior genial tubercle
implants-165.explanation: Option B is correct because the lingual foramen on the lingual cortical plate of the anterior mandible transmits anastomotic branches of the sublingual and submental arteries; lingual cortical perforation during implant osteotomy can trigger massive floor-of-the-mouth hemorrhage, leading to rapid airway obstruction (pseudo-Ludwig angina). The mandibular incisive canal (Option A) contains small neurovascular extensions with low surgical hemorrhage risk, the mental foramen (Option C) is located more posteriorly near teeth 34/35 and 44/45, and the genial tubercles (Option D) represent bony muscular attachments rather than vascular conduits.

implants-198.question: A 58-year-old systemically healthy male presents with a non-restorable root fracture of tooth 24 requiring extraction. Clinical examination reveals healthy gingival architecture and intact buccal bone. A periapical radiograph shows a well-defined, asymptomatic periapical radiolucency (2 mm) at the root apex with no acute suppuration. Following atraumatic extraction and meticulous socket debridement, what is the MOST appropriate timing protocol for implant placement according to ITI (International Team for Implantology) consensus guidelines?
options: Immediate placement (Type 1) at the time of extraction with primary stability achieved in apical native bone
Early placement with soft tissue healing (Type 2) at 4 to 8 weeks post-extraction
Early placement with partial bone healing (Type 3) at 12 to 16 weeks post-extraction
Late placement with complete bone healing (Type 4) at 6 months post-extraction
implants-198.explanation: Option A is correct because current ITI consensus guidelines confirm that a small, localized periapical lesion (≤2 mm) without acute purulent exudate is not a contraindication to immediate (Type 1) implant placement, provided thorough surgical debridement of the socket is performed and primary stability is achieved beyond the alveolus. Deferring placement to Type 2 (Option B), Type 3 (Option C), or Type 4 protocols (Option D) is unnecessary in the absence of acute infection, prolongs treatment time, and leads to inevitable physiological alveolar ridge resorption without improving implant survival rates.

implants-200.question: A 45-year-old female presents for implant replacement of a missing mandibular left second premolar (tooth 35). Pre-operative CBCT reveals 8.0 mm of vertical bone height coronal to the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) canal and 6.5 mm of bucco-lingual ridge width. To respect the mandatory 2.0 mm safety margin from the IAN canal and preserve at least 1.5 mm of surrounding cortical bone, which implant dimension is MOST appropriate?
options: 4.5 mm diameter, 8.0 mm length
4.0 mm diameter, 8.0 mm length
3.5 mm diameter, 6.0 mm length
5.0 mm diameter, 6.0 mm length
implants-200.explanation: Option C is correct because an implant measuring 3.5 mm in diameter and 6.0 mm in length perfectly accommodates the anatomical constraints, maintaining the mandatory 2.0 mm safety buffer coronal to the IAN canal (8.0 mm - 6.0 mm = 2.0 mm) while preserving 1.5 mm of cortical bone on both buccal and lingual aspects (6.5 mm - 3.5 mm = 3.0 mm total bone clearance). Implant lengths of 8.0 mm (Options A and B) leave zero safety margin and risk catastrophic neurosensory transection of the IAN, while diameters of 4.5 mm or 5.0 mm (Options A and D) excessively thin the crestal cortex below the critical 1.5 mm threshold, leading to progressive peri-implant bone resorption.

implants-244.question: Which statement accurately describes a key histological difference between the peri-implant mucosa and the gingiva surrounding natural teeth?
options: Peri-implant collagen fibers run parallel and circumferential to the implant surface without direct insertion, whereas gingival Sharpey's fibers insert perpendicularly into cementum.
Peri-implant mucosa possesses a richer and more extensive microvascular plexus than the gingiva around natural teeth.
Peri-implant connective tissue contains a higher proportion of fibroblasts and fewer collagen fibers compared to natural gingival connective tissue.
The peri-implant junctional epithelium attaches to titanium via mechanical desmosomal junctions rather than a hemidesmosomal basal lamina.
implants-244.explanation: Option A is correct because the peri-implant connective tissue barrier is formed by collagen fiber bundles oriented parallel and circumferential to the titanium surface without perpendicular insertion, unlike natural teeth where Sharpey's fibers insert directly into root cementum. Peri-implant mucosa is relatively hypovascular compared to natural gingiva due to the absence of the periodontal ligament vascular network (Option B), consists of scar-like tissue with fewer fibroblasts and higher collagen density (Option C), and forms an epithelial seal via hemidesmosomes and an internal basal lamina rather than desmosomes (Option D).

implants-256.question: A 55-year-old female presents for implant consultation six months after the extraction of the maxillary left first molar (tooth 26). Clinical examination reveals healthy soft tissue volume and normal interocclusal space. Pre-operative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) demonstrates 7 mm of residual bone height below the maxillary sinus floor and 8 mm of bucco-lingual ridge width. What is the MOST appropriate initial surgical management?
options: Transcrestal osteotome sinus floor elevation with simultaneous implant placement
Lateral window sinus augmentation with a staged healing period of 6 months prior to implant placement
Standard implant placement using an 8 mm length fixture without sinus floor elevation
Placement of a short 4 mm implant to avoid any sinus floor manipulation
implants-256.explanation: Option A is correct because with 7 mm of residual vertical bone height, a transcrestal osteotome approach (crestal sinus lift) with simultaneous implant placement is the gold standard minimally invasive procedure, providing sufficient native bone for excellent initial mechanical stability. A lateral window approach with delayed implant placement (Option B) is unnecessarily invasive when residual height exceeds 5 mm, placing an 8 mm implant without elevation (Option C) breaches the Schneiderian membrane, and ultra-short 4 mm implants (Option D) have reduced predictability and unfavorable crown-to-implant ratios in posterior maxillae compared to crestally augmented implants.

implants-257.question: Which statement MOST accurately characterizes the mucosal epithelial attachment to a titanium dental implant surface in a healthy peri-implant environment?
options: An elongated junctional epithelium that attaches to the titanium dioxide surface via hemidesmosomes and an internal basal lamina
A short junctional epithelium that attaches to the titanium dioxide surface via direct desmosomal interlocking
A keratinized sulcular epithelium with perpendicular collagen fibrils inserting directly into the titanium surface
A modified pseudo-epithelial layer lacking a basal lamina that relies exclusively on a circumferential suction seal
implants-257.explanation: Option A is correct because the peri-implant epithelial seal is histologically characterized by an elongated (long) junctional epithelium, approximately 2 mm in vertical dimension, that attaches to the titanium oxide surface via hemidesmosomes and an internal basal lamina. The epithelial attachment is not short or desmosome-mediated (Option B), lacks collagen fibers which cannot insert into metallic surfaces (Option C), and forms a true histological hemidesmosomal hemiseal rather than a passive mechanical suction barrier (Option D).

implants-258.question: A 40-year-old male presents for implant consultation to replace a missing mandibular right first molar (tooth 46). Clinical examination reveals adequate mesiodistal space and interocclusal clearance. A CBCT scan shows sufficient bucco-lingual ridge width (8 mm) but only 8 mm of vertical bone height coronal to the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) canal. What is the MOST appropriate treatment planning strategy?
options: Inform the patient that implant placement is contraindicated due to proximity to the IAN.
Plan for an 8 mm standard implant to engage the dense cortical roof of the IAN canal for bicortical stability.
Propose an inferior alveolar nerve lateralization to allow placement of a longer 11 mm implant.
Recommend a 6 mm short implant to maintain the mandatory 2 mm safety margin coronal to the IAN canal.
implants-258.explanation: Option D is correct because with 8 mm of vertical bone height above the mandibular canal, placing a 6 mm short implant preserves the mandatory 2 mm safety margin required by Canadian surgical standards to protect the inferior alveolar nerve from traumatic neuropathy. Placing an 8 mm implant (Option B) leaves zero safety buffer and risks irreversible lip paresthesia, nerve lateralization (Option C) carries an unacceptably high risk of permanent neurosensory disturbance, and implant therapy is not contraindicated (Option A) given the high predictability of short implants.

implants-262.question: A 35-year-old female presents for implant placement to replace a missing maxillary right second premolar (tooth 15). Her medical history reveals well-controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus with a recent HbA1c level of 6.8%. She maintains good oral hygiene and presents with no microvascular complications. What is the MOST appropriate clinical consideration regarding implant therapy for this patient?
options: Defer implant placement indefinitely because type 1 diabetes mellitus represents an absolute contraindication to dental osseointegration.
Proceed with standard implant surgical protocols, as patients with well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c < 7.0%) achieve osseointegration and survival rates comparable to non-diabetic patients.
Prescribe a routine 3-week course of postoperative systemic antibiotics to prevent late surgical site infection.
Perform immediate implant loading, as controlled hyperglycemia accelerates bone turnover and secondary stability.
implants-262.explanation: Option B is correct because extensive clinical evidence and Canadian dental consensus demonstrate that patients with well-controlled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c < 7.0%) experience implant osseointegration and long-term survival rates comparable to healthy, non-diabetic individuals. Type 1 diabetes is not an absolute contraindication when glycemic control is maintained (Option A), prescribing a 3-week prophylactic antibiotic course (Option C) violates Canadian antimicrobial stewardship principles without improving clinical outcomes, and immediate loading (Option D) is contraindicated because diabetic microangiopathy may subtly delay rather than accelerate bone remodeling.

implants-264.question: A 68-year-old male presents with chronic food impaction and papillary soreness around an implant-supported crown on tooth 36 placed 5 years ago. The patient reports that daily use of interdental brushes provides temporary debris removal but fails to prevent food entrapment during meals. Clinical examination reveals an open proximal contact with tooth 35, a flat prosthetic emergence profile, and no peri-implant bleeding or mobility. Radiographs confirm stable marginal bone levels. What is the MOST appropriate definitive management to resolve the etiology of this condition?
options: Prescribe a twice-daily 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate rinse and continue using interdental brushes.
Perform a localized excisional gingivectomy to eliminate the interdental soft tissue col.
Advise the patient to continue using interdental brushes as the sole long-term therapy.
Modify or remake the implant crown to establish an anatomical emergence profile and a closed proximal contact.
implants-264.explanation: Option D is correct because the definitive management to resolve chronic food impaction caused by an open proximal contact and flat emergence profile is to modify or remake the implant crown, re-establishing physiological contours and proximal contact tightness. Excisional gingivectomy (Option B) destroys the interproximal papilla and exacerbates food impaction, while chlorhexidine rinses (Option A) and relying solely on interdental brushes (Option C) provide only palliative plaque control without correcting the anatomical open contact.

emergencies-2.question: A 68-year-old male patient with Type 2 diabetes controlled with insulin becomes disoriented, diaphoretic, and tremulous during a restorative procedure on tooth 16. He reports feeling weak and dizzy, having taken his morning insulin without eating lunch. He remains conscious and capable of swallowing. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Administer 0.3 mg epinephrine intramuscularly
Place the patient in a supine position and elevate his legs
Administer 1 mg glucagon intramuscularly
Administer 15 to 20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrates, such as glucose tablets or fruit juice
emergencies-2.explanation: Option D is correct because in a conscious hypoglycemic patient who is able to swallow, immediate administration of 15–20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrates is the definitive Canadian standard of care, and treatment must never be delayed for blood glucose testing. Option C is incorrect because glucagon is reserved for unconscious patients or those unable to take oral carbohydrates safely. Options A and B are incorrect because epinephrine is indicated for anaphylaxis, and supine positioning is indicated for vasovagal syncope rather than hypoglycemia.

emergencies-3.question: A 55-year-old male patient with a known history of stable angina develops sudden dull, retrosternal chest pain radiating to his left arm during a crown preparation on tooth 25. He is conscious, upright, and anxious. His blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, pulse is 88 bpm, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. What is the MOST appropriate initial management step?
options: Administer 160–325 mg of chewable acetylsalicylic acid (ASA)
Activate emergency medical services (EMS) immediately
Administer 0.4 mg of sublingual nitroglycerin
Administer high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask
emergencies-3.explanation: Option C is correct because in a conscious patient with known stable angina and adequate systolic blood pressure (>90–100 mmHg), one dose of sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) is the first-line intervention to relieve myocardial ischemia. Option B is incorrect because EMS activation is indicated only if pain persists after three doses over 15 minutes or if acute myocardial infarction is suspected. Options A and D are incorrect because chewable ASA is indicated when acute coronary syndrome is suspected, and routine oxygen is not recommended when oxygen saturation is normal (≥94%).

emergencies-10.question: During a restorative procedure on tooth 46, an inlay slips into the oropharynx. The 28-year-old male patient sits up, grasps his neck, and begins coughing forcefully and wheezing, but remains fully conscious and is able to speak in short phrases. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) immediately
Encourage the patient to continue coughing forcefully while monitoring breathing
Perform a blind finger sweep to retrieve the object
Place the patient in a supine position and administer back blows
emergencies-10.explanation: Option B is correct because when a patient exhibits forceful coughing and adequate air exchange during a partial airway obstruction, the natural cough reflex is the most effective clearance mechanism and intervention must be limited to close monitoring. Option A is incorrect because abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) are indicated exclusively for severe or complete airway obstruction characterized by a silent cough, inability to speak, or cyanosis. Options C and D are incorrect because blind finger sweeps can push foreign bodies deeper into the pharynx, and placing the patient supine increases the risk of complete airway obstruction.

implants-469.question: A 65-year-old female patient presents with a 7-year-old implant-supported crown at the site of tooth 36. She reports mild, dull pain around the implant during mastication and occasional bleeding upon brushing. Clinical examination reveals localized erythema, edema, and a probing depth of 6 mm with bleeding on probing, but no suppuration or mobility. Radiographs demonstrate 1 mm of crestal bone loss compared to baseline post-remodeling radiographs. What is the MOST appropriate initial management strategy?
options: Immediate explantation followed by socket preservation grafting
Open flap surgical debridement and guided bone regeneration
Non-surgical mechanical debridement combined with oral hygiene instructions
Systemic broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy alone
implants-469.explanation: Option C is correct because non-surgical mechanical debridement using titanium or plastic curettes combined with oral hygiene reinforcement is the essential initial therapy for early peri-implantitis with minimal bone loss. Option B is incorrect because surgical intervention is indicated only when non-surgical therapy fails to arrest disease progression or in advanced bone defects. Options A and D are incorrect because implant removal is indicated only for mobile or fractured fixtures, and systemic antibiotics alone without debridement cannot resolve peri-implant biofilm infections.

implants-471.question: A 40-year-old male patient presents with a non-restorable fracture of tooth 11 at the gingival margin. He has a high smile line and a thin periodontal phenotype. CBCT imaging shows a thin buccal cortical plate (<1 mm). He desires an implant-supported restoration. Which procedure is MOST appropriate to augment the facial bone and maintain long-term peri-implant mucosal esthetics?
options: Maxillary sinus floor augmentation via a lateral window approach
Guided bone regeneration (GBR) for buccal plate augmentation using a particulate graft and barrier membrane
Ridge splitting and expansion technique without a barrier membrane
Coronally advanced flap without hard tissue grafting
implants-471.explanation: Option B is correct because in the maxillary anterior aesthetic zone (tooth 11) with a thin buccal bone wall (<1 mm), guided bone regeneration (GBR) using a particulate bone graft and barrier membrane is required to establish at least 1.5–2 mm of facial bone thickness and prevent mucosal recession. Option A is incorrect because sinus augmentation is performed exclusively in the posterior maxilla to gain vertical height below the antrum. Options C and D are incorrect because ridge splitting carries a high risk of labial cortical fracture in the thin anterior maxilla, and soft-tissue advancement alone cannot compensate for underlying bone deficiency.

implants-475.question: A 68-year-old male patient received two implants at the sites of tooth 33 and tooth 43 to support a mandibular overdenture. During the impression appointment, the implant at tooth 33 exhibits rotational mobility of the impression coping under torque, whereas the implant at tooth 43 is completely rigid. What is the MOST appropriate action regarding the mobile implant at tooth 33?
options: Remove the mobile implant, as rotational mobility indicates definitive failure of osseointegration
Delay prosthetic loading and allow an additional 3 months for re-osseointegration
Proceed with the impression, as minor rotational mobility is acceptable for overdenture abutments
Switch to a closed-tray impression technique using a flexible elastomeric material
implants-475.explanation: Option A is correct because rotational mobility or loosening under torque during the restorative phase indicates fibrous encapsulation and irreversible failure of osseointegration, mandating explantation of the implant. Option B is incorrect because an implant that has undergone fibrous encapsulation cannot achieve secondary osseointegration by simply providing additional healing time. Options C and D are incorrect because taking impressions on or loading a clinically mobile implant violates core prosthodontic principles and will lead to prosthesis failure.

implants-477.question: A 35-year-old healthy female presents with a non-restorable tooth 36. She desires an implant-supported restoration. A CBCT scan reveals adequate mesiodistal space and vertical bone height above the inferior alveolar canal, but a critically narrow bucco-lingual ridge dimension of 4 mm. What is the MOST appropriate surgical management to achieve sufficient ridge width for implant placement?
options: Extract tooth 36 and perform horizontal guided bone regeneration (GBR) using a particulate bone graft and barrier membrane
Perform a ridge splitting and expansion osteotomy with immediate implant placement
Place a 3.0 mm narrow-diameter implant without bone augmentation
Extract tooth 36 and perform a socket shield procedure with immediate implant placement
implants-477.explanation: Option A is correct because a 4 mm bucco-lingual ridge width is insufficient for a standard molar implant, and extraction followed by horizontal guided bone regeneration (GBR) is the predictable standard of care. Option B is incorrect because ridge-splitting osteotomy is contraindicated in the dense, non-compliant cortical bone of the posterior mandible due to high risk of buccal plate fracture. Options C and D are incorrect because narrow-diameter implants are contraindicated under molar occlusal forces, and socket shield procedures are contraindicated in the presence of acute pathology or non-restorable teeth.

implants-479.question: A 50-year-old male presents with a 2-year-old implant-supported crown at the site of tooth 11. He is concerned about a grayish discoloration visible at the mucosal margin and slight gingival recession compared to adjacent tooth 21. Clinical examination reveals 1 mm of labial mucosal recession exposing the titanium abutment margin, with no peri-implant inflammation or bone loss. What is the MOST appropriate management strategy to address this aesthetic complication?
options: Replace the titanium abutment and crown with a custom zirconia abutment and all-ceramic crown
Perform a free gingival autograft to cover the exposed implant collar
Replace the restoration with a porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown with a labial metal collar
Administer subgingival minocycline microspheres and monitor annually
implants-479.explanation: Option A is correct because the grayish marginal discoloration is caused by the optical show-through of the metallic titanium abutment through thin peri-implant mucosa, and replacing it with a tooth-colored zirconia abutment and ceramic crown eliminates the shadow. Option B is incorrect because attempting soft-tissue root coverage over a smooth, non-vascularized implant collar using free gingival grafts is unpredictable and aesthetically compromised. Options C and D are incorrect because a PFM crown with a metal collar worsens mucosal discoloration, and antimicrobial therapy does not address a non-inflammatory prosthetic aesthetic complication.

implants-480.question: Which bone graft material possesses osteogenic potential, defined by the presence of viable cells capable of directly forming new bone?
options: Autograft
Allograft
Xenograft
Alloplast
implants-480.explanation: Option A is correct because autografts uniquely possess osteogenic properties due to the transplantation of viable, living osteoblasts and osteoprogenitor cells capable of direct de novo bone formation. Option B is incorrect because allografts (such as FDBA or DFDBA) are non-vital, processing only osteoconductive or osteoinductive properties. Options C and D are incorrect because xenografts and alloplasts are completely acellular and non-inductive scaffolds that heal exclusively via osteoconduction.

emergencies-104.question: A 68-year-old male with a history of stable angina develops severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to his left arm and mandible during a restoration on tooth 16. He received one dose of sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) 5 minutes ago with no relief. He remains upright and conscious; his blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, pulse is 82 bpm, and SpO2 is 98% on room air. What is the MOST appropriate immediate next step?
options: Administer 160–325 mg of chewable acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) and begin CPR
Administer a second dose of sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg)
Administer high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask
Place the patient in a supine position with legs elevated
emergencies-104.explanation: Option B is correct because under Canadian dental emergency protocols, if angina pain persists 5 minutes after an initial dose and systolic blood pressure remains >90–100 mmHg, a second dose of sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) should be administered. Option A is incorrect because chewable ASA and EMS activation are indicated if pain persists after three nitroglycerin doses or if myocardial infarction is suspected, while CPR is indicated only for pulseless cardiac arrest. Options C and D are incorrect because supplemental oxygen is not indicated for patients with normal oxygen saturation (≥94%), and supine positioning increases venous return and cardiac workload, worsening myocardial ischemia.

emergencies-133.question: A 20-year-old female patient, extremely anxious before the planned surgical extraction of impacted tooth 38, begins hyperventilating. She exhibits rapid, deep respirations, complains of carpopedal spasms and circumoral paresthesia, and feels lightheaded. Her pulse is 98 bpm, blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Administer 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask at 10 L/min
Instruct the patient to breathe repeatedly into an airtight paper bag
Administer 2 mg of intravenous midazolam immediately
Position the patient upright, provide calm reassurance, and coach slow diaphragmatic breathing
emergencies-133.explanation: Option D is correct because the definitive management of acute hyperventilation syndrome in the dental office consists of terminating the procedure, seating the patient comfortably upright, and actively coaching slow, controlled diaphragmatic breathing to restore arterial pCO2 levels. Option A is incorrect because supplemental oxygen is contraindicated in hyperventilation, as the patient is already hyperoxic and hypocapnic. Options B and C are incorrect because rebreathing into a paper bag is obsolete and hazardous due to the risk of severe hypoxia, and parenteral sedatives carry significant risks of respiratory depression.

emergencies-143.question: A 58-year-old male with no prior cardiac history experiences sudden, severe crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm and mandible during a restorative procedure on tooth 26. He is diaphoretic, dyspneic, and clutching his chest. His blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, pulse is 92 bpm, and SpO2 is 98% on room air. What is the MOST appropriate initial emergency management in the dental office?
options: Place the patient in a supine position with feet elevated, administer high-flow oxygen, and administer sublingual nitroglycerin
Position the patient comfortably upright, activate EMS immediately, administer 160–325 mg chewable acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), and administer 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin
Administer 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin every 5 minutes for three doses, and activate EMS only if pain fails to resolve after 15 minutes
Administer two puffs of salbutamol via metered-dose inhaler and 10 mg of oral diazepam for acute anxiety
emergencies-143.explanation: Option B is correct because in a patient with no previous cardiac history presenting with classic signs of acute myocardial infarction, immediate protocol requires keeping the patient upright, activating EMS without delay, administering chewed ASA (160–325 mg), and administering sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) given adequate blood pressure. Option A is incorrect because placing a conscious patient experiencing acute myocardial infarction in a supine position increases cardiac preload and myocardial oxygen demand, worsening ischemia and dyspnea. Options C and D are incorrect because delaying EMS activation to complete a full antianginal trial is contraindicated when myocardial infarction is suspected, and bronchodilators or sedatives do not address myocardial ischemia.

emergencies-310.question: A 68-year-old male patient with Type 2 diabetes managed with insulin presents for restorative treatment on tooth 16. He reports skipping breakfast due to anxiety and presents disoriented, pale, tremulous, and profusely diaphoretic. He is conscious and able to swallow safely. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Administer 15 to 20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrate, such as oral glucose tablets or juice.
Administer 1 mg of glucagon intramuscularly.
Administer 0.4 mg of sublingual nitroglycerin.
Position the patient supine and initiate immediate chest compressions.
emergencies-310.explanation: Option A is correct because Diabetes Canada guidelines recommend administering 15 to 20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrates for conscious individuals with mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia who can swallow safely. Intramuscular glucagon (Option B) is indicated only when the patient is unconscious, seizing, or unable to swallow safely, sublingual nitroglycerin (Option C) is indicated for angina rather than hypoglycemia, and chest compressions (Option D) are strictly indicated for cardiac arrest.

emergencies-254.question: A 58-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension presents to the dental clinic for the routine extraction of tooth 46. During the procedure, he develops sudden, crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his mandible and left arm. He is pale and diaphoretic, with a blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg and a heart rate of 88 bpm. He has no history of phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use in the past 48 hours. What is the MOST appropriate initial pharmacological intervention?
options: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg).
Administer 0.3 mg of 1:1,000 epinephrine intramuscularly.
Administer salbutamol via a metered-dose inhaler.
Administer 50 mg of diphenhydramine orally.
emergencies-254.explanation: Option A is correct because sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) is the initial pharmacological intervention of choice to promote coronary vasodilation and differentiate stable angina from acute myocardial infarction in a hemodynamically stable patient (systolic BP > 90–100 mmHg). Epinephrine (Option B) is contraindicated because it increases myocardial oxygen demand and can precipitate lethal arrhythmias, salbutamol (Option C) is a bronchodilator for bronchospasm, and diphenhydramine (Option D) is an antihistamine with no anti-ischemic properties.

emergencies-262.question: A 30-year-old male patient, with no significant medical history, suddenly begins rapid, deep breathing following a local anesthetic injection for restorative treatment on tooth 24. He reports lightheadedness, perioral tingling, and carpopedal paresthesia. What is the MOST appropriate initial intervention?
options: Position the patient upright, provide calm reassurance, and coach slow, controlled breathing.
Administer high-flow 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask.
Instruct the patient to breathe into an airtight paper bag.
Place the patient in a supine position with legs elevated.
emergencies-262.explanation: Option A is correct because modern Canadian emergency protocols manage acute hyperventilation syndrome by positioning the patient comfortably upright, providing verbal reassurance, and coaching paced, slow breathing to normalize arterial carbon dioxide levels. Administering oxygen (Option B) is inappropriate because the patient is hypocapnic rather than hypoxic, breathing into a paper bag (Option C) is obsolete and strictly contraindicated due to the risk of severe hypoxia, and supine positioning (Option D) increases the sensation of suffocation and restricts thoracic expansion.

emergencies-348.question: A 55-year-old male patient with Type 1 diabetes presents for endodontic treatment on tooth 11. He reports taking his usual morning insulin dose but skipping breakfast due to nausea. During the appointment, he becomes confused, agitated, tremulous, and diaphoretic, but remains conscious and capable of swallowing. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Administer 15 to 20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrates.
Administer 1 mg of glucagon intramuscularly.
Place the patient in a supine position with feet elevated.
Administer 10 units of rapid-acting subcutaneous insulin.
emergencies-348.explanation: Option A is correct because Diabetes Canada guidelines specify administering 15 to 20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrates for conscious patients presenting with acute hypoglycemia who can safely swallow. Intramuscular glucagon (Option B) is indicated only when the patient is unconscious, seizing, or unable to ingest oral carbohydrates safely, supine positioning (Option C) does not correct neuroglycopenia and increases aspiration risk, and administering insulin (Option D) would catastrophically worsen hypoglycemia.

emergencies-353.question: According to the Heart & Stroke Foundation of Canada guidelines, what is the correct sequence of immediate actions for a lone dental healthcare provider who witnesses a sudden adult cardiac arrest in the clinic, after confirming unresponsiveness and absence of normal breathing?
options: Activate emergency medical services (EMS), retrieve the automated external defibrillator (AED), and begin chest compressions.
Begin chest compressions, activate emergency medical services (EMS), and retrieve the automated external defibrillator (AED).
Retrieve the automated external defibrillator (AED), deliver 2 rescue breaths, and begin chest compressions.
Deliver 2 rescue breaths, activate emergency medical services (EMS), and retrieve the automated external defibrillator (AED).
emergencies-353.explanation: Option A is correct because Heart & Stroke Foundation of Canada guidelines dictate that a lone rescuer witnessing an adult cardiac arrest must first activate EMS and retrieve the AED before initiating high-quality chest compressions to minimize the delay to defibrillation. Delaying EMS activation or AED retrieval until after compressions begin (Option B) significantly reduces survival from shockable tachyarrhythmias, while delivering rescue breaths first (Options C and D) contradicts current circulation-first (CAB) resuscitation sequences.

emergencies-354.question: A 40-year-old female patient with a history of epilepsy experiences a generalized tonic-clonic seizure while seated in the dental chair during crown preparation on tooth 47. She becomes unconscious and begins convulsing. What is the MOST appropriate initial response by the dental team?
options: Clear hazardous instruments away, gently protect her head, and allow the seizure to run its course without physical restraint.
Insert a padded tongue depressor or bite block between her teeth to protect her tongue.
Firmly restrain her limbs to the dental chair to prevent bodily movement and falling.
Administer 1 mg of glucagon intramuscularly into her deltoid muscle.
emergencies-354.explanation: Option A is correct because Canadian emergency management for an active tonic-clonic seizure focuses on preventing trauma by clearing dental instruments and surrounding hazards while gently shielding the patient's head without restraint. Forcing objects between clenched teeth (Option B) causes dental fractures, soft tissue lacerations, and airway compromise, active restraint (Option C) can produce musculoskeletal fractures or dislocations, and administering glucagon (Option D) is indicated for severe hypoglycemia rather than an epileptic seizure.

emergencies-363.question: A 65-year-old male patient taking rivaroxaban for non-valvular atrial fibrillation undergoes surgical extraction of tooth 38. Significant post-operative hemorrhage persists despite socket debridement, packing with oxidized cellulose, suturing, and continuous local pressure with tranexamic acid-soaked gauze. What is the MOST appropriate next management step?
options: Transfer the patient immediately to a hospital emergency department for systemic medical management.
Administer 10 mg of vitamin K orally in the dental clinic.
Administer a systemic intravenous dose of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA).
Discharge the patient home with instructions to bite on dry cotton gauze for 2 hours.
emergencies-363.explanation: Option A is correct because when bleeding persists despite comprehensive local hemostatic measures in a patient anticoagulated with a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) like rivaroxaban, immediate transfer to a hospital emergency department is required for systemic evaluation and possible reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate or specific reversal agents. Vitamin K (Option B) reverses vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin but is completely ineffective against direct factor Xa inhibitors, tPA (Option C) is a fibrinolytic that would promote clot breakdown and exacerbate hemorrhage, and discharging the patient (Option D) dangerously neglects uncontrolled surgical bleeding.

emergencies-367.question: A 38-year-old female patient develops generalized urticaria, facial angioedema, audible wheezing, and profound hypotension (blood pressure 75/40 mmHg) 15 minutes after taking 2 g of oral amoxicillin for dental prophylaxis. An initial dose of 0.5 mg epinephrine (1:1,000) has just been administered intramuscularly into her anterolateral thigh. What is the MOST crucial immediate next step in her physical management?
options: Place the patient in a supine position with her lower extremities elevated.
Administer a second intramuscular dose of 0.5 mg epinephrine immediately.
Administer 50 mg of oral diphenhydramine with a glass of water.
Seat the patient fully upright to assist with breathing and monitor vital signs.
emergencies-367.explanation: Option A is correct because positioning a hypotensive anaphylactic patient supine with elevated legs restores central venous return, maintains cardiac preload, and prevents fatal empty ventricle syndrome. Administering a second dose of epinephrine immediately (Option B) is clinically contraindicated because repeat injections require an observation window of 5 to 15 minutes to assess efficacy, oral antihistamines (Option C) have a delayed onset and pose an acute aspiration risk in hypotensive patients, and sitting the patient upright (Option D) can precipitate catastrophic circulatory collapse.

emergencies-369.question: A 52-year-old female patient with a documented history of stable angina develops severe substernal chest pain radiating to her left arm during crown placement on tooth 15. She self-administers one dose of sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) from her own prescription, but the pain remains unrelieved after 5 minutes, and she appears pale, diaphoretic, and dyspneic. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Activate emergency medical services (EMS) immediately.
Reassure the patient and wait an additional 15 minutes to allow delayed nitroglycerin absorption.
Administer 0.3 mg of 1:1,000 epinephrine intramuscularly.
Place the patient in a steep Trendelenburg position.
emergencies-369.explanation: Option A is correct because anginal chest pain that fails to respond within 5 minutes to an initial dose of nitroglycerin must be managed as an evolving acute myocardial infarction, mandating immediate EMS activation. Waiting 15 minutes (Option B) dangerously delays emergency reperfusion therapy, administering epinephrine (Option C) is contraindicated because it increases myocardial oxygen demand and triggers lethal arrhythmias, and Trendelenburg positioning (Option D) increases venous return and cardiac workload while worsening dyspnea.

emergencies-399.question: When preparing to apply an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) to an adult patient in cardiac arrest in the dental clinic, what is the standard recommended placement for the adhesive defibrillator pads?
options: One pad on the upper right anterior chest below the clavicle, and the other on the lower left lateral chest wall along the midaxillary line.
One pad on the upper left anterior chest below the clavicle, and the other on the lower right lateral chest wall along the midaxillary line.
Both pads placed horizontally across the right and left anterior lower costal margins.
One pad placed directly over the mid-sternum and the other placed over the epigastrium.
emergencies-399.explanation: Option A is correct because the standard anterolateral AED pad placement for adults requires placing one pad on the upper right anterior chest wall below the clavicle and the second pad on the lower left lateral chest wall along the midaxillary line, optimizing the transthoracic current vector across both cardiac ventricles. Reversing this alignment to the upper left and lower right (Option B) provides a suboptimal defibrillation vector relative to cardiac anatomy, bilateral lower costal placement (Option C) directs current below the ventricular mass, and vertical sternal-epigastric positioning (Option D) fails to encompass the ventricular myocardium.

emergencies-373.question: A 22-year-old male patient, highly anxious regarding the planned surgical extraction of tooth 48, becomes pale, diaphoretic, and lightheaded. He loses consciousness for 10 seconds but awakens promptly when placed supine. Although conscious and oriented, he remains weak and reports persistent nausea. What is the MOST appropriate next step in his management?
options: Abort the dental procedure, keep the patient supine or semi-reclined while monitoring vital signs until baseline is restored, and arrange an escorted discharge.
Administer a sugary oral drink while keeping the patient flat in the supine position.
Immediately resume the extraction of tooth 48 since consciousness has been regained.
Administer 0.3 mg of 1:1,000 epinephrine intramuscularly to prevent recurrent syncope.
emergencies-373.explanation: Option A is correct because following a vasovagal syncopal episode, the dental procedure should be aborted and the patient kept in a supported supine or semi-reclined position until vital signs return to baseline, followed by discharge with an escort. Administering oral liquids or sugary drinks to a supine, nauseated patient (Option B) poses a serious risk of vomiting and pulmonary aspiration, immediately resuming the procedure (Option C) triggers immediate syncopal relapse due to persistent parasympathetic tone, and administering epinephrine (Option D) is contraindicated in benign neurocardiogenic syncope.

emergencies-422.question: A 62-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension presents for crown cementation on tooth 26. He suddenly complains of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm and mandible. He appears pale, diaphoretic, and dyspneic, with a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg and a heart rate of 98 bpm. Emergency medical services (EMS) have been activated. What is the MOST appropriate initial pharmacological management in the dental clinic?
options: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses, provided systolic blood pressure remains above 90 to 100 mmHg.
Administer 325 mg of enteric-coated aspirin swallowed whole with a glass of water.
Administer 0.3 mg of 1:1,000 epinephrine intramuscularly.
Administer 50 mg of diphenhydramine orally.
emergencies-422.explanation: Option A is correct because sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg every 5 minutes up to 3 doses) is the first-line vasodilator to reduce myocardial ischemia and relieve cardiac pain, provided the patient is hemodynamically stable with systolic blood pressure above 90 to 100 mmHg. Enteric-coated aspirin swallowed whole (Option B) is inappropriate because emergency management requires chewable, non-enteric-coated aspirin (160–325 mg) for rapid buccal and gastric absorption, epinephrine (Option C) is contraindicated as it increases myocardial oxygen consumption and risks lethal arrhythmias, and diphenhydramine (Option D) is an antihistamine with no cardiovascular indication.

emergencies-145.question: A 25-year-old female patient expresses extreme apprehension prior to the surgical extraction of impacted tooth 48. She begins breathing rapidly and deeply at 32 breaths/minute, complaining of dizziness, perioral paresthesia, and carpopedal spasms in her hands. Which of the following physiological mechanisms is primarily responsible for her neuromuscular symptoms?
options: Hypocapnia causing respiratory alkalosis, which decreases serum ionized calcium.
Hypercapnia causing respiratory acidosis, which increases serum extracellular potassium.
Hypoxemia causing metabolic acidosis, which triggers peripheral nerve depolarization.
Hyperoxia causing cerebral vasoconstriction, which induces systemic hypocalcemia.
emergencies-145.explanation: Option A is correct because hyperventilation leads to excessive exhalation of carbon dioxide (hypocapnia) and acute respiratory alkalosis, which increases calcium binding to serum albumin and thereby decreases free ionized calcium, triggering tetany and paresthesias. Hypercapnia and acidosis (Option B) occur in respiratory depression rather than hyperventilation. Hypoxemia with metabolic acidosis (Option C) occurs in tissue ischemia, whereas hyperventilation produces high oxygen saturation, and hyperoxia (Option D) does not directly alter ionized calcium levels.

emergencies-153.question: According to Canadian provincial dental regulatory authorities (e.g., RCDSO) and resuscitation guidelines, which of the following non-pharmacological emergency items is MANDATORY in every dental office, regardless of whether sedation is administered?
options: Laryngeal mask airway (LMA) assortment
Automated external defibrillator (AED)
Intravenous infusion kit with crystalloid fluids
Continuous capnography (end-tidal CO2) monitor
emergencies-153.explanation: Option B is correct because Canadian dental regulatory authorities mandate that an automated external defibrillator (AED) and a positive-pressure oxygen delivery system be readily accessible in every dental facility to manage sudden cardiac arrest. Laryngeal mask airways (Option A), intravenous infusion sets (Option C), and capnography monitors (Option D) are advanced airway and monitoring supplies required specifically for moderate sedation, deep sedation, or general anesthesia facilities rather than basic dental clinics.

emergencies-215.question: A 72-year-old female patient suddenly develops right-sided facial weakness, arm drift, and slurred speech during restorative treatment on tooth 15. The dental team immediately activates emergency medical services (EMS). While awaiting EMS arrival, which of the following supportive measures is MOST appropriate?
options: Administer 160 mg of chewable acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) immediately to prevent thrombus extension.
Place the patient in the Trendelenburg position to maximize cerebral blood flow.
Position the patient comfortably with the head elevated approximately 30 degrees, provide nothing by mouth, and monitor vital signs.
Administer a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet to lower acute blood pressure elevation.
emergencies-215.explanation: Option C is correct because Canadian Stroke Best Practice Recommendations dictate positioning a conscious stroke patient with the head elevated 15 to 30 degrees to minimize intracranial pressure and aspiration risk, maintaining an open airway, and strictly withholding all oral intake. Administering ASA (Option A) is contraindicated prior to neuroimaging because it can cause catastrophic bleeding if the stroke is hemorrhagic. The Trendelenburg position (Option B) increases intracranial pressure and worsens cerebral edema, while administering nitroglycerin (Option D) risks abrupt hypotension that exacerbates cerebral ischemia.

emergencies-219.question: A 30-year-old male patient with a history of asthma presents for restorative treatment on tooth 36. During the procedure, he experiences sudden dyspnea, becomes tachypneic, and exhibits audible expiratory wheezing with accessory muscle use. He states his symptoms are worsening despite using his personal inhaler. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Place the patient in a supine position with legs elevated and administer oral prednisone.
Administer sublingual nitroglycerin to relax bronchial smooth muscle.
Administer oral diphenhydramine to suppress airway hyperresponsiveness.
Administer supplemental oxygen and assist the patient with inhaled salbutamol delivered via a spacer.
emergencies-219.explanation: Option D is correct because Canadian guidelines (Health Canada and Canadian Thoracic Society) recommend treating acute asthma exacerbations by positioning the patient upright, administering supplemental oxygen, and delivering repeated doses of a selective short-acting beta-2 agonist (salbutamol) via a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. Placing the patient supine (Option A) compromises lung volume and diaphragmatic excursion, and oral prednisone has a delayed therapeutic onset of several hours. Nitroglycerin (Option B) is a vasodilator used for angina that provides no bronchodilation, and diphenhydramine (Option C) does not relieve acute smooth muscle bronchospasm.

emergencies-192.question: A 22-year-old female patient undergoing root canal therapy on tooth 21 suddenly experiences palpitations, shortness of breath, and paresthesia around her mouth and in her fingers. She states she feels like she is going to 'pass out'. Her respiratory rate is 30 breaths/minute, and her oxygen saturation is 99%. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Administer 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather face mask at 10 L/min.
Terminate the procedure, position the patient comfortably upright, provide calm reassurance, and coach slow breathing into cupped hands.
Instruct the patient to breathe rapidly and deeply into an airtight paper bag.
Place the patient in a supine position with legs elevated and administer sublingual lorazepam.
emergencies-192.explanation: Option B is correct because initial management of hyperventilation syndrome involves terminating treatment, positioning the patient comfortably upright to assist breathing mechanics, reassuring them, and coaching slow, controlled breathing (or breathing into cupped hands) to restore arterial PaCO2. Administering 100% oxygen (Option A) is inappropriate because the patient is already hyperoxic and oxygen does not correct respiratory alkalosis. Rebreathing into a paper bag (Option C) is obsolete and contraindicated under Canadian guidelines due to the risk of life-threatening hypoxia, while supine positioning (Option D) impairs respiratory mechanics.

emergencies-225.question: A 55-year-old female patient receiving local anesthesia for crown preparation on tooth 16 suddenly loses consciousness in the dental chair. She is unresponsive, but assessment reveals spontaneous breathing and a palpable carotid pulse. What is the MOST appropriate immediate patient positioning?
options: Supine position with the feet and legs slightly elevated.
Recovery position (lateral decubitus) on the dental chair.
Semi-Fowler's position with the head elevated 45 degrees.
Steep Trendelenburg position with the head tilted 45 degrees down.
emergencies-225.explanation: Option A is correct because sudden transient loss of consciousness in the dental setting is most commonly vasovagal syncope, which is treated by placing the patient supine with legs elevated (10-15 degrees) to promote venous return to the heart and restore cerebral perfusion. Placing the patient in the recovery position (Option B) on a narrow dental chair poses a significant fall hazard and does not facilitate venous return. Semi-Fowler's position (Option C) promotes venous pooling in the lower extremities, worsening cerebral ischemia, while steep Trendelenburg (Option D) restricts diaphragmatic excursion by forcing abdominal organs against the diaphragm.

emergencies-295.question: Which medication in a standard dental emergency kit is specifically indicated as the definitive replacement therapy for an acute adrenal crisis, and also serves as a secondary adjunct for severe status asthmaticus refractory to bronchodilators?
options: Diphenhydramine hydrochloride
Epinephrine (1:1,000)
Hydrocortisone sodium succinate
Nitroglycerin
emergencies-295.explanation: Option C is correct because hydrocortisone sodium succinate (100 mg IM/IV) is the essential corticosteroid required to manage acute adrenal crisis in a steroid-dependent patient and acts as an anti-inflammatory adjunct in status asthmaticus. Diphenhydramine (Option A) is an antihistamine used for allergic reactions, and epinephrine (Option B) is the primary drug for anaphylaxis and acute bronchospasm but has no replacement role in adrenal insufficiency. Nitroglycerin (Option D) is a vasodilator used for ischemic cardiac pain.

emergencies-266.question: Following the occurrence of a medical emergency during a restorative procedure on tooth 47, which of the following documentation components is MOST critical for establishing the chronological timeline in the patient's record?
options: The manufacturer lot numbers, expiry dates, and handling records of all dental materials used.
The professional license numbers and clinical duties of all auxiliary personnel present in the clinic.
The cumulative lifetime radiation dosage and radiographic history of the patient.
The exact time of symptom onset, baseline and serial vital signs, and the specific timing of all interventions.
emergencies-266.explanation: Option D is correct because Canadian dental regulatory standards (e.g., RCDSO) require meticulous documentation of the exact time of symptom onset, serial vital signs (blood pressure, pulse, respirations, SpO2), and the chronological sequence of all interventions administered to establish an accurate clinical timeline. Material lot numbers (Option A) are tracked for product quality assurance but do not document emergency progression. Auxiliary license numbers (Option B) and radiographic histories (Option C) are administrative records that do not describe patient status during an acute medical crisis.

emergencies-269.question: An adult patient collapses and becomes unresponsive with no palpable pulse during an operative procedure on tooth 26. When applying an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) in the standard anterolateral configuration, where should the pads be positioned on the patient's bare chest?
options: One pad on the upper left chest below the clavicle, and the other pad on the lower right chest along the midaxillary line.
One pad on the upper right chest below the clavicle, and the other pad on the lower left chest along the midaxillary line.
Both pads placed vertically along the midline of the anterior sternum.
Both pads placed posteriorly over the left and right scapular regions.
emergencies-269.explanation: Option B is correct because the standard anterolateral AED pad placement for an adult patient requires placing one pad below the right clavicle (to the right of the sternum) and the second pad on the lower left chest wall (midaxillary line) to direct the electrical defibrillation current through the myocardium. Reversing this orientation (Option A) is non-standard and impedes optimal transthoracic current vectoring. Placing both pads directly on the sternum (Option C) risks arcing across bone and misses the cardiac mass, while placing both pads on the posterior scapulae (Option D) fails to direct current across the ventricles.

emergencies-270.question: A 10-year-old child presents to the dental office 15 minutes after traumatic avulsion of permanent tooth 11. The tooth was dropped on the ground and has visible debris on the root surface. What is the MOST appropriate initial management of the avulsed tooth prior to replantation?
options: Rinse the tooth gently under a stream of cold saline or milk for a maximum of 10 seconds while holding only the crown.
Scrub the root surface with a soft sterile gauze soaked in 0.12% chlorhexidine to mechanically remove contaminants.
Soak the tooth in 3% hydrogen peroxide for 5 minutes to decontaminate the root surface.
Immerse the tooth in Hank's Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS) and curette the contaminated cementum.
emergencies-270.explanation: Option A is correct because International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines recommend that an avulsed permanent tooth with short extraoral dry time (<60 minutes) should be handled strictly by the crown and gently rinsed with cold saline, milk, or HBSS for up to 10 seconds to flush debris while preserving viable periodontal ligament (PDL) cells. Scrubbing the root surface (Option B) mechanically strips viable PDL fibroblasts. Soaking in cytotoxic antiseptics like hydrogen peroxide (Option C) or curetting the root surface (Option D) kills the cementoblasts and PDL cells, leading to severe replacement root resorption (ankylosis).

emergencies-305.question: A 55-year-old male patient with poorly controlled hypertension presents for emergency extraction of symptomatic tooth 37. His blood pressure is measured at 205/115 mmHg. He reports an acute throbbing headache, blurred vision, and dizziness. What is the MOST appropriate management for this patient?
options: Administer a rapid-acting sublingual calcium channel blocker (e.g., nifedipine) to lower blood pressure before medical transport.
Administer sublingual nitroglycerin and proceed with the extraction using 3% mepivacaine plain.
Activate emergency medical services (EMS) immediately, position the patient comfortably semi-reclined, and monitor vital signs without administering antihypertensive medications.
Keep the patient seated in the clinic for 30 minutes, recheck blood pressure, and discharge him to drive to his primary care physician.
emergencies-305.explanation: Option C is correct because blood pressure > 180/110 mmHg with acute signs of target organ damage (severe headache, blurred vision) represents a hypertensive emergency requiring immediate EMS activation, patient positioning in a comfortable semi-reclined position, and close vital sign monitoring. Administering oral or sublingual antihypertensive agents like nifedipine (Option A) in the dental office is strictly contraindicated under Canadian guidelines because precipitous blood pressure drops can cause ischemic stroke or myocardial infarction. Proceeding with surgical extraction (Option B) poses severe cardiovascular risks, and discharging the patient unescorted (Option D) is medically unsafe.

emergencies-309.question: Following the emergency administration of intramuscular epinephrine for severe anaphylaxis during restorative treatment on tooth 14, which specific information regarding the pharmacotherapy MUST be meticulously documented in the patient's record?
options: The manufacturer expiry date, pharmacy acquisition invoice number, and commercial drug brand.
The formal written counter-signature of the attending EMS paramedic acknowledging the medication.
The storage temperature and inspection certification log of the emergency drug kit.
The exact drug dose, route, anatomical injection site, time administered, and patient clinical response.
emergencies-309.explanation: Option D is correct because Canadian dental regulatory standards (e.g., RCDSO) mandate that any emergency medication administration must be documented with the exact drug name, dosage, route of administration, anatomical site (e.g., anterolateral thigh), time of delivery, and the patient's resulting vital signs and clinical response. Commercial drug invoice details and brand names (Option A) are business inventory records rather than clinical chart entries. Paramedic countersignatures (Option B) are not legally required on dental charts, and storage temperature logs (Option C) belong in clinic facility maintenance documentation.

emergencies-404.question: A 65-year-old male with a history of stable angina and hypertension develops sudden, severe crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw during tooth preparation on tooth 16. The patient is conscious and diaphoretic, with a blood pressure of 140/85 mmHg and a pulse of 96 bpm. After stopping dental treatment and positioning the patient comfortably, what is the MOST appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention in the dental office?
options: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg)
Administer chewable acetylsalicylic acid (160–325 mg)
Administer oral diphenhydramine (50 mg)
Administer inhaled salbutamol (100 mcg per puff)
emergencies-404.explanation: Option A is correct because for a patient with a known history of stable angina experiencing acute chest pain, the immediate first-line chairside pharmacological intervention is sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) to alleviate myocardial ischemia via coronary and systemic vasodilation. Chewable acetylsalicylic acid (Option B) is indicated if pain is not relieved by nitroglycerin and acute myocardial infarction is suspected, but it is not the immediate initial medication administered for an acute anginal episode in a known angina patient. Oral diphenhydramine (Option C) is an antihistamine for mild allergic reactions with no cardiovascular utility, and inhaled salbutamol (Option D) is a beta-2 agonist for bronchospasm that causes tachycardia and increases myocardial oxygen demand.

emergencies-464.question: According to Canadian Dental Association (CDA) and provincial regulatory guidelines (e.g., RCDSO) for dental office emergency preparedness, which of the following medications is classified as a supplementary (advanced) drug rather than a mandatory core emergency medication?
options: Atropine sulfate
Epinephrine (1:1,000)
Nitroglycerin sublingual spray (0.4 mg/metered dose)
Chewable acetylsalicylic acid (81–325 mg)
emergencies-464.explanation: Option A is correct because according to Canadian dental emergency standards (CDA/RCDSO), atropine sulfate is an advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) medication and is categorized as a supplementary/non-core drug in a standard dental practice. Epinephrine (Option B), nitroglycerin (Option C), and chewable acetylsalicylic acid (Option D) are all mandatory core emergency medications that must be immediately accessible in every Canadian dental practice to manage life-threatening anaphylaxis, acute angina, and acute coronary syndromes. Non-core drugs require advanced training, monitoring, and intravenous access that are not standard requirements for basic general dental emergency kits.

operative-dentistry-98.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents for the replacement of a defective composite restoration on tooth 16. During rubber dam isolation, the rubber dam sheet tears repeatedly around the cervical area as it is stretched over the molar clamp and tooth. Which of the following is the most appropriate clinical modification to prevent tearing?
options: Switch from a wingless clamp to a winged clamp
Invert the rubber dam margin into the gingival sulcus using an explorer
Apply a water-soluble lubricant to the tissue-facing surface of the rubber dam sheet
Select a smaller punch hole size on the rubber dam punch plate
operative-dentistry-98.explanation: Option C is correct because applying a water-soluble lubricant to the tissue-facing surface of the rubber dam sheet significantly reduces frictional resistance as the dam passes over clamp jaws and tight proximal contacts, effectively preventing tearing. Using a winged clamp (Option A) increases mechanical interference and tensile stress around the hole, whereas inverting the margin (Option B) is performed after dam placement to achieve a moisture seal rather than preventing tears during isolation. Selecting a smaller punch hole size (Option D) increases tensile strain on the elastomer as it stretches over a molar crown, greatly exacerbating the risk of material tearing.

operative-dentistry-108.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with a deep amalgam restoration on tooth 36. She reports severe, sharp pain to cold stimuli that lingers for more than 30 seconds after the stimulus is removed. Clinical examination reveals no visible recurrent caries, no tooth mobility, and normal periodontal probing depths. Percussion and palpation are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate definitive management for tooth 36?
options: Apply a topical desensitizing agent along the cervical margin and re-evaluate in 6 months
Remove the amalgam restoration, place an indirect pulp cap with a resin-modified glass ionomer base, and place a new restoration
Prescribe a 7-day course of systemic amoxicillin and re-evaluate pulpal symptoms
Initiate therapeutic non-surgical endodontic treatment
operative-dentistry-108.explanation: Option D is correct because thermal pain lingering for more than 30 seconds after stimulus removal is the pathognomonic diagnostic criterion for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, which necessitates therapeutic non-surgical endodontic treatment (or extraction). Desensitizing agents (Option A) only manage dentin hypersensitivity without pulpal inflammation and are completely ineffective for irreversible pulpitis. Restorative replacement or indirect pulp capping (Option B) is contraindicated because inflamed pulpal tissue in symptomatic irreversible pulpitis cannot predictably heal without complete pulpectomy. Systemic antibiotics (Option C) have no efficacy in treating localized pulpal inflammation in the absence of spreading infection and violate Canadian antibiotic stewardship guidelines.

operative-dentistry-111.question: During the restoration of a deep Class II cavity on tooth 46 using a conventional resin composite, what is the primary purpose of placing and light-curing the material in oblique increments of 2 mm or less?
options: To completely eliminate polymerization shrinkage of the composite resin matrix
To prevent monomer conversion at the cavosurface margins
To reduce the cavity configuration factor (C-factor) and minimize polymerization shrinkage stress
To increase the inorganic filler particle fraction within the deepest resin layer
