Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
operative-dentistry-276816295.explanation: Option C is correct because spontaneous nocturnal pain combined with an exaggerated, lingering thermal cold response lasting greater than 30 seconds on a vital tooth are the definitive diagnostic criteria for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis under AAE and NDEB standards. Option A is incorrect because a normal pulp produces only transient cold sensation that dissipates within seconds. Option B is incorrect because reversible pulpitis features non-lingering provoked sensitivity without spontaneous pain, while Option D is incorrect because a necrotic pulp is completely non-responsive to thermal and electric pulp testing.

operative-dentistry-402422667.question: A 24-year-old male patient presents with a deep carious lesion on the distal surface of tooth 36 extending into the inner third of dentin. The tooth is asymptomatic, tests vital, and exhibits no periapical pathology. During selective caries excavation, a small zone of softened, discolored dentin remains over the pulp chamber that, if removed, would result in mechanical pulpal exposure. What is the MOST appropriate next step in management?
options: Excavate all softened dentin until hard dentin is reached, accepting mechanical pulp exposure
Place a hydraulic calcium silicate bioceramic liner over the remaining dentin followed by a definitive adhesive restoration
Perform immediate non-surgical root canal treatment on tooth 36
Place a temporary zinc oxide-eugenol sedative restoration and re-enter the cavity in 6 months
operative-dentistry-402422667.explanation: Option B is correct because indirect pulp therapy using selective caries removal and placement of a bioactive hydraulic calcium silicate material (bioceramic) under an airtight adhesive restoration maximizes pulp vitality and avoids unnecessary mechanical exposure. Option A is incorrect because complete excavation to hard dentin that results in pulp exposure drastically decreases long-term pulpal prognosis. Options C and D are incorrect because complete endodontic therapy is overtreatment for a vital, symptom-free pulp, and traditional stepwise re-entry carries a high risk of iatrogenic pulp exposure without therapeutic benefit.

operative-dentistry-267645055.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with an occlusal (Class I) carious lesion involving the outer two-thirds of dentin in tooth 16. The patient has severe nocturnal bruxism, heavy occlusal forces, and a high caries risk. Which restorative material and preparation design is MOST appropriate to ensure long-term wear resistance and marginal integrity?
options: Dental amalgam placed in a cavity preparation with 90-degree cavosurface margins and adequate bulk depth
Composite resin placed with an incremental layering technique and minimal interproximal reduction
Conventional glass ionomer cement placed in a single bulk increment without surface resin glaze
Direct composite resin placed with deep mechanical undercut grooves extending into axial dentin
operative-dentistry-267645055.explanation: Option A is correct because dental amalgam provides superior wear resistance under severe bruxing forces, requires a 90-degree cavosurface margin for edge strength, and its corrosion products provide self-sealing margins that resist recurrent decay in high-caries-risk patients. Option B is incorrect because Class I preparations do not involve interproximal reduction, and composite resin exhibits accelerated occlusal wear and marginal degradation under heavy bruxism. Options C and D are incorrect because conventional glass ionomer lacks sufficient flexural strength for load-bearing posterior occlusal stress, and deep mechanical undercuts unnecessarily sacrifice healthy dentin without improving composite adhesion.

prosthodontics-11.question: A 62-year-old male presents for the fabrication of a new maxillary complete denture. Clinical examination reveals redundant, mobile, hyperplastic tissue folds in the anterior maxillary vestibule corresponding to the overextended labial flange of his ill-fitting existing denture (epulis fissuratum). What is the MOST appropriate initial management prior to definitive impression making?
options: Immediate surgical excision of the hyperplastic tissue folds before modifying the denture
Border molding and making a definitive secondary impression with high-viscosity elastomeric material
Immediate fabrication of an implant-supported overdenture over the mobile hyperplastic folds
Relief of the overextended denture flange and relining with a resilient tissue conditioner
prosthodontics-11.explanation: Option D is correct because the standard initial management of epulis fissuratum is conservative therapy: reducing the overextended flange and relining with a soft, resilient tissue conditioner to resolve traumatic ulceration and tissue edema prior to reassessing the need for surgical excision. Option A is incorrect because premature surgical excision often leads to unnecessary loss of vestibular depth and scarring that could be avoided once inflammatory edema subsides. Options B and C are incorrect because recording impressions or fabricating prostheses over inflamed, hyperplastic tissue captures distorted anatomy and results in an unstable, unretentive definitive denture.

prosthodontics-13.question: A 55-year-old female patient is having a porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown fitted on tooth 46. At the try-in appointment, light contacts are verified in centric occlusion, but a premature contact (non-working interference) is detected during mediotrusive excursion. What is the MOST appropriate clinical adjustment to eliminate this interference while preserving centric occlusion?
options: Reduce the centric holding cusp tip of the opposing maxillary molar
Adjust the inner incline of the mandibular buccal cusp on the crown of tooth 46
Adjust the inner incline of the mandibular lingual cusp on the crown of tooth 46
Adjust the outer incline of the mandibular buccal cusp on the crown of tooth 46
prosthodontics-13.explanation: Option B is correct because non-working (mediotrusive) interferences occur between the inner inclines of maxillary lingual cusps and mandibular buccal cusps; adjusting the inner incline of the mandibular buccal cusp on the crown eliminates the interference while preserving the patient's opposing natural tooth structure and maintaining centric stops. Option A is incorrect because grinding the centric holding cusp tip destroys essential contacts in maximum intercuspation. Options C and D are incorrect because the mandibular lingual cusp does not participate in non-working movements, and the outer incline of the mandibular buccal cusp is involved in working-side (laterotrusive) rather than non-working excursions.

prosthodontics-14.question: A mandibular removable partial denture is being planned for a patient with Kennedy Class I edentulism. The patient has healthy periodontal support on all remaining teeth and a vertical distance of 12 mm from the active floor of the mouth to the free gingival margins. Which mandibular major connector is the MOST appropriate choice for this patient?
options: Lingual bar
Lingual plate
Sublingual bar
Labial bar
prosthodontics-14.explanation: Option A is correct because a lingual bar is the simplest, most hygienic, and preferred mandibular major connector when there is at least 7 to 8 mm of vertical clearance (12 mm available here) and the remaining anterior teeth have sound periodontal support. Option B (lingual plate) is contraindicated when ample vertical space exists because its unnecessary coverage of gingival margins and tooth structure increases plaque accumulation, gingival inflammation, and caries risk. Options C and D are incorrect because a sublingual bar is reserved for patients with limited vertical space (<6 mm) or high lingual frenal attachments, and a labial bar is indicated only in rare instances of severe lingual tori or pronounced lingual inclination of remaining teeth.

prosthodontics-22.question: A 55-year-old female patient is having a porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown permanently cemented on tooth 46. Marginal adaptation and occlusion have been clinically and radiographically verified. Which of the following luting agents provides the greatest resistance to microleakage and secondary caries through chemical adhesion to tooth structure and sustained fluoride release?
options: Zinc phosphate cement
Resin-modified glass ionomer cement
Zinc polycarboxylate cement
Zinc oxide-eugenol temporary cement
prosthodontics-22.explanation: Option B is correct because resin-modified glass ionomer cement (RMGI) combines chemical ionic bonding to dentin and enamel calcium with low solubility, high compressive strength, and continuous fluoride release, providing superior long-term resistance to microleakage and secondary caries. Option A is incorrect because zinc phosphate relies entirely on mechanical interlocking without chemical adhesion or fluoride release. Options C and D are incorrect because zinc polycarboxylate has low compressive strength and higher solubility, while zinc oxide-eugenol lacks the mechanical properties for permanent crown luting and releases no cariostatic fluoride.

prosthodontics-39.question: A 58-year-old female presents two days after the cementation of a metal-ceramic crown on tooth 16. She reports severe pain upon biting and thermal sensitivity to cold that lingers for more than 15 seconds after stimulus removal. Clinical examination reveals normal periodontal probing depths, negative percussion, and pain on biting with a Tooth Slooth. Pulp vitality testing with cold confirms a heightened, lingering response compared to the contralateral control tooth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Primary occlusal trauma without pulpal involvement
Reversible pulpitis secondary to procedural trauma
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis secondary to procedural trauma
Cement washout leading to acute microleakage
prosthodontics-39.explanation: Option C is correct because sharp pain with prolonged lingering cold sensitivity (>15 seconds) is the definitive clinical indicator of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, indicating irreversible inflammatory damage requiring endodontic therapy. Reversible pulpitis produces transient sensitivity that subsides immediately upon stimulus removal, while occlusal trauma primarily causes tenderness to biting and percussion without prolonged thermal hypersensitivity. Cement washout or microleakage would not cause acute pulpal necrosis or lingering pulpitis within two days of cementation.

prosthodontics-41.question: A patient requires a post and core for endodontically treated tooth 11 to support an all-ceramic crown. Which of the following post systems provides the most favorable stress distribution to the remaining root structure by closely matching the modulus of elasticity of dentin?
options: Titanium threaded active post
Fiber-reinforced resin composite post
Stainless steel parallel-sided serrated post
Cast gold custom post and core
prosthodontics-41.explanation: Option B is correct because fiber-reinforced resin composite posts possess an elastic modulus (~18–20 GPa) very similar to human dentin (~18 GPa), which allows uniform stress distribution and significantly reduces the risk of non-restorable vertical root fracture. Metallic posts (cast gold, stainless steel, and titanium) possess much higher moduli of elasticity (100–200 GPa), concentrating stresses at the post apex and drastically increasing the likelihood of catastrophic root fracture. Active threaded posts (Option A) generate high insertion stresses and are contraindicated in modern restorative dentistry.

prosthodontics-42.question: During the evaluation of a fixed dental prosthesis replacing missing tooth 16, the dentist assesses abutment teeth 15 and 17. According to Ante's Law, what is the requirement regarding the periodontal root surface area of the abutment teeth?
options: The combined pericemental root surface area of the abutment teeth should equal or exceed that of the tooth or teeth to be replaced.
The pericemental root surface area of each individual abutment must equal that of the missing tooth.
The combined root surface area of the abutment teeth must be less than that of the pontic.
The root surface area is clinically irrelevant provided the crown-to-root ratio is at least 1:1.
prosthodontics-42.explanation: Option A is correct because Ante's Law states that the total pericemental root surface area of the abutment teeth should equal or exceed the pericemental surface area of the tooth or teeth being replaced. Individual abutments do not need to match the pontic independently (Option B), but their combined surface area provides the periodontal support necessary to resist functional occlusal loads. Crown-to-root ratio alone does not supersede total root surface area requirements for multi-unit fixed prostheses (Option D).

prosthodontics-48.question: A 55-year-old female patient receives a porcelain-fused-to-metal crown on tooth 16. Two weeks later, she returns complaining of discomfort when biting down on the crown and mild cold sensitivity that subsides immediately upon removal of the stimulus. There is no spontaneous pain. Percussion testing produces mild tenderness on tooth 16, whereas palpation and periodontal probings are within normal limits. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
options: Occlusal interference causing hyperocclusion
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Inadequate marginal seal causing periodontal breakdown
Cement washout leading to acute microleakage
prosthodontics-48.explanation: Option A is correct because pain on biting down combined with mild, non-lingering thermal sensitivity and mild percussion sensitivity shortly after crown cementation is characteristic of hyperocclusion from an occlusal interference. Irreversible pulpitis (Option B) is characterized by spontaneous, lingering pain (>15 seconds) to thermal stimuli. Inadequate marginal seal (Option C) and cement washout (Option D) typically cause recurrent caries or chronic microleakage over months to years rather than acute localized bite discomfort two weeks post-placement.

prosthodontics-49.question: Which of the following maxillary major connectors provides the greatest structural rigidity through an L-beam effect and is considered the first choice for most maxillary removable partial dentures when anterior and posterior abutments are present?
options: Single palatal strap
Anterior-posterior palatal strap
U-shaped palatal connector
Complete palatal plate
prosthodontics-49.explanation: Option B is correct because the anterior-posterior palatal strap provides the greatest structural rigidity due to its components lying in different anatomical planes (the L-beam effect), making it the primary choice for most maxillary removable partial dentures. A single palatal strap (Option A) is indicated primarily for tooth-borne Class III arches with narrow edentulous spans. The U-shaped connector (Option C) lacks rigidity and flexes under load, while a complete palatal plate (Option D) is reserved for extensively compromised dentitions requiring maximal mucosal support rather than being a routine first choice.

prosthodontics-79.question: Which of the following luting agents forms a true chemical bond to tooth structure through chelation of polyacrylic acid carboxyl groups with calcium ions in hydroxyapatite?
options: Zinc phosphate cement
Zinc oxide-eugenol cement
Conventional composite resin cement
Glass ionomer cement
prosthodontics-79.explanation: Option D is correct because glass ionomer cement achieves true chemical adhesion to enamel and dentin through the chelation of its polyacrylic acid carboxyl groups with calcium ions in the hydroxyapatite crystal lattice. Zinc phosphate cement (Option A) and zinc oxide-eugenol cement (Option B) rely strictly on micromechanical interlocking and lack any chemical adhesion to tooth structure. Conventional resin cements (Option C) achieve retention through micromechanical bonding to etched tooth surfaces via an adhesive hybrid layer rather than ionic chelation.

prosthodontics-84.question: A 70-year-old female presents for evaluation to replace missing teeth 14 and 15 with a fixed dental prosthesis using teeth 13 and 16 as abutments. Which biomechanical rule dictates that the total pericemental root surface area of teeth 13 and 16 must equal or exceed that of the teeth being replaced?
options: Posselt's envelope of motion
Curve of Spee
Ante's Law
Bonwill's triangle
prosthodontics-84.explanation: Option C is correct because Ante's Law dictates that the combined pericemental root surface area of the abutment teeth (teeth 13 and 16) must be equal to or greater than the pericemental root surface area of the teeth being replaced (teeth 14 and 15). Posselt's envelope of motion (Option A) illustrates the border movements of the mandible in three planes. The Curve of Spee (Option B) describes the anteroposterior curvature of the occlusal surfaces, and Bonwill's triangle (Option D) is an equilateral 4-inch triangle formed between the condyles and the mandibular incisal contact point.

prosthodontics-87.question: When designing a distal extension removable partial denture using the RPI (rest, proximal plate, I-bar) clasp assembly, what is the primary mechanical purpose of placing the occlusal rest on the mesial surface of the abutment tooth?
options: To direct forces along the long axis of the tooth and allow the I-bar to disengage under occlusal loading
To act as an indirect retainer anterior to the primary fulcrum line
To convert the prosthesis into a Class I lever system to increase retention
To eliminate the need for a major connector across the dental arch
prosthodontics-87.explanation: Option A is correct because placing the rest on the mesial surface of the abutment tooth directs masticatory forces along the long axis of the tooth and shifts the fulcrum anteriorly so that the I-bar and proximal plate move downward and forward, disengaging from the tooth under occlusal load to prevent harmful torquing forces. The mesial rest forms the primary fulcrum line itself and cannot serve as an indirect retainer (Option B). The RPI system prevents a Class I lever rather than creating one (Option C), and a rigid major connector is still required to provide cross-arch stabilization (Option D).

prosthodontics-88.question: A 55-year-old female patient requires a single crown on tooth 16. Preparation guidelines for an all-ceramic lithium disilicate crown require a minimum occlusal reduction of how many millimeters to ensure structural integrity?
options: 1.0 mm
1.5 mm
2.5 mm
3.0 mm
prosthodontics-88.explanation: Option B is correct because the recommended minimum occlusal reduction for an all-ceramic lithium disilicate crown is 1.5 mm to ensure adequate bulk thickness and prevent ceramic fracture under functional occlusal loads. An occlusal reduction of 1.0 mm (Option A) provides insufficient ceramic bulk and significantly elevates the risk of crown fracture. Reductions of 2.5 mm or 3.0 mm (Options C and D) remove excessive sound tooth structure, compromising retention and risking irreversible pulpal injury.

prosthodontics-91.question: During the fabrication of a complete denture, what is the primary purpose of properly contouring the polished surfaces of the mandibular denture to have concave external contours?
options: To prevent food debris from entering the buccal vestibule
To maximize the surface area for salivary adhesion
To allow the surrounding musculature of the cheeks and tongue to aid in denture retention and stability
To increase the total acrylic mass for gravitational retention
prosthodontics-91.explanation: Option C is correct because contouring the buccal and lingual polished surfaces of a mandibular complete denture with concave inclinations allows the buccinator muscle and the lateral borders of the tongue to seat the denture downward onto the basal seat during functional movements, enhancing retention and stability. While proper contours help manage the food bolus, preventing food impaction (Option A) is secondary to neuromuscular stabilization. Salivary adhesion (Option B) is primarily governed by intimate adaptation of the intaglio surface, and modern prosthodontic principles do not rely on adding acrylic weight for gravitational retention (Option D).

prosthodontics-92.question: A 48-year-old male presents with a fractured porcelain-fused-to-metal crown on tooth 21. The metal substructure is intact and clinically visible in an aesthetic area. What is the most appropriate immediate chairside approach to repair this defect?
options: Microetching with alumina, application of a metal primer and silane, and direct bonding with composite resin
Complete removal of the crown and immediate fabrication of a new all-ceramic crown
Etching with 37% phosphoric acid and direct placement of flowable composite resin
Extraction of the tooth followed by immediate implant placement
prosthodontics-92.explanation: Option A is correct because immediate chairside intraoral repair of exposed metal substructure involves microetching with aluminum oxide particles to create micromechanical retention, applying a metal primer (e.g., 10-MDP) and silane to promote chemical adhesion, and restoring the defect with composite resin. Complete crown removal and remanufacture (Option B) is not an immediate chairside repair technique. Phosphoric acid (Option C) cleans the surface but cannot etch metal or porcelain, and extraction (Option D) is completely unjustified for a restorable tooth with an intact substructure.

prosthodontics-97.question: A patient receives a porcelain-fused-to-metal crown on tooth 36. During the crown evaluation prior to final cementation, the dentist checks the eccentric occlusion and detects a heavy contact on the non-working (mediotrusive) side. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Apply a desensitizing agent to the tooth and re-evaluate in 2 weeks
Selectively grind the opposing natural tooth cusps to eliminate the contact
Remake the crown entirely with a reduced occlusal table
Adjust the porcelain of the crown until the non-working contact is completely eliminated
prosthodontics-97.explanation: Option D is correct because non-working (mediotrusive) contacts generate destructive oblique forces that cause mechanical and biological complications; therefore, any interference must be adjusted directly on the artificial restoration before final cementation. Applying desensitizer (Option A) fails to eliminate the damaging mechanical interference. Modifying healthy opposing natural tooth structure (Option B) violates conservative dental principles when the crown itself is causing the prematurity. Remaking the crown (Option C) is unnecessary when the interference can be quickly and effectively eliminated by chairside occlusal adjustment.

prosthodontics-24.question: A patient requires a full-coverage crown preparation on tooth 16. To ensure adequate resistance form for the preparation, which of the following geometric features is MOST critical?
options: Maximizing surface area through deep occlusal reduction regardless of axial wall length
Creating a heavy chamfer finish line with an unsupported 90-degree cavosurface angle
Increasing total occlusal convergence to at least 20 degrees to eliminate all undercuts
Providing adequate height and minimizing convergence taper of the axial walls
prosthodontics-24.explanation: Option D is correct because resistance form against dislodging tipping forces is primarily governed by maintaining adequate axial wall height (at least 3-4 mm in molars) and minimal total occlusal convergence taper (ideally 6 to 10 degrees). Deep occlusal reduction (Option A) compromises resistance by shortening axial walls, while excessive convergence taper (Option C) dramatically reduces resistance to rotation under lateral forces. Finish line configuration (Option B) establishes marginal integrity and bulk of restorative material rather than primary preparation resistance form.

operative-dentistry-298966122.question: A 65-year-old male patient requires routine extraction of a non-restorable tooth 37. His medical history includes non-valvular atrial fibrillation treated with dabigatran 150 mg twice daily, and coronary artery disease treated with daily aspirin 81 mg. According to Canadian consensus guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate management of his antithrombotic therapy prior to the extraction?
options: Discontinue both dabigatran and aspirin 7 days prior to extraction to normalize hemostasis.
Continue dabigatran and aspirin without interruption, and manage post-extraction bleeding using local hemostatic measures.
Discontinue dabigatran 48 hours prior to extraction and bridge with low-molecular-weight heparin.
Withhold aspirin for 5 days prior to extraction while continuing dabigatran as scheduled.
operative-dentistry-298966122.explanation: Option B is correct because consensus guidelines from the Canadian Dental Association (CDA) and Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) recommend continuing direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs like dabigatran) and antiplatelet agents (aspirin) without interruption for minor dental extractions, managing bleeding with local hemostatic measures such as gelatin sponges, sutures, and tranexamic acid mouthwashes. Interruption or heparin bridging (Options A and C) significantly increases the risk of fatal thromboembolic events without providing a clinical benefit in minor oral surgery. Stopping aspirin alone (Option D) is unindicated without medical consultation and does not significantly reduce intraoperative bleeding risk.

operative-dentistry-499645845.question: An 8-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic 30 minutes after completely avulsing tooth 11 during a playground fall. The tooth was recovered immediately, rinsed briefly with cold water, and transported in cold milk. Radiographs show an immature root with a wide open apex and no alveolar fracture. According to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate clinical management?
options: Replant the tooth immediately, place a flexible splint for up to 2 weeks, and monitor closely for pulp revascularization without prophylactic pulpectomy.
Replant the tooth immediately, place a rigid splint for 6 weeks, and initiate root canal therapy within 7 to 10 days.
Scrape the root surface with a curette to remove debris, soak the tooth in chlorhexidine, replant, and perform immediate pulpectomy.
Advise against replantation due to high risk of ankylosis, and plan for an immediate removable space maintainer.
operative-dentistry-499645845.explanation: Option A is correct because according to IADT guidelines recognized by Canadian dental authorities, an avulsed immature permanent tooth with an open apex and short extraoral dry time (< 60 minutes) has high potential for spontaneous pulp revascularization and should be replanted immediately, stabilized with a flexible splint for up to 2 weeks, and monitored without elective pulpectomy. Prophylactic pulpectomy within 7-10 days (Option B) is indicated only for mature teeth with closed apices, and rigid splinting for 6 weeks promotes dentoalveolar ankylosis. Mechanical scraping of the root (Option C) destroys viable periodontal ligament cells, and discarding the tooth (Option D) is premature and clinically inappropriate.

operative-dentistry-570184664.question: A 30-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of dark grey intrinsic discoloration of tooth 11 following trauma 10 years ago and root canal treatment 5 years ago. Clinical examination reveals intact coronal tooth structure, and radiographic examination shows a well-condensed obturation with healthy periapical tissues. What is the MOST appropriate initial conservative treatment to address this discoloration?
options: Fabrication and placement of a full-coverage all-ceramic crown
Preparation and placement of a direct composite resin veneer
External at-home tray bleaching using 10% carbamide peroxide alone
Internal bleaching (walking bleach) using sodium perborate and sterile water after placing a 2 mm cervical barrier
operative-dentistry-570184664.explanation: Option D is correct because the walking bleach technique using sodium perborate mixed with sterile water (or saline), protected by a 2 mm cervical barrier placed at the cementoenamel junction to prevent invasive cervical resorption, is the gold-standard conservative initial treatment for an endodontically treated anterior tooth with intact coronal structure. Full-coverage crowns (Option A) and facial composite veneers (Option B) involve invasive preparation and unnecessary loss of healthy tooth structure. External tray bleaching alone (Option C) cannot predictably penetrate through the pulp chamber to eliminate dense internal endodontic discolouration.

operative-dentistry-941613092.question: A dental healthcare worker sustains an accidental puncture injury to the finger from a contaminated local anesthetic needle following a dental procedure. According to Canadian dental infection prevention and control (IPAC) guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate immediate action at the exposure site?
options: Wash the wound immediately and thoroughly with liquid soap and water without squeezing or expressing blood, and report promptly for post-exposure medical assessment.
Vigorously squeeze and express blood from the puncture wound, cleanse with concentrated sodium hypochlorite, and continue clinical duties.
Immerse the affected finger in 70% isopropyl alcohol for 10 minutes and apply a topical antibiotic ointment before reporting.
Send the contaminated needle to an external microbiology laboratory for viral culture prior to cleaning the wound.
operative-dentistry-941613092.explanation: Option A is correct because Canadian IPAC guidelines mandate immediately washing percutaneous puncture wounds thoroughly with liquid soap and water and reporting the exposure without delay to initiate risk assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Squeezing or expressing the wound (Option B) is explicitly contraindicated as it causes localized tissue trauma and increases the risk of microbial inoculate spread. Alcohol soaks or caustic agents like bleach (Options B and C) cause cellular damage without reducing viral transmission, while sending contaminated needles for culturing (Option D) is clinically useless, poses needle-handling hazards, and is strictly prohibited.

operative-dentistry-408248071.question: A 12-year-old male presents to the clinic 2 hours after sustaining a sports-related impact to tooth 11. Clinical examination reveals an enamel-dentin fracture with a pinpoint pulp exposure (< 1 mm) that bleeds brightly and no mobility. Radiographic examination reveals an immature root with a wide open apex and no root fracture. What is the MOST appropriate pulpal therapy for tooth 11?
options: Complete pulpectomy followed by immediate single-visit gutta-percha obturation
Direct pulp capping with calcium hydroxide covered by an unbonded temporary crown
Partial pulpotomy (Cvek pulpotomy) using mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) and a bonded coronal restoration
Complete coronal pulpotomy using formocresol and zinc oxide-eugenol cement
operative-dentistry-408248071.explanation: Option C is correct because for a vital immature permanent tooth with an open apex and small traumatic pulp exposure, a partial pulpotomy (Cvek technique) using mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) removes only the superficial inflamed tissue (1-2 mm) while preserving healthy radicular pulp tissue to enable apexogenesis. Complete pulpectomy with gutta-percha obturation (Option A) arrests root development and is impossible to condense properly against an open divergent apex. Direct pulp capping (Option B) has a lower clinical success rate than partial pulpotomy in traumatic exposures due to superficial bacterial contamination. Formocresol pulpotomy (Option D) is cytotoxic, devitalizing, and obsolete in permanent teeth.

operative-dentistry-196779280.question: A 48-year-old female presents with a fractured tooth 36. Clinical examination reveals a preexisting, extensive MOD amalgam restoration with a fracture of the functional distolingual cusp extending slightly below the free gingival margin. The tooth is asymptomatic, responds normally to vitality testing, and displays no periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST appropriate definitive restorative management?
options: Full-coverage crown designed with a minimum 1.5 to 2.0 mm circumferential ferrule
Direct multi-surface composite resin restoration without cuspal coverage
Complex pin-retained amalgam restoration without full occlusal protection
Long-term provisional restoration with reinforced zinc oxide-eugenol cement
operative-dentistry-196779280.explanation: Option A is correct because an endodontically vital mandibular molar with an extensive MOD restoration and loss of a functional supporting cusp subjected to heavy masticatory forces requires a full-coverage crown with a minimum 1.5 to 2.0 mm ferrule to provide structural resistance form and prevent catastrophic longitudinal fracture. Direct resin restoration without cuspal reduction (Option B) leaves undermined remaining cusps vulnerable to biomechanical flexure and fracture. Pin-retained amalgams without cuspal protection (Option C) generate internal dentinal stress lines and carry high failure rates. Long-term temporary cementation (Option D) fails to provide structural stability and invites marginal microleakage and recurrent decay.

operative-dentistry-843211725.question: A 35-year-old male presents with localized gingival recession on tooth 13. Clinical examination reveals 3 mm of buccal marginal tissue recession extending to the mucogingival junction, complete absence of attached gingiva, and no loss of interdental bone or clinical attachment. The patient maintains excellent oral hygiene. What is the MOST appropriate surgical management to achieve root coverage and augment keratinized tissue?
options: Free gingival graft placed apical to the recession defect without root coverage
Subepithelial connective tissue graft combined with a coronally advanced flap
Gingivectomy and external bevel excision to level the marginal gingiva
Application of topical desensitizing varnish and continued observational monitoring
operative-dentistry-843211725.explanation: Option B is correct because a subepithelial connective tissue graft (SCTG) combined with a coronally advanced flap represents the gold-standard surgical therapy for Cairo RT1 (Miller Class I/II) recession defects lacking attached gingiva, providing the highest predictability for complete root coverage and aesthetic augmentation of keratinized tissue. A free gingival graft placed apically (Option A) augments attached gingiva but yields poor aesthetic color matching and fails to cover the denuded root. Gingivectomy (Option C) is contraindicated because it excises existing keratinized tissue and exacerbates recession. Topical varnish and monitoring alone (Option D) does not address the progressive mucogingival defect or lack of attached tissue.

operative-dentistry-478080227.question: A 50-year-old male presents with an acute odontogenic infection and diffuse facial swelling originating from a non-vital tooth 27 with an acute apical abscess. The patient has a confirmed medical history of IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to penicillin. In addition to urgent surgical intervention (incision, drainage, and debridement), which systemic oral antibiotic is MOST appropriate to prescribe according to Canadian dental guidelines?
options: Azithromycin
Amoxicillin
Cephalexin
Clindamycin
operative-dentistry-478080227.explanation: Option A is correct because according to Health Canada and Canadian dental regulatory guidelines (including RCDSO and CDA), azithromycin is the recommended first-line oral antibiotic for spreading odontogenic infections in patients with true IgE-mediated anaphylactic penicillin allergy. Amoxicillin (Option B) is strictly contraindicated due to the verified history of anaphylaxis. Cephalexin (Option C) carries cross-reactivity risks with beta-lactams and is contraindicated in patients with severe immediate-type penicillin hypersensitivity. Clindamycin (Option D) has been removed from standard Canadian dental guidelines due to its strong association with severe and potentially fatal Clostridioides difficile colitis.

prosthodontics-27.question: When selecting maxillary anterior denture teeth for a completely edentulous patient, which anatomical facial landmark is most reliable for approximating the combined mesiodistal width of the two maxillary central incisors?
options: The distance between the corners of the mouth at rest
The interpupillary distance
The width of the philtrum of the upper lip
The ala-tragus line (Camper's line)
prosthodontics-27.explanation: Option C is correct because the width of the philtrum of the upper lip closely correlates with the combined mesiodistal width of the two maxillary central incisors. The distance between the corners of the mouth at rest (Option A) corresponds to the distal surfaces of the maxillary canines and estimates the total combined width of all six anterior teeth. The interpupillary distance (Option B) and the ala-tragus line (Option D) are craniofacial orientation planes used to align the horizontal incisal plane and posterior occlusal plane, respectively, rather than anterior tooth mold dimensions.

prosthodontics-32.question: A patient is scheduled for surgical crown lengthening on tooth 15 prior to fabrication of a full-coverage crown. To respect the supracrestal tissue attachment (biologic width) and prevent chronic periodontal inflammation, what is the MINIMUM vertical distance required from the proposed restorative margin to the alveolar crest?
options: 2.0 mm
3.0 mm
1.0 mm
0.5 mm
prosthodontics-32.explanation: Option B is correct because a minimum vertical distance of 3.0 mm between the proposed restorative margin and the alveolar bone crest is required to accommodate the supracrestal tissue attachment (approximately 1.0 mm of connective tissue attachment and 1.0 mm of junctional epithelium) plus a 1.0 mm healthy gingival sulcus. Providing only 2.0 mm or less (Options A, C, and D) encroaches upon the biologic width, inevitably resulting in chronic gingival inflammation, localized pocketing, or uncontrolled crestal bone resorption.

prosthodontics-38.question: When designing a cast removable partial denture (RPD) for a Kennedy Class II mandibular arch with a tooth-bounded modification space, which of the following clasp designs is indicated to provide direct retention on the premolar abutment adjacent to the modification space?
options: A cast circumferential (Akers) clasp engaging an undercut in the middle third directed toward the edentulous space
An I-bar retainer crossing the gingival margin to engage a 0.030-inch undercut located in the occlusal third
A cast circumferential (Akers) clasp engaging a 0.010-inch undercut in the cervical third directed away from the edentulous space
A continuous lingual bar acting as an active direct retainer on the lingual cingula
prosthodontics-38.explanation: Option C is correct because on a tooth-bounded abutment adjacent to a modification space, a standard cast circumferential (Akers) clasp originates from the occlusal rest and minor connector adjacent to the edentulous space and traverses the tooth to terminate its flexible retentive tip in a 0.010-inch undercut in the cervical third, pointing away from the rest. Engaging an undercut in the middle third facing the edentulous space (Option A) is biomechanically invalid and causes clasp distortion. An I-bar clasp (Option B) engages a 0.010-inch undercut in the cervical third rather than a 0.030-inch undercut in the occlusal third. A continuous lingual bar (Option D) functions as a major connector or indirect retainer, not a direct retainer.

prosthodontics-99.question: A 58-year-old female patient requires a single crown on tooth 14. Clinical evaluation of the preparation reveals a total occlusal convergence of 20 degrees, an axial wall height of 2 mm, and a chamfer finish line. Which factor is most critically compromising the retention and resistance form of this restoration?
options: The selection of a chamfer finish line
The choice of definitive luting cement
The combination of inadequate axial height and excessive convergence angle
The location of the tooth within the maxillary arch
prosthodontics-99.explanation: Option C is correct because an axial wall height of only 2 mm paired with an excessive total occlusal convergence of 20 degrees severely shortens the preparation's limiting dimension and arc of displacement, critically compromising retention and resistance form. A chamfer finish line (Option A) provides adequate marginal integrity and bulk for ceramic or metal crowns and does not compromise retention. While luting cement properties (Option B) aid retention, cementation cannot compensate for fundamentally inadequate preparation geometry. Tooth position in the arch (Option D) does not alter the physical laws of retention and resistance.

prosthodontics-101.question: What is the primary purpose of incorporating beading along the borders of a maxillary major connector, such as a palatal strap, on the master cast?
options: To establish an intimate tissue seal that prevents food particles from collecting beneath the connector
To provide relief over the hard median palatal raphe during functional loading
To act as a primary stress-breaker for distal extension denture bases
To provide mechanical retention for the attachment of acrylic denture base resin
prosthodontics-101.explanation: Option A is correct because beading produces a slightly elevated, smooth border on the tissue surface of the casting that gently indents the resilient palatal soft tissues, creating an intimate seal that prevents food impaction beneath the major connector. Relief (Option B) is deliberately avoided under maxillary major connectors unless an unyielding torus or prominent median suture is present. Stress-breakers (Option C) are distinct mechanical devices, and mechanical retention for denture resin (Option D) is provided by minor connector mesh or lattice designs.

prosthodontics-58.question: A patient requires a full-coverage crown on tooth 14, but the preparation exhibits minimal clinical crown height. Which preparation modification is most effective for providing adequate retention and resistance form?
options: Further reducing the axial walls to decrease the rotational radius
Converting the margin design to a circumferential knife-edge finish line
Placing auxiliary retentive features such as proximal grooves or boxes
Increasing the total occlusal convergence angle to 20 degrees
prosthodontics-58.explanation: Option C is correct because auxiliary retentive features such as proximal grooves or boxes limit the rotational paths of withdrawal and restore necessary resistance form when axial wall height is compromised. Shortening axial walls (Option A) reduces total surface area and accelerates rotational dislodgement. A knife-edge margin (Option B) offers poor marginal definition and structural bulk without enhancing resistance. Increasing the convergence angle (Option D) catastrophically degrades both retention and resistance.

prosthodontics-61.question: When establishing the occlusal scheme for an implant-supported full-arch fixed dental prosthesis in the mandible opposing a conventional maxillary complete denture, which occlusal scheme is recommended to direct forces axially and stabilize the opposing denture?
options: Canine-protected occlusion
Unilateral group function occlusion
Balanced lingualized occlusion
Mutually protected occlusion with immediate anterior disclusion
prosthodontics-61.explanation: Option C is correct because balanced lingualized occlusion utilizes prominent maxillary lingual cusps articulating within shallow mandibular fossae to direct forces axially and provide smooth bilateral contact during excursive movements, which preserves the peripheral seal and stability of the opposing maxillary complete denture. Canine-protected occlusion (Option A) and mutually protected occlusion (Option D) produce immediate anterior tipping levers that dislodge the complete denture during excursions. Unilateral group function (Option B) creates unilateral lateral torquing forces that destabilize the denture base.

prosthodontics-67.question: What is the primary clinical objective of scoring a posterior palatal seal bead into the maxillary master cast prior to complete denture processing?
options: To establish the correct vertical dimension of occlusion
To engage hard tissue undercuts for mechanical retention
To compensate for volumetric polymerization shrinkage of the acrylic resin during processing
To create relief over the compressible submucosal tissues of the soft palate
prosthodontics-67.explanation: Option C is correct because heat-polymerized polymethyl methacrylate undergoes significant volumetric polymerization shrinkage (approximately 6% to 7%) across the broad palatal vault, causing the processed denture base to pull away from the mucosal tissues; scoring the cast ensures the cured denture maintains intimate contact with the palate. Scoring the master cast compresses tissue rather than providing relief (Option D). The posterior palatal seal does not determine the vertical dimension of occlusion (Option A) nor does it engage hard bony undercuts (Option B).

prosthodontics-68.question: A 62-year-old male presents with severe generalized tooth wear due to attrition and erosion. Before planning full-mouth rehabilitation, which diagnostic evaluation is most critical to determine whether the patient has experienced a true loss of vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO) versus compensatory dentoalveolar extrusion?
options: Measurement of the interocclusal rest space (freeway space) by comparing vertical dimension at rest to vertical dimension of occlusion
Measurement of the clinical crown length of mandibular incisors on diagnostic casts
Assessment of the angle of the articular eminence on a panoramic radiograph
Evaluation of the maximum bite force using an intraoral pressure transducer
prosthodontics-68.explanation: Option A is correct because compensatory dentoalveolar extrusion frequently accompanies severe tooth wear to maintain facial height; evaluating the interocclusal rest space (freeway space = VDR - VDO, normal 2 to 4 mm) determines whether VDO is truly lost or if the apparent loss of crown height is compensated. If freeway space is within normal limits, VDO is preserved and restorative space must be created surgically or orthodontically. Crown length alone (Option B) does not account for continuous alveolar bone remodelling. Articular eminence morphology (Option C) and maximum bite force (Option D) do not assess or quantify vertical jaw relationships.

prosthodontics-70.question: During the clinical try-in stage of complete dentures, the patient closes into centric relation. The anterior teeth make heavy contact, but the posterior teeth fail to contact, leaving a bilateral posterior open bite. Which error during the jaw relation registration most likely caused this discrepancy?
options: An excessive vertical dimension of occlusion was recorded
The posterior record bases contacted prematurely or had excessive recording medium during centric relation registration
The facebow transfer was mounted with the bite fork positioned too far anteriorly
The incisal guidance angle on the articulator was set with excessive inclination
prosthodontics-70.explanation: Option B is correct because premature posterior contact between record base heels or excessive posterior thickness of registration material compresses the underlying displaceable mucosa or props open the posterior jaws during registration; once mounted and checked intraorally without the interocclusal medium, the anterior teeth contact prematurely while the posterior teeth remain separated. Excessive vertical dimension of occlusion (Option A) causes generalized premature contacts and eliminates freeway space rather than producing an isolated posterior open bite. Facebow mounting errors (Option C) affect the arc of closure and occlusal plane orientation but do not create an isolated centric relation posterior gap. Incisal guide angle settings (Option D) only affect excursive movements on the articulator, not static centric relation closure.

prosthodontics-71.question: A patient requires a three-unit fixed dental prosthesis replacing missing tooth 36, utilizing teeth 35 and 37 as abutments. Periodontal assessment reveals that tooth 37 has 30% bone loss with Class II mobility (2 mm), whereas tooth 35 has normal physiologic mobility and 15% bone loss. What is the primary biomechanical and prognostic concern for this proposed prosthesis?
options: The combined root surface area of the abutments violates Ante's law
Differential mobility between the abutments creates a fulcrum effect, leading to cement seal failure on the more rigid abutment (tooth 35)
The short span length generates excessive bending moments and ceramic fracture
Secondary caries will inevitably occur around tooth 37 due to gingival recession
prosthodontics-71.explanation: Option B is correct because splinting a hypermobile abutment (tooth 37) to a rigid abutment (tooth 35) generates a destructive cantilever-like fulcrum under masticatory forces, subjecting the cement interface of the rigid abutment to high tensile stresses and resulting in decementation. While Ante's law evaluates pericemental area, the combined root area here is adequate for a single pontic, but mechanical stability is compromised by mobility (Option A). A single pontic replacement represents a short span with minimal flexure (Option C). Secondary caries (Option D) is a consequence of uncemented margins rather than the primary biomechanical failure mechanism.

prosthodontics-109.question: A 48-year-old female presents with severe generalized tooth wear resulting in a confirmed loss of vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO). Before permanently altering her VDO with definitive fixed prosthodontics, which diagnostic procedure is most critical to perform?
options: Immediate preparation and placement of definitive monolithic zirconia crowns at the anticipated VDO
Full-mouth surgical crown lengthening of all posterior teeth prior to diagnostic planning
Immediate extraction of all worn anterior teeth followed by insertion of immediate dentures
Fabrication of diagnostic mounted casts, aesthetic wax-ups, and provisional restorations to verify phonetics, aesthetics, and temporomandibular joint tolerance
prosthodontics-109.explanation: Option D is correct because altering the vertical dimension of occlusion requires a reversible, phased approach using accurately mounted diagnostic casts, diagnostic wax-ups, and provisional restorations or an occlusal appliance to confirm patient adaptation, phonetics, aesthetics, and temporomandibular joint comfort before irreversible preparation. Immediately delivering definitive crowns (Option A) is contraindicated due to the irreversibility of the procedure and high risk of functional failure. Surgical crown lengthening (Option B) is performed only after restorative margins and gingival contours are determined by the diagnostic wax-up. Extractions (Option C) are unwarranted for restorable worn dentition.

prosthodontics-113.question: A 55-year-old female requires a fixed dental prosthesis replacing missing tooth 36. The clinical crown height of the abutments is short, but teeth 35 and 37 are periodontally healthy. Which preparation modification is most effective for increasing the resistance and retention form of these full-coverage crown preparations?
options: Adding proximal grooves or boxes to the axial walls
Shortening the axial wall height to decrease the rotational radius
Polishing the prepared dentin surfaces to a high gloss
Increasing the total occlusal convergence angle beyond 20 degrees
prosthodontics-113.explanation: Option A is correct because placing proximal axial grooves or boxes establishes definitive internal limiting planes that resist rotational displacement along the tipping axis, significantly improving retention and resistance form on short clinical crowns. Shortening axial walls (Option B) further diminishes total surface area and resistance form. Polishing dentin (Option C) removes micro-roughness needed for the mechanical interlocking of luting agents. Increasing the convergence angle (Option D) dramatically diminishes retention and resistance.

prosthodontics-115.question: A 42-year-old patient presents with an unesthetic porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown on tooth 11, exhibiting dark labial gingival shadowing caused by cervical metal show-through. When designing a replacement metal-ceramic crown, which modification best resolves this esthetic concern while preserving structural coping strength?
options: Fabricating a standard 360-degree subgingival metal collar
Utilizing a full-cast gold labial apron placed supragingivally
Incorporating a collarless design with a 90-degree facial shoulder and porcelain butt margin
Preparing a knife-edge facial margin and extending the metal substructure into the junctional epithelium
prosthodontics-115.explanation: Option C is correct because a collarless metal-ceramic restoration featuring a 90-degree facial shoulder with an all-porcelain butt joint eliminates the opaque metal coping at the labial margin, enabling natural light transmission through cervical tissues while maintaining lingual and occlusal metal framework strength. A facial metal collar (Option A) is the exact cause of dark cervical shadowing. Full-cast gold (Option B) is unesthetic and unacceptable in the anterior maxilla. Extending knife-edge margins subgingivally (Option D) violates the biologic width and causes chronic inflammation and discolouration.

prosthodontics-118.question: A patient requires a three-unit fixed dental prosthesis to replace missing tooth 15, utilizing teeth 14 and 16 as abutments. According to Ante's Law, which criterion must be satisfied regarding the periodontal ligament root surface area of the abutments?
options: The clinical attachment loss on each abutment tooth must not exceed 2 mm
The root length of each abutment must be at least twice the clinical crown height
The occlusal table width of the pontic must be identical to that of the adjacent abutments
The combined periodontal ligament area of the abutment teeth must equal or exceed that of the missing teeth being replaced
prosthodontics-118.explanation: Option D is correct because Ante's Law states that the total pericemental (periodontal ligament) surface area of the abutment teeth must be equal to or greater than the pericemental surface area of the teeth being replaced by pontics. Clinical attachment loss thresholds (Option A) and crown-to-root ratios (Option B, ideally 2:3, minimum 1:1) are independent periodontal parameters rather than the definition of Ante's Law. Pontic occlusal tables (Option C) are typically reduced in buccolingual width to decrease occlusal forces rather than matched to abutment dimensions.

prosthodontics-150.question: A 68-year-old patient presents with a midline fracture of a mandibular complete denture that has been in service for five years. What is the primary underlying cause of this midline fatigue failure?
options: Continuous alveolar ridge resorption leading to loss of uniform support and repetitive midline flexure
Inadequate denture base resin thickness confined strictly to the anterior lingual sulcus
Bilateral balanced occlusal contacts distributing masticatory loads during excursive movements
Impact failure resulting from an inadequate border seal causing the prosthesis to drop
prosthodontics-150.explanation: Option A is correct because midline complete denture fractures are primarily fatigue failures caused by progressive residual ridge resorption, which creates a midline fulcrum effect and repetitive cyclic flexure under masticatory loads. Inadequate resin thickness (Option B) is a secondary contributing factor rather than the primary progressive cause, balanced occlusion (Option C) protects against rather than causes denture fractures, and dropping the denture (Option D) produces acute impact fractures rather than classic midline fatigue fractures.

prosthodontics-166.question: A patient presents with a fractured provisional crown on tooth 36. When selecting a provisional restorative material for this posterior tooth, which physical property is LEAST critical to clinical success?
options: High flexural and compressive strength
Biocompatibility with adjacent gingival and pulpal tissues
Ease of repair and marginal modification
Long-term color stability
prosthodontics-166.explanation: Option D is correct because for an interim provisional restoration on a posterior molar such as tooth 36, long-term color stability is clinically the least critical physical requirement compared to functional and biological demands. High compressive and flexural strength (Option A) is vital to withstand masticatory forces and avoid fracture, pulpal and gingival biocompatibility (Option B) is essential to preserve tissue health, and ease of repair (Option C) is necessary for chairside adjustments.

prosthodontics-167.question: According to the Aramany classification for maxillectomy defects, which class presents the greatest challenge for prosthetic obturator rehabilitation due to the bilateral loss of palatal and alveolar support?
options: Class IV (bilateral defect crossing the midline)
Class I (unilateral defect along the midline with contralateral dentition intact)
Class II (unilateral defect posterior to the canine retaining contralateral teeth)
Class III (central defect of the hard palate sparing bilateral dentition)
prosthodontics-167.explanation: Option A is correct because an Aramany Class IV maxillectomy defect crosses the midline with extensive bilateral loss of hard palate and alveolar support, resulting in the poorest prognosis for obturator retention and stability. Aramany Class I (Option B) and Class II (Option C) retain an intact contralateral dental arch that provides linear or tripoded retention, while Class III (Option D) preserves dentition bilaterally, offering the most stable mechanical support.

prosthodontics-173.question: A patient requires a full-coverage crown on tooth 41. During tooth preparation, the facial margin is extended 1.0 mm subgingivally into the crevice. What is the most significant biological concern associated with this margin depth?
options: Invasion of the supracrestal tissue attachment leading to persistent periodontal inflammation
Loss of coronal dentin compromising the mechanical resistance form of the preparation
Accelerated coronal microleakage due to luting agent dissolution
Irreversible pulpal necrosis caused by excessive thermal injury
prosthodontics-173.explanation: Option A is correct because placing a crown margin 1.0 mm subgingivally on tooth 41 frequently invades the supracrestal tissue attachment (biologic width), initiating chronic periodontal inflammation, apical migration of the junctional epithelium, and localized bone loss. Resistance form (Option B) is primarily governed by axial wall height and convergence angle rather than subgingival extension, microleakage (Option C) is prevented by an accurate marginal seal, and pulpal necrosis (Option D) is prevented by appropriate water coolant during preparation rather than determined by margin depth.

prosthodontics-176.question: Which pontic design is most recommended for a posterior fixed partial denture to combine optimal cleansability with the prevention of food entrapment along the edentulous ridge?
options: Saddle (ridge-lap) pontic
Modified ridge-lap pontic
Ovate pontic
Conical pontic
prosthodontics-176.explanation: Option B is correct because the modified ridge-lap pontic possesses a convex tissue surface that contacts only the facial aspect of the residual ridge, facilitating plaque removal with floss while preventing food entrapment. A saddle pontic (Option A) has a concave tissue-contacting surface that causes plaque accumulation and tissue inflammation, an ovate pontic (Option C) requires surgical soft tissue sculpting primarily indicated for the anterior esthetic zone, and a conical pontic (Option D) creates food entrapment when used over wide posterior residual ridges.

prosthodontics-179.question: A 65-year-old edentulous patient presents for complete maxillary denture fabrication. Which anatomical landmark determines the posterior termination of the denture base and the location of the posterior palatal seal?
options: The vibrating line, extending laterally through the hamular notches
The fovea palatini, demarcating the absolute posterior denture border
The posterior nasal spine, establishing the posterior border seal
The pterygomandibular raphe, defining the anterior seal limit
prosthodontics-179.explanation: Option A is correct because the posterior palatal seal is located along the vibrating line on compressible soft palatal tissue, extending bilaterally through the pterygomaxillary (hamular) notches to create an effective peripheral seal. The fovea palatini (Option B) are variable anatomical landmarks that lie within 1 to 2 mm of the vibrating line but do not dictate the posterior border, the posterior nasal spine (Option C) is non-compressible bone anterior to the seal area, and the pterygomandibular raphe (Option D) is an anatomical band that does not define the anterior limit of the posterior palatal seal.

prosthodontics-180.question: A patient presents for partial denture treatment with missing maxillary teeth: tooth 15, tooth 16, and tooth 25. All other natural teeth are present, and third molars are not being replaced. According to Kennedy's classification and Applegate's rules, how is this maxillary arch classified?
options: Kennedy Class III, Modification 1
Kennedy Class II, Modification 2
Kennedy Class I, Modification 1
Kennedy Class IV, Modification 1
prosthodontics-180.explanation: Option A is correct because the edentulous space on the maxillary right quadrant (missing teeth 15 and 16) is bounded by natural teeth anteriorly and posteriorly, establishing a Kennedy Class III, while the single additional bounded edentulous area on the left quadrant (missing tooth 25) constitutes Modification 1. Kennedy Class II (Option B) requires a unilateral distal extension, Kennedy Class I (Option C) requires bilateral distal extensions, and Kennedy Class IV (Option D) is a single bilateral anterior space that cannot possess modifications by definition.

prosthodontics-227.question: A 38-year-old patient requires a full-coverage monolithic lithium disilicate crown on tooth 26. What is the recommended minimum axial wall reduction required to ensure adequate structural durability and esthetics?
options: 0.5 to 0.8 mm
1.0 to 1.2 mm
1.8 to 2.2 mm
2.5 to 3.0 mm
prosthodontics-227.explanation: Option B is correct because monolithic lithium disilicate restorations require a minimum axial reduction of 1.0 to 1.2 mm with a rounded shoulder or deep chamfer finish line to ensure adequate ceramic bulk for fracture resistance and natural optical properties. A reduction of 0.5 to 0.8 mm (Option A) provides insufficient thickness for glass-ceramics and risks catastrophic fracture, while reductions of 1.8 to 2.2 mm (Option C) or 2.5 to 3.0 mm (Option D) correspond to occlusal reductions or excessive, destructive preparations that jeopardize pulpal vitality.

prosthodontics-226.question: A 55-year-old patient requires a mandibular Kennedy Class I removable partial denture with primary abutments on tooth 34 and tooth 44. To effectively counteract rotational displacement of the distal extension base away from the basal seat, which indirect retainer design is most appropriate?
options: A distal occlusal rest prepared on tooth 34
An occlusal rest prepared on tooth 45
A cingulum rest prepared on tooth 33
A mesial occlusal rest prepared on tooth 34
prosthodontics-226.explanation: Option C is correct because an indirect retainer must be located perpendicular to and as far anterior from the primary fulcrum line (connecting the rests on tooth 34 and tooth 44) as possible, making a cingulum rest on tooth 33 mechanically optimal. Rests on tooth 34 (Options A and D) lie directly on the fulcrum line and act as primary direct retainer rests rather than indirect retainers, while tooth 45 (Option B) is missing in a Kennedy Class I arch.

prosthodontics-206.question: A 70-year-old edentulous patient presents with an atrophied anterior maxillary alveolar ridge displaying mobile, hyperplastic (flabby) soft tissue. Which impression technique is most appropriate to record this tissue without displacement during complete denture fabrication?
options: A mucocompressive technique using a custom tray with high-viscosity heavy-body polyvinyl siloxane
A single-stage impression using an overextended stock tray and irreversible hydrocolloid
A functional closed-mouth impression technique using high-viscosity border molding compound across the ridge
A mucostatic (minimal pressure) technique using a custom tray with a relief window and low-viscosity material
prosthodontics-206.explanation: Option D is correct because hyperplastic, mobile tissues must be recorded in an undistorted, resting state using a minimal pressure (mucostatic) technique, such as a custom tray with a relief window and low-viscosity impression material (e.g., light-body silicone or zinc oxide-eugenol). Mucocompressive techniques using heavy-body elastomers (Option A) or modeling compound (Option C) displace the mobile tissue, resulting in elastic recoil and denture dislodgement during function, while stock tray hydrocolloid impressions (Option B) lack border control and exert uncontrolled tissue displacement.

prosthodontics-207.question: A patient requires a mandibular Kennedy Class I removable partial denture. The terminal abutment, tooth 35, has adequate clinical crown height, healthy vestibular depth, no tissue undercuts, and a 0.25 mm undercut in the cervical third of the mid-facial surface. Which direct retainer assembly is most indicated to minimize harmful torqueing forces on this abutment during functional loading?
options: An RPI system (mesial rest, distal proximal plate, and I-bar clasp)
A conventional circumferential (Akers) clasp with a distal occlusal rest
A reverse circlet clasp originating from a distal occlusal rest
A continuous bar clasp with rests on adjacent anterior teeth
prosthodontics-207.explanation: Option A is correct because the RPI system (mesial rest, distal proximal plate, and I-bar clasp) is the design of choice on distal extension abutments with sufficient vestibule depth and facial undercuts, as occlusal loading causes the I-bar and plate to disengage into the undercut, releasing torqueing leverage. A conventional Akers clasp with a distal rest (Option B) creates a destructive Class I lever arm that tilts the abutment distally, a reverse circlet clasp (Option C) requires a mesial rest and is bulkier, and a continuous bar clasp (Option D) does not provide direct clasp retention on the terminal abutment.

prosthodontics-208.question: A 45-year-old patient requires a three-unit fixed partial denture to replace missing tooth 36. Clinical examination reveals that abutment tooth 35 and abutment tooth 37 are tilted in opposing directions, creating divergent paths of insertion. To establish a path of insertion while avoiding excessive tooth reduction, which design modification is most appropriate?
options: Perform extensive axial reduction on the divergent surfaces of tooth 35 and tooth 37
Incorporate a non-rigid connector on the distal aspect of the mesial retainer on tooth 35
Increase the convergence angle of both preparations beyond 20 degrees
Fabricate a cantilever fixed partial denture supported solely by tooth 35
prosthodontics-208.explanation: Option B is correct because incorporating a non-rigid connector (key and keyway) within the contour of the mesial retainer (distal surface of tooth 35) accommodates divergent insertion paths without requiring destructive over-reduction of abutment teeth. Aggressively reducing divergent axial walls (Option A) sacrifices sound tooth structure and risks pulpal exposure, increasing preparation convergence beyond 20 degrees (Option C) severely compromises retention and resistance form, and a cantilever design on tooth 35 (Option D) exposes the anterior abutment to destructive occlusal leverage.

prosthodontics-246.question: A 72-year-old edentulous female presents for complete denture fabrication. During the jaw relation records appointment, you are establishing the vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO). Which method provides the most reliable and objective reference for determining VDO when available?
options: Pre-extraction records, such as articulated diagnostic casts and facial profile photographs
Physiological rest position (VDR) minus 2 to 4 mm of interocclusal rest space
Swallowing threshold and patient tactile perception of muscular comfort
Phonetic assessment of the closest speaking space using sibilant sounds
prosthodontics-246.explanation: Option A is correct because pre-extraction records, such as diagnostic articulated casts or profile radiographs, provide the most reliable and objective anatomical baseline for re-establishing the vertical dimension of occlusion. Physiological rest position, swallowing threshold, and phonetics are dynamic neuromuscular measurements subject to patient fatigue, emotional state, and postural changes, making them less consistently reproducible when used alone.

prosthodontics-249.question: When using a dental surveyor during the diagnostic design of a removable partial denture, what is the primary function of the analyzing rod?
options: To determine the parallelism of axial tooth surfaces and identify the optimal path of insertion
To mark the survey line denoting the height of contour on abutment teeth
To measure the precise depth of retentive undercuts in millimeters
To trim excess wax during the blockout of undercut areas on the master cast
prosthodontics-249.explanation: Option A is correct because the analyzing rod is a smooth diagnostic tool used on a dental surveyor to assess relative parallelism among axial surfaces of abutments and soft tissues to establish the most favorable path of insertion. Scribing the height of contour is performed by the carbon marker, measuring the depth of undercut requires an undercut gauge, and contouring wax blockout is accomplished with a wax trimmer.

prosthodontics-252.question: A 58-year-old male with prominent, non-resectable bilateral mandibular lingual tori requires a Kennedy Class I removable partial denture. Which major connector design is indicated to provide adequate rigidity while preventing soft tissue impingement?
options: Lingual plate with relief provided over the tori
Sublingual bar positioned inferior to the tori
Conventional lingual bar positioned superior to the tori
Continuous bar retainer without an inferior major connector
prosthodontics-252.explanation: Option A is correct because when bilateral mandibular tori cannot be surgically excised, a lingual plate designed with adequate relief over the tori is the major connector of choice, as it bridges the bony exostoses without compromising rigidity or mucosal health. A sublingual bar or conventional lingual bar is strictly contraindicated because their vertical placement directly impinges upon the elevated tori or displaces the floor of the mouth, while a continuous bar alone lacks sufficient rigidity without a primary major connector.

prosthodontics-254.question: When designing a fixed partial denture in the anterior maxilla to replace missing tooth 11, which pontic design provides superior esthetics while maintaining cleansability, assuming adequate alveolar ridge height and width?
options: Saddle (ridge lap) pontic
Sanitary (hygienic) pontic
Ovate pontic
Conical pontic
prosthodontics-254.explanation: Option C is correct because an ovate pontic set into a surgically prepared soft tissue depression provides the most natural emergence profile in the anterior esthetic zone while allowing effective plaque control with dental floss. A saddle pontic is unhygienic due to its concave tissue-facing surface that promotes tissue inflammation, a sanitary pontic is functionally non-esthetic and restricted to non-visible posterior teeth, and a conical pontic creates unsightly dark triangles in anterior sites.

prosthodontics-286.question: A 58-year-old female presents with missing teeth 35, 36, 45, and 46, requiring a mandibular Kennedy Class I bilateral distal extension removable partial denture. Which mechanical feature is most critical for counteracting the rotational dislodgement of the denture base away from the residual ridge during mastication of sticky foods?
options: Rigid major connector providing cross-arch stabilization
Maximum anatomical coverage of the residual ridge
Selective pressure physiologic impression technique
Indirect retention positioned anterior to the fulcrum line
prosthodontics-286.explanation: Option D is correct because indirect retainers placed anterior to the primary retentive fulcrum line provide resistance against the rotational displacement of distal extension denture bases away from the supporting ridge when sticky foods are chewed. Maximum basal seat coverage and selective pressure impressions resist tissueward displacement under occlusal loading rather than movement away from the ridge, while cross-arch stabilization counteracts horizontal and lateral displacement forces.

prosthodontics-304.question: A 52-year-old male requires a three-unit fixed partial denture to replace missing tooth 15. The patient exhibits a moderate smile line and prioritizes ease of cleaning to prevent plaque accumulation. Which pontic design is indicated for this maxillary site?
options: Saddle pontic
Conical pontic
Modified ridge lap pontic
Sanitary (hygienic) pontic
prosthodontics-304.explanation: Option C is correct because a modified ridge lap pontic contacts the facial aspect of the ridge to satisfy esthetic demands in the premolar zone while featuring a convex lingual contour that facilitates easy plaque removal with floss. A conical pontic creates large triangular food traps when placed against broad maxillary residual ridges, a saddle pontic has an unhygienic concave tissue surface that causes chronic mucosal inflammation, and a sanitary pontic leaves an unsightly clearance gap that is esthetically unacceptable in the maxilla.

prosthodontics-305.question: A 62-year-old male presents for fabrication of a mandibular Kennedy Class II Modification 1 removable partial denture, with missing teeth 36, 45, 46, and 47. Diagnostic evaluation demonstrates healthy periodontium and 9 mm of vertical space between the active floor of the mouth and the free gingival margin. Which major connector is the first choice for this patient?
options: Double lingual bar (Kennedy bar)
Lingual bar
Sublingual bar
Lingual plate
prosthodontics-305.explanation: Option B is correct because a lingual bar is the first-choice mandibular major connector whenever at least 7 to 8 mm of vertical clearance exists between the marginal gingiva and the elevated floor of the mouth, as it avoids covering anterior teeth and minimizes plaque accumulation. A lingual plate unnecessarily covers cervical gingival tissues and increases the risk of caries and periodontal breakdown when anterior splinting is not required, while double lingual bars and sublingual bars are complex secondary designs indicated only when vertical height is severely limited or large diastemas exist.

prosthodontics-257.question: A 35-year-old female requires an all-ceramic lithium disilicate crown on tooth 14. Which finish line design is recommended to minimize internal stress concentration and ensure adequate marginal ceramic thickness?
options: Shoulder finish line with a sharp 90-degree internal line angle
Shoulder finish line with a rounded internal line angle
Knife-edge (feather-edge) finish line
Beveled finish line
prosthodontics-257.explanation: Option B is correct because a shoulder with a rounded internal line angle provides the recommended 1.0 to 1.5 mm of marginal ceramic bulk while dispersing internal stresses that could otherwise propagate fractures in all-ceramic restorations. A sharp 90-degree internal line angle creates high localized stress concentrations that promote ceramic fracture, whereas knife-edge and beveled finish lines produce an unsupported, ultra-thin margin of brittle ceramic prone to chipping and deformation.

prosthodontics-266.question: A patient with a mandibular Kennedy Class I arch presents with a lingual alveolar ridge that slopes significantly downward and posteriorly toward the floor of the mouth. Which major connector design is most prone to soft tissue impingement during tissueward rotational movement of the distal extension base under occlusal loading?
options: Lingual bar
Lingual plate
Continuous bar retainer
Labial bar
prosthodontics-266.explanation: Option A is correct because when an alveolar ridge slopes downward and posteriorly, tissueward rotation of a distal extension base causes the inferior edge of a conventional lingual bar to travel along an arc that drives it directly into the sloping lingual mucosa. A lingual plate is specifically contoured to prevent this impingement and distribute forces across multiple teeth, a continuous bar is an auxiliary component rather than a standalone connector, and a labial bar is placed on the facial aspect of the arch.

prosthodontics-267.question: A 45-year-old male presents with non-restorable caries on tooth 31 requiring extraction. He requests a fixed partial denture to replace tooth 31. Radiographic assessment reveals that tooth 32 has a short, tapered root with moderate bone loss, whereas tooth 41 has normal bone support and favorable root anatomy. Which abutment configuration presents the poorest long-term prognosis?
options: Using tooth 32 as a solitary cantilever abutment
Using tooth 41 as a solitary cantilever abutment
Splinting tooth 32 to tooth 33 to support a fixed partial denture
Using teeth 32 and 41 as abutments for a conventional three-unit fixed partial denture
prosthodontics-267.explanation: Option A is correct because using tooth 32—which has a compromised crown-to-root ratio, short tapered root, and reduced periodontal support—as a solitary cantilever abutment subjects it to destructive unreciprocated class I lever forces, resulting in rapid bone loss and prosthesis failure. Using an abutment with intact bone support (tooth 41), splinting to include canine tooth 33, or fabricating a conventional bilateral fixed partial denture significantly reduces tipping stresses and provides favorable biomechanical load distribution.

prosthodontics-268.question: A 58-year-old patient undergoes placement of an endosseous dental implant to replace missing tooth 11. High primary stability is achieved with an implant stability quotient (ISQ) greater than 70. According to bone biology principles, what is the primary physiological advantage of controlled immediate provisional loading?
options: It significantly increases the biological rate of osseointegration
