options: Dentigerous cyst; enucleation of the cyst with surgical extraction of tooth 48
Radicular cyst; non-surgical root canal treatment of tooth 48
Odontogenic keratocyst; complete segmental resection with 1 cm osseous margins
Ameloblastoma; marginal hemimandibulectomy and immediate reconstruction
prosthodontics-961405961.explanation: Option A is correct because a well-circumscribed, unilocular radiolucency surrounding the crown of an impacted tooth and attached at the cementoenamel junction is characteristic of a dentigerous cyst, which is definitively managed by complete enucleation of the lesion and removal of the impacted tooth 48. A radicular cyst develops at the apex of a non-vital erupted tooth rather than pericoronally around an impacted crown. Radical surgical interventions such as segmental resection or hemimandibulectomy are overly aggressive and contraindicated for benign developmental odontogenic cysts.

prosthodontics-365518478.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents following the premature extraction of tooth 75 (mandibular left primary second molar) due to non-restorable caries. Clinical and radiographic examinations demonstrate that tooth 36 (mandibular left permanent first molar) is fully erupted into stable functional occlusion, while tooth 35 (mandibular left second premolar) remains unerupted within alveolar bone. What is the MOST appropriate appliance to maintain arch length?
options: Distal shoe space maintainer
Band and loop space maintainer
Nance holding arch appliance
Passive observation without appliance placement
prosthodontics-365518478.explanation: Option B is correct because a unilateral band and loop space maintainer is the standard appliance indicated to prevent the mesial drifting and tipping of an erupted permanent first molar (tooth 36) after the premature loss of a primary second molar (tooth 75). A distal shoe space maintainer is indicated only when the primary second molar is lost prior to the eruption of the permanent first molar to guide its eruption path. A Nance appliance is a maxillary bilateral space maintainer that cannot be utilized in the mandibular arch, and passive observation often results in space loss and subsequent premolar impaction.

prosthodontics-356134356.question: According to Canadian infection prevention and control (IPAC) guidelines and provincial regulatory standards, how should heat-sensitive critical instruments (instruments that penetrate oral soft tissue or bone) be processed if they cannot tolerate conventional steam autoclave sterilization?
options: Immersion in a 2% glutaraldehyde solution for 20 minutes
Processing through a validated low-temperature sterilization method or replacing with single-use sterile devices
Wiping the instrument surfaces thoroughly with an intermediate-level hospital disinfectant
Cold chemical immersion in a quaternary ammonium compound solution for 10 hours
prosthodontics-356134356.explanation: Option B is correct because under Canadian IPAC and RCDSO guidelines, all critical instruments that penetrate soft tissue or contact bone must achieve true sterility; when instruments are heat-sensitive, they must be processed using a validated low-temperature sterilization method (such as hydrogen peroxide gas plasma) or replaced with single-use sterile disposable items. Immersion in 2% glutaraldehyde for 20 minutes or wiping with intermediate-level disinfectants achieves only disinfection, not sporicidal sterilization. Quaternary ammonium compounds are low-level disinfectants incapable of sterilizing surgical items and cannot be biologically monitored with spore tests.

prosthodontics-150177789.question: A 50-year-old female patient with a confirmed medical history of Sjögren syndrome presents with severe xerostomia and rampant cervical dental caries. Clinical examination reveals dry, fissured lips, atrophic oral mucosa, and a complete absence of salivary pooling in the floor of the mouth. What is the MOST appropriate long-term preventive and therapeutic home-care regimen for this patient?
options: Daily at-home application of 1.1% sodium fluoride (5,000 ppm) dentifrice/gel combined with salivary substitutes and frequent water hydration
Daily self-application of 5% sodium fluoride (22,600 ppm) varnish in custom dental trays
Twice-daily oral rinsing with 70% isopropyl alcohol and complete dietary sugar restriction
Prophylactic long-term broad-spectrum systemic antibiotic therapy and bilateral parotidectomy
prosthodontics-150177789.explanation: Option A is correct because high-risk xerostomic patients with rampant caries require intensive daily at-home fluoride therapy utilizing 1.1% sodium fluoride (5,000 ppm) gel or dentifrice, supplemented with salivary substitutes and frequent hydration to promote remineralization and comfort. In contrast, 5% sodium fluoride (22,600 ppm) varnish is strictly indicated for periodic professional in-office application and is never prescribed for daily home use due to systemic fluoride toxicity risks. Alcohol-based rinses exacerbate oral mucosal xerosis, while systemic antibiotics and salivary gland excision have no valid role in managing xerostomia-induced caries.

prosthodontics-409010348.question: A 7-year-old female presents after falling on a playground, sustaining trauma to her anterior maxilla. Clinical examination reveals that the permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth 11) is displaced palatally and apically with limited mobility, an intact crown, and no gingival laceration. Radiographic examination confirms palatal and apical displacement of tooth 11 with an intact root and an open apex. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Gently reposition tooth 11 with digital pressure and place a flexible splint for 4 weeks.
Perform immediate pulpectomy and root canal instrumentation on tooth 11.
Surgically extract tooth 11 to prevent injury to adjacent structures.
Observe tooth 11 without intervention to allow for spontaneous repositioning.
prosthodontics-409010348.explanation: Option A is correct because lateral luxation with palatal and apical displacement locks the root apex into the alveolar bone, requiring immediate gentle digital repositioning and flexible splinting for 4 weeks per International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines. Immediate pulpectomy is contraindicated in immature permanent teeth because pulpal revascularization remains possible unless persistent necrosis is diagnosed, extraction is overly destructive for a salvageable permanent incisor, and spontaneous repositioning does not occur in apically locked permanent teeth.

prosthodontics-390048020.question: A 42-year-old male presents for a routine recall examination. His medical history is non-contributory and he has no history of smoking. Clinical examination reveals generalized pocket depths of 4 to 5 mm, bleeding on probing across 35% of sites, and interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm, with slight mobility of the mandibular left central incisor (tooth 31). Full-mouth periapical radiographs demonstrate horizontal bone loss extending between 15% and 33% of root length coronal to the root apex, with no tooth loss attributable to periodontal disease. According to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, what is the MOST appropriate diagnosis?
options: Periodontitis, Stage II
Periodontitis, Stage I
Periodontitis, Stage III
Dental biofilm-induced gingivitis
prosthodontics-390048020.explanation: Option A is correct because interdental clinical attachment loss of 3 to 4 mm, probing depths up to 5 mm, and horizontal bone loss confined to the coronal third (15% to 33%) without periodontal-related tooth loss definitively defines Stage II Periodontitis under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification. Stage I represents early disease characterized by attachment loss of 1 to 2 mm and bone loss under 15%, Stage III involves severe attachment loss of 5 mm or greater with bone loss extending into the mid-third of the root, and gingivitis presents with bleeding on probing but completely lacks interdental attachment or bone loss.

prosthodontics-51344434.question: A 6-year-old female presents with her mother, who is concerned about a discolored primary maxillary right central incisor (tooth 51) that appears grey-brown. There is no parental recollection of dental trauma or pain. Clinical examination reveals tooth 51 is asymptomatic with physiologic mobility, no sinus tract, and normal surrounding gingiva. Radiographs demonstrate advanced physiologic root resorption of tooth 51 and an intact, developing permanent successor. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Monitor tooth 51 clinically and radiographically for pathological symptoms until exfoliation.
Perform an immediate pulpectomy and root canal obturation on tooth 51.
Extract tooth 51 immediately under local anesthesia.
Perform an indirect pulp capping procedure on tooth 51.
prosthodontics-51344434.explanation: Option A is correct because an asymptomatic, discolored primary incisor undergoing physiologic root resorption without signs of infection or swelling requires only periodic clinical and radiographic monitoring until natural exfoliation. Pulpectomy is contraindicated due to advanced physiologic root resorption and the risk of mechanical or chemical trauma to the permanent tooth germ, extraction is unnecessarily invasive in the absence of active infection or pain, and indirect pulp therapy is indicated only for vital pulps beneath deep active dental caries.

prosthodontics-569690316.question: A 70-year-old male presents complaining that his 3-month-old complete mandibular denture has become loose and causes pain during mastication. Clinical examination reveals reduced denture retention, localized erythematous, inflamed mucosal sore spots under the denture base, and generalized residual ridge resorption. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Relieve denture pressure areas, place a temporary resilient tissue conditioner, and re-evaluate once tissues heal.
Perform an immediate definitive hard laboratory reline of the existing mandibular denture.
Fabricate a completely new maxillary and mandibular complete denture set.
Refer the patient for pre-prosthetic mandibular surgical vestibuloplasty.
prosthodontics-569690316.explanation: Option A is correct because sore, abused, and inflamed bearing tissues must be relieved of occlusal and base pressure and treated with a temporary tissue conditioner to restore tissue health before any definitive impression or reline is attempted. Performing a definitive hard reline or fabricating new dentures directly over deformed, inflamed mucosa locks in registration errors and perpetuates prosthesis instability, while surgical vestibuloplasty is an invasive intervention reserved for severe anatomical deficits after conservative prosthodontic measures are exhausted.

prosthodontics-24148590.question: A 9-year-old female presents for a recall appointment. Clinical examination reveals that the primary maxillary left canine (tooth 63) is clinically firm and the permanent maxillary left canine (tooth 23) is unerupted. A panoramic radiograph reveals that tooth 23 is palatally displaced and impacted, with its crown overlapping the distal half of the root of the permanent maxillary left lateral incisor (tooth 22). What is the MOST appropriate interceptive management?
options: Extract the primary maxillary left canine (tooth 63) to encourage normal eruption of tooth 23.
Perform immediate surgical exposure and orthodontic traction on tooth 23.
Extract the impacted permanent maxillary left canine (tooth 23).
Initiate comprehensive fixed orthodontic appliance therapy with rapid palatal expansion.
prosthodontics-24148590.explanation: Option A is correct because interceptive extraction of the primary canine (tooth 63) in 9- to 10-year-old patients provides space and allows palatally displaced permanent canines to normalize their eruptive path in up to 80% of cases per the Ericson and Kurol protocol. Surgical exposure and orthodontic traction are premature and contraindicated prior to the physiological eruption age of 11 to 12 years, surgical removal of tooth 23 sacrifices an essential cornerstone of the dentition, and full fixed appliances are unnecessary before evaluating the outcome of interceptive primary tooth extraction.

prosthodontics-838530716.question: A 35-year-old female presents with a slowly enlarging, painless swelling in the anterior palate. Clinical examination reveals a well-circumscribed, fluctuant swelling in the midline of the anterior hard palate, palatal to the permanent maxillary central incisors (teeth 11 and 21). Both tooth 11 and tooth 21 respond normally to cold and electric pulp testing. An occlusal radiograph shows a well-defined, unilocular, heart-shaped radiolucency with a corticated border located between the roots of teeth 11 and 21, causing divergence of their roots. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Nasopalatine duct cyst
Periapical cyst
Odontogenic keratocyst
Conventional ameloblastoma
prosthodontics-838530716.explanation: Option A is correct because a well-defined midline anterior palatal radiolucency, often heart-shaped due to the superimposed anterior nasal spine, situated between vital maxillary central incisors (teeth 11 and 21) is classic for a nasopalatine duct (incisive canal) cyst. A periapical cyst requires a non-vital pulp, which is ruled out by positive thermal and electric testing, an odontogenic keratocyst develops predominantly in the posterior mandible with high recurrence and distinct histopathology, and an ameloblastoma is an aggressive odontogenic neoplasm that typically causes substantial cortical expansion and root resorption in the molar-ramus region of the mandible.

prosthodontics-103484513.question: A 9-year-old male presents following bicycle trauma to his anterior maxilla. Clinical examination reveals that the permanent maxillary right central incisor (tooth 11) is displaced labially with slight mobility. A periapical radiograph reveals that tooth 11 has an open apex with no root fracture or alveolar bone comminution. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Digitally reposition tooth 11 and place a flexible splint for 2 weeks.
Extract tooth 11 to prevent acute infection of the developing anterior arch.
Apply a rigid orthodontic splint to tooth 11 and adjacent teeth for 8 weeks.
Initiate immediate pulpectomy and root canal obturation on tooth 11.
prosthodontics-103484513.explanation: Option A is correct because a luxated permanent incisor with an open apex should be gently repositioned with digital pressure and stabilized with a flexible splint for 2 weeks to allow periodontal healing while optimizing chances for pulpal revascularization. Extraction is contraindicated because immature permanent incisors have exceptional regenerative potential, prolonged rigid splinting for 8 weeks significantly increases the risk of ankylosis and replacement root resorption, and immediate endodontic intervention is contraindicated until clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpal necrosis is established.

prosthodontics-207536064.question: When administering a conventional inferior alveolar nerve block, which palpable anatomical landmark on the anterior border of the ramus is used to establish the correct vertical height of needle insertion?
options: Coronoid notch
Pterygomandibular raphe
Mental foramen
Mandibular lingula
prosthodontics-207536064.explanation: Option A is correct because palpating the greatest depression of the coronoid notch on the anterior border of the ramus establishes the horizontal plane and vertical height of needle insertion (approximately 6 to 10 mm above the mandibular occlusal plane). The pterygomandibular raphe is a soft-tissue landmark that defines the anteroposterior or medial insertion boundary rather than the ramus height, the mental foramen is located on the external surface of the mandibular body near the premolars, and the lingula is an internal bony prominence that shields the foramen and cannot be directly palpated prior to injection.

general-medicine-13.question: A 75-year-old male who suffered an ischemic stroke 6 months ago presents for restorative dental treatment. He exhibits residual right-sided hemiparesis and is currently maintained on low-dose aspirin therapy. What is the MOST appropriate protocol for his safe dental management?
options: Schedule short morning appointments to minimize physical and cardiovascular fatigue.
Place the patient in a fully supine chair position throughout the dental procedure.
Discontinue low-dose aspirin therapy 7 days prior to treatment to avoid bleeding.
Administer prophylactic antibiotics prior to routine restorative care due to stroke history.
general-medicine-13.explanation: Option A is correct because post-stroke patients should be scheduled for short, mid-morning appointments to minimize physical exertion, endogenous catecholamine release, and cardiovascular fatigue. Fully supine positioning is contraindicated because stroke-induced pharyngeal weakness impairs airway protective reflexes and elevates aspiration risk, discontinuing antiplatelet therapy for routine dental procedures exposes the patient to life-threatening rebound thromboembolism, and antibiotic prophylaxis is neither indicated nor recommended for patients with a history of stroke.

general-medicine-40.question: Prior to administering general anesthesia for extensive dental treatment in an outpatient dental facility, which pre-anesthetic assessment is CRITICAL to ensure patient safety and assess anesthetic risk?
options: Comprehensive medical history, physical examination, and airway assessment.
Routine screening coagulation panel and baseline bleeding time analysis.
Nutritional dietary intake log and caloric expenditure assessment.
Full-mouth periodontal probing depth charting and radiographic survey.
general-medicine-40.explanation: Option A is correct because a thorough medical history, physical examination, and airway assessment (evaluating Mallampati class, thyromental distance, and neck mobility) are mandatory to assign an ASA physical status score and anticipate difficult airway management. Routine coagulation screening in healthy patients without a bleeding history is non-contributory and not indicated per preoperative guidelines, dietary nutritional logs do not evaluate cardiopulmonary or airway anesthetic tolerance, and dental/periodontal charting assesses dental disease rather than physiological anesthetic stability.

general-medicine-45.question: Which of the following local anesthetic agents is metabolized primarily by hepatic microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes and must be used with caution in patients with severe hepatic dysfunction?
options: Lidocaine
Articaine
Procaine
Tetracaine
general-medicine-45.explanation: Option A is correct because lidocaine is an amide local anesthetic cleared and metabolized almost exclusively (approximately 90% to 95%) by hepatic microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes, requiring significant dosage reduction in severe liver disease to avoid toxicity. Articaine is an amide containing an ester side-chain that undergoes 90% to 95% of its biotransformation in the bloodstream via plasma carboxylesterases, while procaine and tetracaine are ester local anesthetics hydrolyzed rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterases rather than liver microsomal enzymes.

general-medicine-58.question: A 45-year-old patient with a prosthetic cardiac valve and a documented history of immediate hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis) to penicillin requires antibiotic prophylaxis prior to dental scaling. According to current Canadian Dental Association (CDA) and American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines, which of the following is the MOST appropriate oral prophylactic regimen?
options: Azithromycin 500 mg orally administered 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure.
Cephalexin 2 g orally administered 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure.
Clindamycin 600 mg orally administered 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure.
Amoxicillin 2 g orally administered 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure.
general-medicine-58.explanation: Option A is correct because current CDA and AHA guidelines recommend azithromycin 500 mg (or clarithromycin 500 mg) orally 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure for high-risk patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria to penicillins. Cephalexin and other first-generation cephalosporins are contraindicated in patients with a history of penicillin anaphylaxis due to the risk of cross-reactivity, clindamycin has been completely eliminated from antibiotic prophylaxis guidelines due to its high association with fatal Clostridioides difficile colitis, and amoxicillin is strictly contraindicated in penicillin-allergic individuals.

prosthodontics-678861105.question: A 45-year-old male patient presents with a missing tooth 46 and requests an implant-supported restoration. Clinical examination reveals adequate interocclusal space and ridge width. A cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scan demonstrates a residual bone height of 8 mm coronal to the mandibular canal in the area of tooth 46. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate implant treatment approach?
options: Placement of a 6 mm short dental implant to maintain a 2 mm safety margin above the mandibular canal
Vertical guided bone regeneration (GBR) to place a standard 10 mm dental implant
Inferior alveolar nerve transposition followed by placement of a standard 10 mm dental implant
Placement of an 8 mm standard implant bicortically engaging the superior border of the mandibular canal
prosthodontics-678861105.explanation: Option A is correct because placing a 6 mm short dental implant in an 8 mm bone crest satisfies the mandatory 2 mm radiographic safety margin coronal to the inferior alveolar canal while providing predictable long-term survival. Vertical guided bone regeneration (option B) entails significantly higher surgical morbidity, prolonged healing times, and elevated complication rates in the posterior mandible compared to short implants. Inferior alveolar nerve transposition (option C) carries an unacceptable risk of permanent neurosensory paresthesia, and bicortical engagement encroaching directly upon the canal (option D) risks traumatic nerve injury.

prosthodontics-914782944.question: A 10-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic after falling from a skateboard, sustaining trauma to his anterior teeth. Clinical examination reveals tooth 11 is displaced palatally, locked in bone, and sensitive to percussion with absence of mobility. Radiographs confirm lateral luxation with periodontal ligament space widening and no root fracture. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Reposition tooth 11 with gentle digital pressure and stabilize with a flexible splint for 4 weeks
Reposition tooth 11 using extraction forceps and apply a rigid wire splint for 2 weeks
Perform an immediate pulpectomy and place an intracanal calcium hydroxide dressing
Allow tooth 11 to re-erupt spontaneously without manual repositioning or splinting
prosthodontics-914782944.explanation: Option A is correct because current International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines mandate that laterally luxated teeth be gently repositioned and stabilized with a passive, flexible splint for 4 weeks to facilitate periodontal ligament reattachment and alveolar bone remineralization. Rigid splinting or abbreviated 2-week durations (option B) impair physiological periodontal healing and significantly elevate the risk of replacement resorption and ankylosis. Immediate pulpectomy (option C) is contraindicated before confirming pulp necrosis, and awaiting spontaneous re-eruption (option D) is inappropriate because laterally luxated permanent incisors are locked into alveolar bone and require prompt manual reduction.

general-medicine-159.question: A 65-year-old patient with well-controlled hypertension managed with a non-selective beta-blocker presents for the extraction of tooth 47. Which of the following is the MOST important clinical management consideration related to this antihypertensive medication?
options: Monitor for postural hypotension when raising the dental chair and limit epinephrine to 0.04 mg
Completely avoid the administration of any local anesthetic containing epinephrine
Instruct the patient to discontinue the beta-blocker 24 hours prior to the extraction
Advise the patient to double their morning dose of the beta-blocker to prevent perioperative hypertension
general-medicine-159.explanation: Option A is correct because non-selective beta-blockers suppress compensatory reflex vasoconstriction, creating a significant risk for postural (orthostatic) hypotension when returning the dental chair upright, while systemic absorption of epinephrine requires limiting the vasoconstrictor dose to a cardiac maximum of 0.04 mg. Epinephrine does not need to be completely avoided (option B), as low doses (up to two cartridges of 1:100,000 epinephrine) can be safely administered with careful aspiration. Abruptly discontinuing beta-blockers (option C) risks rebound hypertension, tachycardia, and angina, whereas doubling the medication dose (option D) risks profound bradycardia, hypotension, and cardiovascular collapse.

general-medicine-168.question: A 68-year-old patient who suffered an acute ischemic stroke 2 months ago and is currently stabilized on daily aspirin (81 mg) presents for the elective extraction of an asymptomatic, non-restorable tooth 36. What is the PRIMARY clinical concern regarding this patient's immediate dental care?
options: Elevated risk of recurrent stroke or cardiovascular event triggered by procedure-related stress
Excessive uncontrollable post-extraction intraoral hemorrhage due to antiplatelet therapy
Severe toxic drug-drug interaction between low-dose aspirin and amide local anesthetics
Development of infective endocarditis requiring mandatory pre-procedural antibiotic prophylaxis
general-medicine-168.explanation: Option A is correct because the risk of recurrent stroke, myocardial infarction, and cardiovascular mortality is exceptionally high within the first 6 months following an acute ischemic stroke; consequently, Canadian medical protocols dictate deferring elective invasive dental treatment until after this 6-month recovery window. Postoperative bleeding on low-dose aspirin monotherapy (option B) is minor and predictably controlled using local hemostatic agents like gelatin sponges and sutures without interrupting antiplatelet therapy. Low-dose aspirin does not interact dangerously with amide local anesthetics (option C), and a cerebrovascular accident carries zero risk or indication for infective endocarditis prophylaxis (option D).

general-medicine-172.question: Which of the following represents the MOST severe and debilitating long-term chronic complication affecting the gnathic bones in patients receiving high-dose radiation therapy (>60 Gy) for head and neck cancer?
options: Osteoradionecrosis of the jaw
Pseudomembranous oral candidiasis
Recurrent intraoral herpes simplex virus infection
Major recurrent aphthous stomatitis
general-medicine-172.explanation: Option A is correct because osteoradionecrosis of the jaw is the most severe, chronic, and devastating complication of head and neck radiotherapy exceeding 60 Gy, stemming from permanent radiation-induced endarteritis obliterans, hypovascularity, hypoxia, and hypocellularity. Oral candidiasis (option B) is a common, superficial opportunistic fungal infection that occurs frequently during radiotherapy but is easily treated and managed with antifungals. Herpetic viral lesions (option C) and aphthous ulcers (option D) are self-limiting mucosal conditions that do not cause irreversible bone necrosis or structural jaw destruction.

general-medicine-194.question: A 62-year-old patient with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents for restorative dental treatment. Which of the following dental chair positions is the MOST appropriate to minimize respiratory distress during the appointment?
options: Upright or semi-supine position
Fully flat supine position
Trendelenburg position
Prone position
general-medicine-194.explanation: Option A is correct because positioning a patient with severe COPD upright or semi-supine utilizes gravity to facilitate diaphragmatic descent, maximizing functional residual capacity and preventing acute dyspnea. The fully flat supine position (option B) severely impairs ventilation by causing abdominal viscera to compress the diaphragm and increase the work of breathing. The Trendelenburg position (option C) is strictly contraindicated because cephalad visceral displacement critically splints the diaphragm, while the prone position (option D) impairs thoracic expansion and prevents proper clinical airway monitoring.

general-medicine-244.question: A 32-year-old patient with a documented history of recurrent herpes labialis presents for routine periodontal scaling. Clinical examination reveals intact, healthy tissues with no prodromal symptoms or active vesicular or crusted lesions. What is the MOST appropriate clinical management?
options: Proceed with the periodontal scaling as scheduled using standard infection control precautions
Prescribe systemic valacyclovir for 5 days prior to rescheduling the scaling
Apply topical acyclovir 5% ointment to the vermilion border immediately prior to scaling
Postpone the appointment for 14 days to monitor for latent subclinical viral shedding
general-medicine-244.explanation: Option A is correct because patients with a history of recurrent herpes labialis who are entirely asymptomatic with no prodromal signs or active lesions can safely undergo routine periodontal scaling using standard precautions without treatment alteration. Prescribing prophylactic systemic antivirals (option B) is clinically unwarranted for routine dental prophylaxis and is reserved exclusively for major surgical or laser procedures in patients with frequent, severe recurrences. Topical acyclovir (option C) is ineffective for prophylaxis on intact perioral skin, and postponing treatment (option D) in the absence of active lesions is clinically unnecessary.

general-medicine-237.question: A 55-year-old male with a mechanical prosthetic mitral valve requires the simple extraction of tooth 37. He is stably anticoagulated on warfarin. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management strategy regarding his anticoagulant therapy prior to this extraction?
options: Verify a recent therapeutic INR of 3.5 or less, continue warfarin without interruption, and utilize local hemostatic measures
Discontinue warfarin 3 days prior to the extraction and restart the medication the day following surgery
Discontinue warfarin 5 days prior to the procedure and bridge with subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin
Instruct the patient to reduce their warfarin dose by half for 2 days prior to the extraction
general-medicine-237.explanation: Option A is correct because Canadian Dental Association and CHEST guidelines recommend continuing warfarin therapy uninterrupted for minor dental extractions provided the patient's international normalized ratio (INR) is therapeutic (≤ 3.5), relying on local hemostatic agents such as gelatin sponges, sutures, and tranexamic acid mouthwash. Discontinuing warfarin (option B) or reducing the dose (option D) exposes a patient with a mechanical mitral valve to catastrophic risks of valve thrombosis and embolic stroke. Heparin bridging therapy (option C) substantially increases the risk of severe post-extraction hemorrhage without offering protective thromboembolic benefits over uninterrupted warfarin.

general-medicine-240.question: A 45-year-old patient with poorly controlled asthma presents for elective restorative treatment, reporting daily wheezing, nocturnal awakenings, and using a salbutamol rescue inhaler multiple times per day. What is the MOST appropriate clinical course of action?
options: Postpone elective dental treatment and refer the patient to their physician for medical optimization
Proceed with the restorative appointment after placing the patient's salbutamol inhaler on the bracket table
Administer a single dose of oral prednisone 50 mg in the dental clinic and proceed after 30 minutes
Prescribe an oral long-acting beta-2 agonist for the patient to take one hour prior to treating
general-medicine-240.explanation: Option A is correct because elective dental care must be deferred for patients with poorly controlled, unstable asthma—characterized by daily symptoms and frequent rescue inhaler usage—until medical evaluation and disease stabilization are achieved by their physician. Proceeding with care simply because a rescue inhaler is present (option B) creates an unacceptable risk of precipitating acute, severe bronchospasm or status asthmaticus from dental anxiety and aerosols. Chairside administration of oral prednisone (option C) has a delayed onset of several hours and does not rapidly stabilize acute airway hyperresponsiveness, while prescribing long-acting beta-agonists (option D) falls outside dental scope and fails to provide safe, immediate disease control.

general-medicine-218.question: A 50-year-old patient with a mechanical prosthetic mitral valve requires the simple extraction of tooth 48. The patient takes warfarin with a stable therapeutic INR of 2.8. Which of the following represents the MOST appropriate management protocol prior to the extraction?
options: Prescribe 2 g of amoxicillin orally 30 to 60 minutes prior to the extraction, maintain warfarin without interruption, and utilize local hemostatic measures
Omit antibiotic prophylaxis because the prosthetic valve is endothelially covered, discontinue warfarin 3 days prior, and restart postoperatively
Consult the patient's cardiologist to determine the need for antibiotic prophylaxis and bridge warfarin with low-molecular-weight heparin
Prescribe 600 mg of clindamycin for infective endocarditis prophylaxis and hold warfarin for 48 hours prior to the procedure
general-medicine-218.explanation: Option A is correct because Canadian Dental Association and AHA guidelines mandate that dentists autonomously prescribe infective endocarditis prophylaxis (first-line: 2 g amoxicillin orally 30–60 minutes preoperatively) for mechanical heart valves, while maintaining warfarin uninterrupted at a therapeutic INR (≤ 3.5) supported by local hemostatics. Withholding prophylaxis (option B) is negligent because prosthetic valves permanently carry the highest risk of fatal endocarditis, and stopping warfarin introduces significant thromboembolic risk. Deferring the prophylaxis decision to a cardiologist and bridging with heparin (option C) contradicts established dental standards and unnecessarily elevates bleeding risks, while clindamycin (option D) is strictly contraindicated by Canadian guidelines due to fatal Clostridioides difficile colitis.

general-medicine-257.question: A 62-year-old male patient with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease presents for the extraction of non-restorable tooth 26. His daily medications include metformin, ramipril, atorvastatin, and clopidogrel (75 mg). Which of the following is the MOST critical management consideration prior to proceeding with the extraction?
options: Measure baseline blood pressure immediately prior to treatment and maintain clopidogrel without interruption
Instruct the patient to discontinue clopidogrel 5 to 7 days before the extraction to avoid intraoperative hemorrhage
Order an immediate International Normalized Ratio (INR) blood test to assess antiplatelet therapy efficacy
Administer prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent surgical site infection due to diabetes
general-medicine-257.explanation: Option A is correct because preoperative blood pressure monitoring is critical to verify cardiovascular stability in a patient with hypertension and coronary artery disease, and antiplatelet monotherapy (clopidogrel) must be continued uninterrupted for minor oral surgery to avoid fatal stent thrombosis or myocardial infarction. Discontinuing clopidogrel (option B) dramatically elevates ischemic cardiovascular risk, whereas minor surgical bleeding is easily controlled using local hemostatic measures. An INR test (option C) monitors vitamin K antagonists like warfarin and has no utility for antiplatelet agents like clopidogrel, and routine prophylactic antibiotics (option D) are not indicated for dental extractions in well-managed diabetic patients.

general-medicine-291.question: A 25-year-old patient presents for the surgical extraction of tooth 38. The patient reports a childhood history of rheumatic fever with no current symptoms and normal cardiac function. In accordance with Canadian Dental Association and AHA guidelines, what is the recommendation regarding antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis (IE) prior to this procedure?
options: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated for patients with a history of rheumatic fever, regardless of whether residual valvular damage is present
Antibiotic prophylaxis is mandatory because any past history of acute rheumatic fever warrants lifelong bacteremia protection
Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated only if echocardiography demonstrates residual rheumatic valvular damage
Antibiotic prophylaxis is required only if the surgical procedure involves extensive manipulation of the gingival sulcus
general-medicine-291.explanation: Option A is correct because under current Canadian Dental Association and AHA guidelines, rheumatic heart disease and a history of rheumatic fever—even with residual valvular dysfunction—are not indications for infective endocarditis prophylaxis. Antibiotic prophylaxis is strictly restricted to highest-risk cardiac conditions, including prosthetic heart valves, prosthetic valve repair materials, prior infective endocarditis, specific congenital heart diseases, and heart transplants with valvulopathy. Consequently, a past history of rheumatic fever (option B), residual valvular damage (option C), or invasive sulcular manipulation in this patient (option D) does not justify antibiotic administration.

prosthodontics-260614220.question: A 10-year-old male patient presents with severe pain and swelling in the upper left posterior maxilla of two days' duration. Clinical examination reveals significant facial swelling involving the left cheek and infraorbital region, tenderness over the left maxillary sinus, and extensive caries on tooth 26 (maxillary left first molar). Tooth 26 is exquisitely tender to percussion and demonstrates Grade 1 mobility. A periapical radiograph shows a large periapical radiolucency associated with tooth 26 and mucosal clouding of the adjacent maxillary sinus floor. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Prescribe broad-spectrum oral antibiotics and analgesics alone, with re-evaluation in 3 to 5 days
Initiate root canal debridement on tooth 26 and prescribe systemic oral antibiotics
Refer immediately to an otolaryngologist for primary maxillary sinusitis management
Perform immediate surgical extraction of tooth 26 under local anesthesia
prosthodontics-260614220.explanation: Option B is correct because Canadian dental standards mandate immediate source control via pulpal debridement combined with adjunctive systemic antibiotics for spreading odontogenic infections with fascial space involvement to prevent serious sequelae like cavernous sinus thrombosis. Prescribing antibiotics alone without mechanical intervention (Option A) is clinically hazardous and contraindicated as it delays essential infection elimination. Referral to an otolaryngologist (Option C) overlooks the evident odontogenic source, while immediate extraction (Option D) is unnecessarily aggressive when tooth 26 can be preserved through endodontic therapy.

prosthodontics-231876806.question: A 7-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic following a traumatic fall while playing. Clinical examination reveals that tooth 51 (primary maxillary right central incisor) is intruded (displaced apically into the alveolar bone), appearing distinctly shorter than the adjacent incisors. Radiographic examination indicates that the root apex is displaced labially, away from the developing permanent tooth germ, with no alveolar bone fracture or mobility. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Immediately reposition tooth 51 using extraction forceps and stabilize with a rigid splint
Perform immediate extraction of tooth 51 to safeguard the succedaneous tooth
Initiate immediate endodontic pulpectomy on tooth 51 to prevent inflammatory root resorption
Monitor the tooth clinically and radiographically for spontaneous re-eruption
prosthodontics-231876806.explanation: Option D is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) and Canadian pediatric dental guidelines, an intruded primary incisor whose apex is directed labially away from the permanent successor should be monitored conservatively for spontaneous re-eruption, which typically occurs within 2 to 6 months. Forceps repositioning (Option A) or immediate extraction (Option B) inflicts unnecessary iatrogenic trauma to the underlying permanent tooth germ. Immediate pulpectomy (Option C) is contraindicated unless clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpal necrosis or periapical pathosis develops during subsequent follow-up.

prosthodontics-210679547.question: A 50-year-old male patient who is a chronic cigarette smoker presents for a routine dental examination. Intraoral examination reveals an asymptomatic, solitary, flat white plaque on the left buccal mucosa that does not rub off with sterile gauze. The patient's medical history is non-contributory except for well-controlled hypertension. What is the MOST appropriate initial step in the management of this lesion?
options: Perform an immediate incisional biopsy of the buccal mucosal lesion
Prescribe a 14-day course of topical nystatin oral suspension
Provide smoking cessation counseling and re-evaluate the lesion in 2 to 3 weeks
Prescribe a 7-day course of systemic amoxicillin
prosthodontics-210679547.explanation: Option C is correct because Canadian oral medicine standards dictate that an unexplained solitary white keratotic lesion in a smoker must first be managed by eliminating the suspected local irritant followed by clinical re-evaluation in 2 to 3 weeks. An incisional biopsy (Option A) is prematurely invasive and indicated only if the lesion persists after the observation period. Topical nystatin (Option B) is ineffective because non-wipeable keratotic lesions are not candidal, and systemic antibiotics (Option D) have no therapeutic role in treating mucosal hyperkeratosis.

prosthodontics-938843726.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with persistent pain, localized swelling, and mild trismus associated with partially erupted tooth 18 (maxillary right third molar). Clinical examination confirms acute pericoronitis with regional lymphadenopathy. The patient's medical history includes a penicillin allergy that manifested strictly as a mild maculopapular rash during childhood, with no history of anaphylaxis, urticaria, or angioedema. If adjunctive systemic antibiotic therapy is indicated alongside local debridement, which of the following is the MOST appropriate antibiotic?
options: Amoxicillin
Metronidazole alone
Clindamycin
Cephalexin
prosthodontics-938843726.explanation: Option D is correct because Canadian dental guidelines and Health Canada endorse first-generation cephalosporins such as cephalexin for patients with a mild, non-IgE-mediated (rash-only) penicillin allergy due to cross-reactivity rates below 1%. Amoxicillin (Option A) is contraindicated given the documented penicillin allergy, while metronidazole alone (Option B) is ineffective because it lacks activity against aerobic oral streptococci. Clindamycin (Option C) is strictly contraindicated due to Health Canada warnings regarding its disproportionate risk of severe Clostridioides difficile-associated colitis.

prosthodontics-882589986.question: A 30-year-old male patient presents with a history of difficulty achieving profound pulpal anesthesia on tooth 36 (mandibular left first molar) during previous dental procedures. Despite successful subjective signs of an inferior alveolar nerve block (lip and anterior tongue numbness), he experiences sharp pain during dentinal instrumentation of the mesial pulp horn of tooth 36. Which of the following anatomical variations is the MOST likely cause of this anesthetic failure?
options: Accessory innervation from the long buccal nerve
Presence of a bifid mandibular canal
Higher than average position of the mandibular foramen
Accessory sensory innervation from the mylohyoid nerve
prosthodontics-882589986.explanation: Option D is correct because according to Malamed's local anesthesia principles, accessory sensory innervation from the mylohyoid nerve entering lingual mandibular foramina is the primary anatomical cause of localized pulpal anesthesia failure when soft tissue signs of an inferior alveolar block are fully present. The long buccal nerve (Option A) supplies only the buccal gingiva and periosteum of mandibular molars rather than pulpal tissues. A bifid mandibular canal (Option B) or an abnormally high mandibular foramen (Option C) would cause complete block failure with absent or incomplete lip and tongue anesthesia.

prosthodontics-291526328.question: A 58-year-old male patient presents for a comprehensive dental examination. Periapical radiography reveals a well-obturated root canal system and a distinct periapical radiolucency associated with the mesiobuccal root apex of tooth 17 (maxillary right second molar), which underwent endodontic therapy 5 years ago. Clinical examination reveals that tooth 17 is completely asymptomatic, responding normally to palpation and showing no tenderness to percussion. There is no swelling, mobility, or sinus tract present. According to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic terminology, what is the MOST appropriate apical diagnosis for tooth 17?
options: Acute apical abscess
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
Chronic apical abscess
prosthodontics-291526328.explanation: Option C is correct because according to AAE diagnostic consensus, asymptomatic apical periodontitis is defined by apical radiolucency representing bone destruction of pulpal origin without clinical symptoms such as pain to percussion or palpation. Symptomatic apical periodontitis (Option B) and acute apical abscess (Option A) both require acute clinical symptoms including pain to percussion, biting, or palpation. Chronic apical abscess (Option D) is characterized by the pathognomonic presence of an active draining sinus tract or stoma.

prosthodontics-47603626.question: A 30-year-old female patient presents for the surgical extraction of non-restorable tooth 48 (mandibular right third molar). Her medical history is unremarkable except for the daily use of a combined oral contraceptive pill. Which of the following statements regarding her medication and post-operative risks is MOST accurate according to Canadian clinical guidelines?
options: Oral contraceptives increase the risk of alveolar osteitis due to estrogen-induced elevation of plasma fibrinolytic activity
Oral contraceptives must be discontinued 24 hours prior to surgery to minimize the risk of post-operative thromboembolism
Adjunctive amoxicillin must be prescribed post-operatively alongside backup barrier contraception
Oral contraceptives significantly impair platelet aggregation, leading to an increased risk of secondary hemorrhage
prosthodontics-47603626.explanation: Option A is correct because exogenous estrogens in oral contraceptives elevate plasma fibrinolytic activity, promoting early lysis of the extraction socket blood clot and significantly increasing the incidence of alveolar osteitis (dry socket). Discontinuing oral contraceptives (Option B) is contraindicated due to the risk of unintended pregnancy and does not immediately normalize fibrinolytic balance. Canadian clinical guidelines confirm that routine non-rifamycin dental antibiotics do not compromise oral contraceptive efficacy (Option C), and oral contraceptives do not impair platelet aggregation or promote systemic bleeding (Option D).

prosthodontics-18734731.question: A 9-year-old male patient presents to the dental clinic one hour after sustaining a sports injury to his anterior maxilla. Clinical examination reveals that permanent tooth 11 is displaced palatally and extruded by 3 mm, but remains responsive to cold pulp testing. Permanent tooth 21 exhibits an uncomplicated crown fracture confined to enamel and dentin without pulpal exposure. Radiographic evaluation shows that tooth 11 has an intact root with an immature, open apex and no alveolar fracture. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for tooth 11?
options: Avulse and immediately replant tooth 11 fully into the socket
Gently reposition tooth 11 with digital pressure and stabilize with a flexible splint
Initiate immediate pulpectomy and root canal treatment on tooth 11
Extract tooth 11 to prevent replacement resorption and ankylosis
prosthodontics-18734731.explanation: Option B is correct because according to International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines, an extruded or laterally luxated permanent incisor should be gently repositioned with digital pressure into its anatomical socket and stabilized with a flexible splint for 2 weeks. Intentional avulsion and replantation (Option A) causes severe iatrogenic damage to the periodontal ligament and is restricted to exarticulated teeth. Immediate pulpectomy (Option C) is contraindicated because immature permanent teeth with open apices possess strong potential for pulpal revascularization, and extraction (Option D) is needlessly destructive for a restorable tooth.

prosthodontics-184121119.question: On an intraoral periapical radiograph of the maxillary canine-premolar region, a distinct radiopaque landmark resembling an inverted 'Y' is visualized. Which two anatomical structures intersect to create this classic radiographic appearance?
options: The floor of the maxillary sinus and the inferior border of the zygomatic process
The lateral wall of the nasal cavity and the medial cortical plate of the incisive canal
The floor of the nasal fossa and the anterior-inferior border of the maxillary sinus
The inferior border of the piriform aperture and the cortical outline of the canine fossa
prosthodontics-184121119.explanation: Option C is correct because the 'inverted Y' of Ennis is an intraoral periapical radiographic landmark formed by the superimposition of the radiopaque cortical line of the nasal fossa floor and the anterior-inferior cortical wall of the maxillary sinus. The zygomatic process (Option A) forms a U-shaped radiopacity superior to the roots of the maxillary molars. The incisive canal (Option B) is an anterior midline landmark seen on central incisor projections, while the piriform aperture and canine fossa (Option D) do not produce an inverted Y intersection.

prosthodontics-552628237.question: A 55-year-old male patient diagnosed with Parkinson disease 5 years ago presents for periodontal maintenance. He takes levodopa/carbidopa and an antihypertensive medication. Clinical examination reveals resting hand tremors, muscle rigidity, xerostomia, generalized moderate periodontitis, and heavy plaque accumulation resulting from impaired manual dexterity. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate oral hygiene recommendation for this patient?
options: Recommend daily interdental cleaning using traditional un-waxed string floss
Advise using an oscillating-rotating powered toothbrush and involving a caregiver for oral hygiene assistance
Prescribe a 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate rinse as a sole replacement for mechanical toothbrushing
Instruct the patient to brush three times daily using a stiff-bristled manual toothbrush
prosthodontics-552628237.explanation: Option B is correct because clinical guidelines for patients with Parkinson disease and motor tremors recommend powered toothbrushes with ergonomic handles to compensate for diminished dexterity, alongside caregiver support to ensure thorough plaque removal. Traditional string floss (Option A) requires complex two-handed fine motor coordination that is unfeasible for a patient with tremors and rigidity. Chlorhexidine mouthwash (Option C) cannot substitute for mechanical biofilm disruption and causes taste alteration, while stiff-bristled manual brushes (Option D) fail to overcome motor deficits and cause severe cervical abrasion.

prosthodontics-699705515.question: A 38-year-old female patient presents with severe, spontaneous, throbbing pain in tooth 36 (mandibular left first molar) that has progressively worsened over the last 24 hours. The pain is intensely exacerbated by thermal stimuli and lingers for several minutes after removal of the cold stimulus. Clinical examination reveals deep occlusal caries and tenderness to percussion on tooth 36. Periapical radiography shows deep caries approximating the pulp horn with a normal periodontal ligament space and no periapical radiolucency. According to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) diagnostic terminology, what is the MOST likely pulpal diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis
Symptomatic apical periodontitis
prosthodontics-699705515.explanation: Option A is correct because severe spontaneous pain accompanied by heightened, lingering responses to thermal stimuli is the hallmark definition of symptomatic irreversible pulpitis under AAE diagnostic criteria. Reversible pulpitis (Option B) produces sharp, transient discomfort that subsides immediately upon removal of the thermal stimulus without lingering. Pulp necrosis (Option C) results in non-responsive, non-vital pulpal tissue with absent response to thermal testing, while symptomatic apical periodontitis (Option D) is an apical classification denoting inflammation of the periodontal ligament rather than a pulpal diagnosis.

prosthodontics-630001943.question: A 55-year-old male patient presents for the extraction of non-restorable tooth 16 (maxillary right first molar) due to extensive crown-root caries. His medical history includes well-controlled chronic sinusitis. A periapical radiograph reveals pneumatization of the maxillary sinus with the sinus floor extending between the divergent roots and closely approximating the root apices of tooth 16. What is the MOST significant potential intraoperative complication to anticipate during the extraction of tooth 16?
options: Oroantral communication
Fracture of the maxillary tuberosity
Inferior alveolar nerve paresthesia
Inadvertent displacement of the tooth into the infratemporal fossa
prosthodontics-630001943.explanation: Option A is correct because the anatomical proximity of the divergent roots of tooth 16 to a pneumatized maxillary sinus creates a high risk of sinus floor perforation and subsequent oroantral communication during extraction. Fracture of the maxillary tuberosity (Option B) characteristically occurs during the extraction of an isolated or ankylosed maxillary second or third molar rather than a first molar. Inferior alveolar nerve paresthesia (Option C) is a complication specific to the mandible, not the maxilla, and displacement into the infratemporal fossa (Option D) is a rare risk associated almost exclusively with impacted maxillary third molars.

general-medicine-895390589.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the mesiobuccal root of the permanent maxillary first molar (tooth 16 or tooth 26)?
options: Posterior superior alveolar nerve
Anterior superior alveolar nerve
Nasopalatine nerve
Middle superior alveolar nerve
general-medicine-895390589.explanation: Option D is correct because the middle superior alveolar (MSA) nerve innervates the maxillary premolars and the mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar (tooth 16 or tooth 26). The posterior superior alveolar (PSA) nerve (Option A) innervates the distobuccal and palatal roots of the maxillary first molar, as well as the entire second and third molars. The anterior superior alveolar (ASA) nerve (Option B) innervates the maxillary incisors and canines, while the nasopalatine nerve (Option C) provides sensory supply to the palatal mucosa of the anterior maxilla.

general-medicine-232191122.question: A 25-year-old female patient in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with acute, severe pain from tooth 16 diagnosed with symptomatic irreversible pulpitis. Her medical history is otherwise non-contributory. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Prescribe amoxicillin and acetaminophen, deferring operative dental treatment until after delivery.
Perform an immediate extraction of tooth 16 under nitrous oxide sedation to minimize maternal distress.
Initiate endodontic therapy (pulpectomy) using 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine for local anesthesia.
Administer 4% prilocaine without epinephrine to initiate a pulpectomy, strictly avoiding vasoconstrictors.
general-medicine-232191122.explanation: Option C is correct because acute irreversible pulpitis requires immediate operative intervention (pulpectomy) to eliminate pain and infection regardless of the trimester; 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine is safe, standard, and recommended under Canadian guidelines during pregnancy. Deferring treatment and prescribing antibiotics (Option A) is contraindicated because antibiotics are ineffective for irreversible pulpitis and prolong maternal pain. Nitrous oxide sedation and extraction (Option B) are inappropriate for a restorable tooth, and avoiding epinephrine (Option D) increases the risk of inadequate analgesia, leading to high maternal endogenous catecholamine release.

general-medicine-448830295.question: A 55-year-old male patient with a history of stable angina controlled by sublingual nitroglycerin experiences retrosternal chest pain and shortness of breath during a crown preparation on tooth 46. His blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg and heart rate is 90 bpm. What is the MOST immediate clinical action to take?
options: Terminate the procedure, administer supplemental oxygen, and assist the patient in administering sublingual nitroglycerin.
Activate emergency medical services (911) immediately and prepare the automated external defibrillator.
Administer 325 mg chewable aspirin and place the patient in a supine position.
Initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) immediately.
general-medicine-448830295.explanation: Option A is correct because in a conscious patient with known stable angina presenting with acute chest pain and stable hemodynamics (BP 140/90 mmHg), the immediate office protocol is terminating the procedure, administering supplemental oxygen, and assisting with sublingual nitroglycerin. Calling 911 immediately (Option B) is premature before evaluating the response to initial nitroglycerin in known stable angina, although EMS must be activated if pain persists beyond 5 minutes or after three doses. Aspirin (Option C) is indicated if myocardial infarction is suspected or pain is unresolved by nitroglycerin, and CPR (Option D) is indicated only for unresponsive, pulseless cardiac arrest.

general-medicine-329988089.question: A 55-year-old male patient presents for a comprehensive periodontal examination. His medical history is significant for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus with an HbA1c of 8.4%. Clinical examination reveals generalized probing depths of 6–8 mm, clinical attachment loss of >= 5 mm, Class II furcation involvement on tooth 16 and tooth 46, and radiographic bone loss extending to the middle third of the root affecting 45% of teeth. What is the MOST appropriate periodontal diagnosis according to the 2017 AAP/EFP classification?
options: Generalized Periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C
Generalized Periodontitis, Stage II, Grade B
Localized Periodontitis, Stage III, Grade C
Generalized Periodontitis, Stage IV, Grade A
general-medicine-329988089.explanation: Option A is correct because under the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, clinical attachment loss >= 5 mm, probing depths >= 6 mm, furcation involvement, and bone loss extending to the middle third of the root define Stage III; involvement of > 30% of teeth defines generalized extent, and an HbA1c >= 7.0% serves as a grade modifier establishing Grade C. Stage II (Option B) is incorrect because it is restricted to coronal-third bone loss and attachment loss of 3–4 mm. Localized extent (Option C) requires < 30% of teeth to be affected, and Stage IV, Grade A (Option D) incorrectly categorizes extent, severity, and diabetic progression.

general-medicine-78755939.question: A 70-year-old male patient requires a single simple extraction of tooth 36. He is currently taking rivaroxaban daily for a history of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism that occurred 8 months ago. What is the MOST appropriate management regarding his anticoagulant medication prior to this procedure?
options: Advise the patient to stop rivaroxaban 48 hours prior to the procedure and resume 24 hours later.
Perform the extraction without interrupting rivaroxaban therapy, employing local hemostatic measures.
Bridge the patient with subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin for 5 days prior to surgery.
Withhold the morning dose of rivaroxaban and require an immediate INR test before extraction.
general-medicine-78755939.explanation: Option B is correct because Canadian dental and surgical guidelines recommend that minor oral surgical procedures (such as a single simple extraction of tooth 36) proceed without interrupting direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs like rivaroxaban), controlling bleeding with local hemostatic agents (e.g., gelatin sponge, sutures). Discontinuing rivaroxaban (Option A) unnecessarily elevates the risk of life-threatening thromboembolism, which far exceeds the risk of minor, manageable dental bleeding. Heparin bridging (Option C) is contraindicated for DOACs, and rivaroxaban does not require routine INR monitoring (Option D).

general-medicine-881797299.question: A 35-year-old male patient with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presents for emergency treatment of tooth 46. During the appointment, he becomes confused, diaphoretic, and tremulous, but remains conscious and capable of swallowing. A glucometer is not immediately available. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Administer subcutaneous regular insulin and immediately activate emergency medical services.
Administer 15 to 20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrates (glucose) and monitor vital signs.
Recline the patient in a supine position and withhold all fluids and sugars.
Administer sublingual nitroglycerin and monitor the patient for recovery.
general-medicine-881797299.explanation: Option B is correct because in an outpatient dental emergency involving an altered conscious diabetic patient where blood glucose cannot be immediately confirmed, fast-acting oral glucose must be administered immediately according to Canadian emergency protocols (Malamed). Additional glucose will not cause acute harm in hyperglycemia, whereas untreated hypoglycemia rapidly causes irreversible neuroglycopenia and death. Administering insulin (Option A) in the dental office is strictly contraindicated due to the risk of fatal hypoglycemia and hypokalemia. Withholding carbohydrates (Option C) is hazardous in suspected hypoglycemia, and nitroglycerin (Option D) is indicated for angina, not diabetic emergencies.

general-medicine-808094588.question: A 50-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of severe pain when chewing on tooth 36. Clinical examination reveals a large, previously restored tooth 36 with no visible recurrent caries. The tooth responds normally to cold testing, but percussion elicits mild discomfort. A bite test with a Tooth Slooth elicits exquisite sharp pain specifically when releasing pressure from the distolingual cusp. Radiographs reveal no periapical radiolucency. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Acute apical abscess
Cracked tooth syndrome
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Periodontal abscess
general-medicine-808094588.explanation: Option B is correct because sharp pain elicited upon release of biting pressure on an individual cusp (positive bite test) in a restored tooth with a vital pulp and no periapical lesion is classic for cracked tooth syndrome affecting tooth 36. Acute apical abscess (Option A) involves a non-vital pulp, continuous throbbing pain, and periapical pathology. Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (Option C) is characterized by lingering pain to thermal stimuli rather than sharp, isolated bite-release pain, and periodontal abscess (Option D) presents with a localized swelling and deep periodontal pocketing.

general-medicine-349757276.question: A 35-year-old female patient presents to your dental clinic with a chief complaint of an acute, painful crusted ulcer on her lower lip that developed two days after intense sun exposure. Clinical examination reveals a cluster of vesicular and shallow ulcerative lesions with a golden-yellow crust localized to the vermilion border of the lower lip. Her medical history is non-contributory. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
options: Recurrent herpes labialis
Squamous cell carcinoma
Major aphthous ulcer
Traumatic ulcer
general-medicine-349757276.explanation: Option A is correct because an acute eruption of clustered vesicles that rupture into crusted, painful lesions on the vermilion border of the lip following ultraviolet exposure in a young adult is pathognomonic for recurrent herpes labialis (HSV-1). Squamous cell carcinoma (Option B) presents as a chronic, indurated, slow-growing, painless ulcer or exophytic lesion, typically in older patients with long-term actinic damage. Aphthous ulcers (Option C) develop almost exclusively on non-keratinized movable intraoral mucosa rather than the keratinized vermilion border, and traumatic ulcers (Option D) are non-vesicular lesions directly linked to mechanical trauma.

ethics-20.question: A dentist delegates the taking of final impressions for orthodontic clear aligners and the intra-oral adjustment of these appliances to an uncertified dental assistant who has received only informal on-the-job training. Provincial regulatory standards (such as RCDSO guidelines) explicitly restrict these controlled intra-oral procedures to licensed dentists or qualified dental hygienists. This delegation primarily violates which ethical duty?
options: Duty to maintain patient confidentiality and privacy of dental records.
Duty to respect professional boundaries between health care professionals.
Duty to promote patient autonomy in choosing treatment modalities.
Duty to ensure non-maleficence by protecting patients from substandard care and potential harm.
ethics-20.explanation: Option D is correct because non-maleficence mandates that clinicians do no harm; delegating restricted, irreversible intra-oral procedures to unqualified staff exposes patients to substandard care and risk of injury, violating provincial regulatory standards. Confidentiality (Option A) governs the protection of private personal health information. Professional boundaries (Option B) govern the therapeutic relationship and prevent exploitation (e.g., dual relationships) between clinician and patient rather than delegation scopes of practice, and autonomy (Option C) concerns the patient's right to self-determination and informed consent.

ethics-8.question: A patient provides informed consent specifically for the surgical extraction of tooth 37. During the procedure, the dentist discovers that adjacent tooth 38 is partially impacted and, believing it may cause pericoronitis in the future, proceeds to extract tooth 38 as well without discussing it or obtaining consent from the patient. Which essential element of informed consent was MOST directly violated regarding the extraction of tooth 38?
options: Adequacy of disclosure of information
Voluntariness of the decision-making process
Assessment of patient decision-making capacity
Evaluation of patient comprehension
ethics-8.explanation: Option A is correct because Canadian informed consent law requires adequate disclosure of the nature, risks, benefits, and alternatives of any proposed intervention before it is performed; extracting tooth 38 without prior discussion represents a complete failure of disclosure. Voluntariness (Option B) requires that consent be given freely without coercion or manipulation, which was not the operative issue because no consent was ever requested or given for tooth 38. Patient capacity (Option C) and comprehension (Option D) evaluate the patient's ability to understand disclosed information, which cannot occur when disclosure is absent.

ethics-59.question: During an informed consent discussion for the surgical removal of tooth 48, a dentist discloses all common and significant risks but decides not to mention a very remote, minor complication (less than 0.01% probability with no permanent sequelae). Under Canadian dental ethics and jurisprudence (Reibl v. Hughes), is this disclosure approach legally and ethically justifiable?
options: Yes, because Canadian informed consent doctrine requires the disclosure of material risks that a reasonable person in the patient's position would consider significant.
No, because Canadian regulatory standards require the disclosure of every possible complication, regardless of rarity or severity.
Yes, because the dentist's therapeutic privilege allows unilateral withholding of risks to prevent patient apprehension.
No, unless the patient has explicitly signed a legal waiver releasing the clinician from disclosure obligations.
ethics-59.explanation: Option A is correct because under Canadian law established by the Supreme Court in Reibl v. Hughes, informed consent requires disclosing all 'material risks'—defined as common risks or serious, rare risks that a reasonable person in the patient's position would deem significant in making their decision. Canadian law does not require clinicians to list every infinitesimal or non-material risk (Option B). Therapeutic privilege (Option C) is narrowly restricted to grave psychiatric emergencies and does not permit paternalistic withholding of surgical risks, and patients cannot simply execute blank waivers of their right to informed consent (Option D).

ethics-66.question: During endodontic therapy on a 40-year-old patient's permanent mandibular first molar (tooth 46), an endodontic file separates in the apical third of the mesial root. The fragment cannot be safely retrieved. The patient is currently unaware of the occurrence. What is the dentist's MOST ethical and professional course of action?
options: Attempt aggressive ultrasonic retrieval at a subsequent visit before disclosing the event to the patient.
Promptly inform the patient of the separated file, explain the clinical implications, management options, and prognosis, and document the disclosure in the patient's chart.
Complete obturation coronal to the fragment and monitor the tooth radiographically without informing the patient to prevent undue anxiety.
Refer the patient to an endodontist without prior discussion, delegating the disclosure decision to the specialist.
ethics-66.explanation: Option B is correct because Canadian dental regulatory authorities (such as the RCDSO) and codes of ethics mandate prompt disclosure of clinical incidents under the principles of veracity and patient autonomy, including discussing options, prognosis, and thoroughly documenting the discussion. Concealing the separated instrument (Option C) violates truthfulness and breaches informed consent. Attempting hazardous retrieval without consent (Option A) risks root perforation, and referring without disclosure (Option D) inappropriately abdicates the treating dentist's primary professional and ethical responsibility.

general-medicine-294.question: A 65-year-old male patient presents with acute odontogenic pain requiring an urgent extraction of tooth 46. His medical history includes hypertension controlled with an ACE inhibitor and a myocardial infarction 3 months ago. He also takes clopidogrel daily. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Consult the patient's cardiologist to assess cardiovascular stability and determine the appropriate procedural setting.
Discontinue clopidogrel for 5 to 7 days prior to performing the extraction in the dental office.
Prescribe oral antibiotics and analgesics, deferring the extraction until at least 6 months post-myocardial infarction.
Proceed immediately with the extraction in the dental office without consultation, as single antiplatelet therapy requires no alteration.
general-medicine-294.explanation: Option A is correct because a myocardial infarction 3 months ago carries an intermediate-to-high risk of perioperative cardiac complications, requiring urgent consultation with the cardiologist to assess cardiac stability and evaluate whether surgery should occur in a hospital-based or monitored setting. Clopidogrel must not be stopped empirically due to the high risk of stent thrombosis and recurrent myocardial infarction (Option B), urgent surgical care cannot be delayed for months with antibiotics alone because untreated infection worsens cardiac stress (Option C), and proceeding unmonitored without risk stratification is unsafe (Option D).

general-medicine-272.question: A 55-year-old male patient presents for an elective extraction of non-restorable tooth 37. His medical history is significant for an acute myocardial infarction that occurred 3 weeks ago, and he is currently stable on cardiac medications. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate clinical management?
options: Defer the elective extraction and consult the cardiologist, as elective dental surgery is contraindicated within 30 days of an acute myocardial infarction.
Proceed with the extraction using 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine, limiting the dose to a maximum of two cartridges.
Proceed with the extraction using 3% mepivacaine plain, as local anesthetics without vasoconstrictors eliminate cardiac risk.
Administer 300 mg of aspirin chairside and proceed with the extraction in the outpatient dental clinic.
general-medicine-272.explanation: Option A is correct because elective dental surgical procedures are strictly contraindicated within 30 days of an acute myocardial infarction due to the exceptionally high risk of recurrent infarction, fatal arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest during this unstable recovery period. Proceeding with elective surgery regardless of vasoconstrictor dose reduction or omission (Options B and C) fails to mitigate this major systemic cardiac risk. Administering aspirin chairside before elective surgery (Option D) does not lower the acute perioperative cardiac event risk.

general-medicine-276.question: A 55-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes presents with acute severe pain and localized swelling associated with tooth 46 requiring urgent extraction. The patient reports a recent HbA1c of 9.5% along with polydipsia and polyuria. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Measure chairside capillary blood glucose to evaluate for acute metabolic decompensation and proceed with the urgent extraction to eliminate the source of infection.
Defer all surgical intervention and refer the patient to their physician for chronic HbA1c optimization below 7.0%.
Prescribe a 10-day course of broad-spectrum antibiotics and dismiss the patient without surgical intervention.
Administer 10 units of subcutaneous regular insulin chairside prior to performing the extraction.
general-medicine-276.explanation: Option A is correct because active odontogenic infection directly exacerbates insulin resistance and glycemic decompensation; therefore, acute surgical intervention must not be deferred once acute metabolic crisis (such as diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state) is ruled out via chairside blood glucose assessment. Deferring urgent care for chronic HbA1c optimization (Option B) allows severe infection to spread and worsens glycemic control. Antibiotics alone without source control are ineffective (Option C), and dentists must not empirically administer insulin chairside due to the risk of inducing fatal hypoglycemia (Option D).

general-medicine-282.question: A patient with end-stage renal disease receiving hemodialysis on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday requires an elective extraction of non-restorable tooth 26. Which of the following represents the MOST appropriate time to schedule the extraction?
options: The day following a hemodialysis session (e.g., Tuesday).
The same day, immediately prior to the start of a hemodialysis session.
The same day, immediately following the completion of a hemodialysis session.
Two days following a hemodialysis session, immediately prior to the next scheduled treatment.
general-medicine-282.explanation: Option A is correct because scheduling invasive dental procedures the day after hemodialysis provides optimal metabolic stability, fluid balance, and allows adequate time for systemic heparin to be completely cleared (heparin half-life is 1-2 hours), thereby minimizing bleeding risk. Scheduling immediately before dialysis on the same day (Option B) exposes the patient to peak metabolic waste accumulation and anticoagulation during subsequent hemodialysis. Scheduling immediately after dialysis (Option C) carries a high risk of hemorrhage from active circulating heparin, and waiting two days until immediately before the next session (Option D) risks hyperkalemia, fluid overload, and uremic platelet dysfunction.

general-medicine-367.question: A 45-year-old patient with a prosthetic aortic valve and a documented history of an IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction to penicillin requires an extraction of tooth 47. According to current Canadian Dental Association (CDA) and American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines, which of the following is the MOST appropriate oral antibiotic regimen for infective endocarditis prophylaxis?
options: Azithromycin 500 mg orally 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
Clindamycin 600 mg orally 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
Cephalexin 2 g orally 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure
general-medicine-367.explanation: Option A is correct because oral azithromycin (500 mg) is the recommended first-line alternative for infective endocarditis prophylaxis in patients with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria to penicillins. Clindamycin (Option B) was officially discontinued and is strictly contraindicated under current CDA and AHA guidelines due to high risks of severe, potentially fatal Clostridioides difficile colitis. Cephalexin (Option C) is contraindicated due to potential cross-reactivity in patients with IgE-mediated penicillin anaphylaxis, and amoxicillin (Option D) is an aminopenicillin that would trigger a severe allergic reaction.
